title: 10  Membership inference
text:
10.1 Why this matters
A hospital publishes a model that predicts a disease, and you hold a patient’s record. Was that record in the training set? If it was, the patient was treated there for that disease. This is membership inference, the standard measure of leakage, because a model that cannot hide whether a record was used hides little else. Membership is a test about one record, so the attack to use in an audit compares each record with itself.

title: 10  Membership inference
section: 10.2 Membership as a test about one record
text:
10.2 Membership as a test about one record
In the game of Threat models and privacy games, the attacker gets a training member or a fresh record and says “member” or “not”. It is scored by its true positive rate (TPR), the share of members it flags, and its false positive rate (FPR), the share of non-members it flags.
Fix a target record, written \(z\), and look at the model’s output on it, such as its loss. Retrain on fresh random draws of the data, and that output has one distribution over the runs that include \(z\) and another over the runs without it. Call them the IN and OUT distributions of \(z\). The best test of membership compares their likelihoods at the observed output (the Neyman–Pearson lemma), so it does well only where the two lie far apart. A typical record’s distributions almost overlap, because the rest of the data already predict it. An outlier’s lie far apart, because the model gets it right only if it trained on it. So the records an attack finds at a low FPR are mostly outliers.
The numbers in this chapter come from practitioner_lira.py. It trains 64 logistic-regression classifiers, each on a random half of scikit-learn’s 1,797 images of handwritten digits. Each model takes a turn as the target, while the other 63 serve as the attacker’s shadow models, copies trained the same way whose training images the attacker knows.

title: 10  Membership inference
section: 10.3 The quick check: the generalization gap
text:
10.3 The quick check: the generalization gap
Before any attack, compare the training and test errors. A model fits its training data, so it gets members right more often than fresh records, and Yeom et al. (2018) turned that into the attack “member if correctly classified”. When members and non-members come from the same population, its advantage, the TPR minus the FPR, equals the gap between the two errors: \[\mathrm{Adv} = \text{test error} - \text{training error}. \tag{10.1}\] On the digits, averaged over the 64 models, the gap is 0.0422.
So a large gap shows a leak at no cost. But a small gap does not mean a private model, because the gap averages over records and hides who is exposed. The loss attack, which flags every record whose loss falls below one threshold, shows this. At an FPR of \(10^{-3}\) it reaches a TPR of 0.0009 on the digits, no better than a coin that says “member” one time in a thousand.
The classic attack of Shokri et al. (2017) also applies one rule to all records, learned from shadow models. The script runs it from the Adversarial Robustness Toolbox (ART), a Python library of attacks, with four shadow models.
# ART copies the target's recipe and trains each shadow on a random half of the images.
shadows = ShadowModels(models.first, num_shadow_models=N_ART_SHADOWS, random_state=seed)
(x_in, y_in, pred_in), (x_out, y_out, pred_out) = shadows.generate_shadow_dataset(x, onehot)
# One attack model learns "member" from a shadow's probabilities and the true label.
attack = MembershipInferenceBlackBox(models.first, attack_model_type="rf")
attack.fit(x_in, y_in, x_out, y_out, pred=pred_in, test_pred=pred_out)
# The same attack model scores every target's probabilities on every image.
scores = [attack.infer(x, onehot, pred=p, probabilities=True)[:, 0] for p in models.probs]
Its one rule fails at a low FPR too, finding only 0.0014 of the members at an FPR of \(10^{-3}\).

title: 10  Membership inference
section: 10.4 LiRA: a likelihood-ratio test per record
text:
10.4 LiRA: a likelihood-ratio test per record
The likelihood ratio attack (LiRA) of Carlini et al. (2022) uses the shadow models to estimate each record’s own IN and OUT distributions instead. Its statistic is the logit of the model’s confidence \(p_y\) in the true label \(y\), \[\phi = \ln\frac{p_y}{1 - p_y}. \tag{10.2}\] The logit is close to normal over retrainings, while the confidence itself piles up against 1.
For each record, the attacker fits a normal distribution to the record’s logit over the shadow models that trained on it. Its mean is written \(\mu_{\mathrm{in}}\) and its standard deviation \(\sigma_{\mathrm{in}}\). A second fit, over the shadow models that did not, has mean \(\mu_{\mathrm{out}}\) and standard deviation \(\sigma_{\mathrm{out}}\).
Online LiRA scores the target model’s logit \(\phi_z\) on the record by how much more likely it is under the IN fit than under the OUT fit. Writing \(\mathcal N(\phi; \mu, \sigma^2)\) for the normal density, the score is \[\ln\Lambda_z = \ln\mathcal N\big(\phi_z;\, \mu_{\mathrm{in}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{in}}^2\big) - \ln\mathcal N\big(\phi_z;\, \mu_{\mathrm{out}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{out}}^2\big). \tag{10.3}\] Offline LiRA uses only OUT models, which need not contain the record being tested, so they can be trained once and reused for every new record. It asks how many OUT standard deviations the logit lies above its usual value, \[\frac{\phi_z - \mu_{\mathrm{out}}}{\sigma_{\mathrm{out}}}. \tag{10.4}\]
Each score already compares a record with its own fits, so one threshold serves for all records. In the script, ART’s SklearnClassifier wraps the scikit-learn recipe, trains every model and returns its probabilities.
# Each image is in each model's training set with probability 1/2.
member = rng.random((n_models, n)) < 0.5
for k in range(n_models):
    model = recipe()  # a fresh, untrained copy of the target's recipe
    model.fit(x[member[k]], onehot[member[k]])
    probs[k] = model.predict(x)  # the probabilities the attacker sees, for every image
    p = np.clip(probs[k, np.arange(n), y], 1e-15, 1 - 1e-15)  # confidence on the true label
    phi[k] = np.log(p) - np.log(1 - p)  # its logit, close to Gaussian over retrainings
    confidence[k] = p
The LiRA scores come from a helper, because no library installed with this book computes them. Its lira_scores, in practitioner_privacy_tests.py, fits the two normals per image and returns Equation 10.3 and Equation 10.4.
The command uv run python code/part02-attacks/practitioner_lira.py runs in seconds. It compares the attacks by their TPR at two low FPRs and by their area under the curve (AUC) of the TPR against the FPR.
  loss attack: AUC=0.518  TPR@0.001=0.0009  TPR@0.01=0.0105
  ART shadow-model attack: AUC=0.570  TPR@0.001=0.0014  TPR@0.01=0.0146
  LiRA offline: AUC=0.577  TPR@0.001=0.0087  TPR@0.01=0.0345
  LiRA online: AUC=0.623  TPR@0.001=0.0318  TPR@0.01=0.0790
  LiRA online, global variance: AUC=0.614  TPR@0.001=0.0250  TPR@0.01=0.0737
By AUC the attacks look close, and ART’s attack nearly matches offline LiRA. At an FPR of \(10^{-3}\) they are not, because online LiRA finds 0.0318 of the members and the loss attack only 0.0009. All of them see the same model outputs, so the whole gain comes from comparing each record’s output with that record’s own fits. Online LiRA beats offline LiRA because its IN fit also tells it how far training on a record moves that record’s logit.
Noisy fits are the main practical failure. Each record’s variance comes from only about half the shadow models. An underestimated one makes an ordinary output look like a far-tail event, a false positive at the strict thresholds that matter. With few shadow models, Carlini et al. therefore recommend one global variance shared by all records. It makes 16 shadows usable, while per-record variances need about 64.

title: 10  Membership inference
text:
10.5 Running LiRA on your model
The recipe is the same for any model. Train the target and its shadows each on a random half of the data pool, all with exactly the target’s recipe. A shadow trained differently, even with another augmentation, estimates the wrong IN and OUT distributions. Fit the IN and OUT normals to each record’s logits, let each model take a turn as the target, and score every pair of target model and record. Each shadow is a training run, so the shadow count is the budget decision. Pre-release privacy risk assessment runs the whole job on the digits.
For a confident model, the confidence \(p_y\) in the true label nears 1, so \(1 - p_y\) rounds to 0 and the logit becomes infinite. Compute it instead from the class scores \(f\) before the softmax, as \(f_y - \ln\sum_{y' \ne y}e^{f_{y'}}\), or from log_softmax. Clipping the probabilities is no substitute. On a nearly separable model most confidences hit the clip, so their fits have no spread and those pairs drop out, taking the most exposed records with them. Treat such dropped pairs as a failed audit. The script clips only because no digits model comes near the clip.
The most common mistake is to draw members and non-members from different distributions. If non-members come from a later period, another site or another preprocessing pipeline, the attack measures that shift rather than the model, so split one pool at random.
Two more facts matter in practice. Returning only labels does not stop the attack, because a label-only attack measures how much an input must change before its label flips (Choquette-Choo et al. 2021). And libraries differ: TensorFlow Privacy’s run_attacks and ART’s MembershipInferenceBlackBox treat all records alike, while ML Privacy Meter implements LiRA.
To catch a training change that makes a model leak, rerun a cheaper LiRA on every release candidate. Train 16 models with the candidate’s own recipe and score online LiRA with a global variance. On the digits, practitioner_lira.py --models 16 runs in seconds and blocks the model under the release rule of the next section, as the 64-model run does. Compare candidates by their intervals, not their point values, which differ by seed noise alone.

title: 10  Membership inference
text:
10.6 Reading the result
Report the TPR at an FPR of \(10^{-3}\) or lower, with the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve on log axes. Put Clopper–Pearson intervals on both rates, as in Part 1’s recipe for evaluating a detector at a low FPR. That recipe also sets the thresholds on a separate split, a step the script, like the literature, skips.
  LiRA offline: TP=502/57704  TPR=0.0087 [0.0080, 0.0095]  FP=56/57304  FPR=0.00098 [0.00074, 0.00127]  ln(TPR/FPR)=2.19  pass
  LiRA online: TP=1833/57704  TPR=0.0318 [0.0303, 0.0332]  FP=57/57304  FPR=0.00099 [0.00075, 0.00129]  ln(TPR/FPR)=3.46  block
The last word on each line applies the risk assessment’s blocking rule. It blocks a release when, at an FPR of \(10^{-3}\), the lower end of the TPR’s 95% interval is above ten times that FPR. Online LiRA’s lower end, 0.0303, is above 0.01, so it blocks this model, which offline LiRA alone would have passed. For online LiRA, the logarithm of the ratio of the rates is 3.46. It estimates how large the privacy level \(\varepsilon\) of differential privacy (Part 3) would have to be to allow this attack. It is not a certified lower bound, because the pairs share models and so are not independent trials. A certified bound needs independent ones, such as the canaries of Auditing.

title: 10  Membership inference
section: 10.7 Who is exposed, and what helps
text:
10.7 Who is exposed, and what helps
The records an attack scores highest are usually outliers, rare subgroups or mislabelled points, which the rest of the data do not predict. On the digits, the most exposed image is a 9 that the models classify with confidence 0.812 when they trained on it and 0.003 when they did not. Online LiRA flags it at an FPR of \(10^{-3}\) in all 33 target models that trained on it.
Removing the exposed records does not help, because the next layer then becomes exposed, which Carlini et al. (2022b) call the onion effect. Closing the generalization gap is not enough either, because the worst records, not the average, set the low-FPR end.
Differential privacy does help. Private training limits how far any one record can move the model, and so how far apart every record’s IN and OUT distributions can lie. Expect a trade-off, because when many subgroups are rare, memorizing them can be what makes a model accurate (Feldman 2020).

title: 10  Membership inference
text:
10.8 Cheat sheet



Table 10.1: Which attack or check to use.










Situation
Use
Notes




A first look, no attack budget
Test error \(-\) training error
A lower bound on the leak; a small gap proves nothing


A release decision
Online LiRA, Equation 10.3, 64 shadows
Report TPR at FPR \(10^{-3}\) with intervals


Few shadow models

16 shadows are usable this way






Rules of thumb

title: 10  Membership inference
text:
10.9 References

title: 11  Attribute inference and model inversion
text:
11.1 What it is
An attribute inference attack uses a trained model to recover one sensitive field of a person’s record, such as smoking status, from the fields the attacker already knows. An insurer who knows your age and diagnosis could query a hospital’s model that predicts the disease from age and smoking, and guess whether you smoke. But a published study on smoking would allow the same guess, so success alone is not a privacy failure. What matters is whether the model reveals more about you because your record was in its training data.
Yeom et al. (2018) turned this question into a game (Threat models and privacy games). A fair coin decides whether the target is a training record, a member, or a fresh draw from the same population. The attacker knows the target’s public features and label, queries the model and guesses the sensitive value. Its score is the attribute advantage, \[\mathrm{Adv}^{\mathrm{attr}} = \Pr[\text{guess right} \mid \text{member}] - \Pr[\text{guess right} \mid \text{non-member}]. \tag{11.1}\] A guess that rests only on the whole population, called population inference, helps members and non-members equally, because both come from that population. So it cancels in the difference, and what is left is the leak about individuals.
crumbs: 11  Attribute inference and model inversion

title: 11  Attribute inference and model inversion
text:
11.2 When you meet it
You meet it when someone claims that “the model reveals” a sensitive field, or asks whether dropping a column made a model safe. Success up to what the population allows is then a question for policy and fairness, because it would be there without the person’s record. Only success on members beyond non-members is a privacy leak.
crumbs: 11  Attribute inference and model inversion

title: 11  Attribute inference and model inversion
text:
11.3 How to use it
Start with the imputation baseline, the success of the best guess of the sensitive value from the public features and label alone, without the model. Many published attacks do no better (Jayaraman & Evans 2022), so it is the number to beat. Estimate it with a classifier that predicts the sensitive field from the public features and label, fitted on population records the model never saw.
Then run the attack. Model inversion (Fredrikson et al. 2014) scores each candidate value \(s\) of the sensitive field by two numbers. The first is the probability \(p(s \mid x)\) that a person with the target’s public features \(x\) has that value, estimated from population data. The second is \(f_y(x, s)\), the model’s confidence in the known label \(y\) when it is fed \(x\) and the candidate. The inversion attack guesses the value that maximizes their product, \[\hat s = \arg\max_s\; p(s \mid x)\, f_y(x, s). \tag{11.2}\] Give the attacker every column it could hold, because a near-copy of the sensitive field, such as a relationship column next to marital status, moves the baseline most. Run the attack on training members and on as many held-out non-members. Report the baseline and both success rates with confidence intervals, including one on the advantage, since Pre-release privacy risk assessment blocks a release when that interval lies above zero.
The script practitioner_attribute.py, run with uv run python code/part02-attacks/practitioner_attribute.py, applies the Adversarial Robustness Toolbox (ART) to Adult, census records of 45,222 people. A random forest predicts whether income exceeds $50K from every column, and sex is the sensitive field. The attacker holds 4,000 records of its own, and everyone’s other columns and income.
def label(rows: IntArray) -> Array:  # the label the model returns for each record, as a column
    return np.argmax(target.predict(x[rows]), axis=1).reshape(-1, 1).astype(np.float64)

np.random.seed(seed)  # ART builds its random forests unseeded, from NumPy's global generator
attack = AttributeInferenceBlackBox(target, attack_model_type="rf", attack_feature=SENSITIVE)
attack.fit(x[attacker])  # the attacker's own records, sensitive field included
baseline = AttributeInferenceBaselineTrueLabel(attack_model_type="rf", attack_feature=SENSITIVE)
baseline.fit(x[attacker], y[attacker])  # the same records and the true label, without the model
hits: dict[str, list[int]] = {}
for name, rows in (("members", members), ("non-members", others)):
    known = np.delete(x[rows], SENSITIVE, axis=1)  # everything but the sensitive field
    guess = attack.infer(known, pred=label(rows), values=[0.0, 1.0])
    imputed = baseline.infer(known, y=y[rows], values=[0.0, 1.0])
    hits[name] = [int(np.count_nonzero(np.equal(g.ravel(), female[rows]))) for g in (guess, imputed)]
ART black-box attack: right on members 0.8300 [0.8180, 0.8415]  on non-members 0.8423 [0.8306, 0.8534]
ART black-box attack: advantage -0.0123 [-0.0285, +0.0040]
imputation baseline: right on members 0.8307 [0.8188, 0.8423]  on non-members 0.8417 [0.8301, 0.8529]
The attack is right on 0.8300 of the members, and the baseline, which never queries the model, on 0.8307. So the success comes from the population, and the advantage’s interval contains zero, which passes the rule. On a synthetic population the full edition does find a small leak: inversion is right on 0.7832 of members and 0.7262 of non-members, an advantage of 0.0569.
crumbs: 11  Attribute inference and model inversion

title: 11  Attribute inference and model inversion
text:
11.4 What goes wrong
The commonest error is to report one success rate, such as that 0.7832 on members, without the baseline and the rate on non-members, which overstates the leak. Measuring only on fresh records understates it. A model is surer of the true label on its own members, the generalization gap of Membership inference, so the attack does better on them.
Dropping the sensitive column from the inputs does not stop population inference, because its correlates remain. Confidence masking, rounding the confidences or returning only the top label, puts no bound on the gap between members and non-members, and that gap can grow. In the full edition’s experiment, returning labels only raised the advantage from 0.0569 to 0.0650, because success fell more on non-members than on members. Less overfitting shrinks the gap, and differential privacy bounds it for every attacker and every output format.
crumbs: 11  Attribute inference and model inversion

title: 11  Attribute inference and model inversion
text:
11.5 References

Fredrikson, Jha & Ristenpart, “Model Inversion Attacks that Exploit Confidence Information and Basic Countermeasures” (CCS 2015): inversion from confidences, and rounding as a countermeasure.
Jayaraman & Evans, “Are Attribute Inference Attacks Just Imputation?” (CCS 2022): the imputation baseline, and what it takes to beat it.

title: 12  Property inference
text:
12.1 What it is
A property is a fact about a training set as a whole, such as the share of a hospital’s patients who are over 65. Property inference recovers it from a trained model. In the property game (Threat models and privacy games), the data owner flips a fair coin to pick one of two shares for a subgroup. It then trains a model on data with that share. The attacker knows both shares, can train models the way the owner does, and guesses which share was used, so a random guess is right half the time.
A property can leak when no single record does. Write \(n\) for the number of training records and \(g\) for the gap between the two shares. Switching shares changes about \(n g\) records at once, so it moves the model far more than one record can. The leak grows with \(n\), while the risk to one record shrinks. Even a release of only the exact count of subgroup records shows this. At 10,000 records, the best attacker asking whether one patient is in the data is right with probability 0.502. The best one asking whether the share was 0.45 or 0.55 is right with probability 1.0000.

title: 12  Property inference
text:
12.2 When you meet it
You meet it when you share or publish a model trained on your organization’s data. First decide whether the property is a secret at all. It is harmful to reveal only when it describes the data owner rather than the world. One hospital’s patient mix is a secret, but that smokers get more lung cancer is the point of a medical study. If it is not a secret, record that in the threat model of Pre-release privacy risk assessment and move on.
If it is a secret, differential privacy (DP) does not protect it. DP protects one record at a time, and its guarantee for a group multiplies the privacy level \(\varepsilon\) by the group’s size (Post-processing, group privacy and composition). For a hospital of 1,000 patients and shares a tenth apart, the group is the \(n g = 100\) patients that differ between the two datasets. So the property gets only \(100\varepsilon\), which promises nothing at any useful \(\varepsilon\).

title: 12  Property inference
text:
12.3 How to use it
To measure the risk, run the shadow-model attack of Ateniese et al. (2015), which treats whole models as data points. Draw many datasets of your training set’s size at each of the two shares, from auxiliary data of the same population or from your own data. Train a shadow model on each with your architecture and training code, and record its outputs on a fixed set of probe inputs. A linear meta-classifier, such as scikit-learn’s LogisticRegression, learns to tell the two shares apart from those outputs, and its accuracy on held-out shadow models is the attack’s accuracy. If the property is a secret, block the release when that accuracy’s confidence interval lies above one half (Pre-release privacy risk assessment).
Use probe outputs rather than raw weights, because reordering hidden units, or flipping the signs of tanh units, changes the weights but not the network’s function. On the full edition’s small tanh networks, every raw weight therefore averages to zero under both shares. A linear meta-classifier on raw weights scores 0.497, which is chance, and on the probe outputs 1.000. Probes need only query access, so a model behind an application programming interface is exposed too.

title: 12  Property inference
text:
12.4 What goes wrong
The commonest error is to assume that DP, or a passed membership audit, covers the property. Nor is a weak measured attack evidence of safety, because with few records and a small gap, a meta-classifier fitted to noisy shadow models finds the shift badly.
There is no cheap defence. Removing the group column leaves its correlates, and noise large enough to hide \(n g\) records destroys the model’s use. If the property is a secret, the strongest option is not to release a model trained on that mix. If you must, report the attack’s accuracy and state in the release notes that DP protects individuals only.

title: 12  Property inference
text:
12.5 References

Ganju, Wang, Yang, Gunter & Borisov, “Property Inference Attacks on Fully Connected Neural Networks using Permutation Invariant Representations” (CCS 2018): the practical attack on neural networks, and why raw weights fail.
Zhang, Tople & Ohrimenko, “Leakage of Dataset Properties in Multi-Party Machine Learning” (USENIX Security 2021): property inference through queries alone.

title: 13  Memorization and training-data extraction
text:
13.1 Why this matters
A language model trained on scraped text or support tickets sees phone numbers, addresses, keys and private messages. Asked to continue “Anna Smith’s phone number is”, it may finish with the real number. This is training-data extraction. Membership inference needs the record in hand to ask whether it was used, while extraction hands the attacker the record itself.

title: 13  Memorization and training-data extraction
text:
13.2 Which memorization to measure
The notions of memorization in Table 13.1 give rates that differ by orders of magnitude, so a report must say which one it measures. All use greedy decoding, which writes out the most likely next token at each step.



Table 13.1: The notions of memorization and when to use each. The first three are verbatim, needing an exact match, and each implies approximate. Discoverable implies extractable.










Definition
The string counts as memorized if
Use it for




Discoverable (Carlini et al. 2023)
The text before it in the training data makes greedy decoding produce it
Measuring memorization on a model you own


Extractable (Carlini et al. 2021)
Some prompt, any at all, makes greedy decoding produce it
The real risk, which attacks find but no test measures


\(k\)-eidetic
It is extractable and appears in at most \(k\) documents
Flagging the dangerous case, \(k = 1\)


Approximate (Ippolito et al. 2023)
Greedy decoding comes within a set edit distance of it
Near copies, such as a number with one digit changed






Discoverable memorization is the one you can measure, because you hold the training text it uses as the prompt. Treat any verbatim rate as a lower bound on the leak, because near copies leak too. A filter that blocks only verbatim training text is easy to bypass (Ippolito et al. 2023).
Deployed systems sample rather than decode greedily, so whether a string comes out depends on how many samples the attacker draws. A sample at temperature 1 writes out a string with probability \(p\), the model’s probability of that string after the prompt. Write \(\beta\) for the chance of failure the attacker accepts. Then a number \(m\) of independent samples suffices when \[m \ge \frac{\ln(1/\beta)}{p}. \tag{13.1}\] For a string of probability \(10^{-3}\) and \(\beta = 0.01\), that is about 4,600 samples. So report a sampling budget alongside the greedy rate, and measure with the decoding settings you deploy.

title: 13  Memorization and training-data extraction
section: 13.3 What gets memorized, and the first defences
text:
13.3 What gets memorized, and the first defences
Memorization grows with the copies of a string. On open models, the largest reproduced at least 1% of its training data in the discoverable sense (Carlini et al. 2023). A sequence repeated ten times is generated about a thousand times more often than one seen once (Kandpal, Wallace & Raffel 2022).
So the cheapest defence is deduplication, which lowers the copies of every repeated string. Models trained on deduplicated data emit memorized text about ten times less often without losing quality (Lee et al. 2022). Deduplicate before you plant the canaries of the next section, so that only they carry known copy counts.
The second defence removes personal data before training. A detector of personally identifiable information (PII), such as Microsoft’s Presidio, finds names, phone numbers and similar fields so you can mask them, but it misses whatever its patterns do not cover. Neither defence helps a secret seen once in a large model, where one copy is enough. Only fine-tuning with differential privacy, which limits how much any one training sequence can change the model, gives a guarantee for such singletons.

title: 13  Memorization and training-data extraction
text:
13.4 Auditing with canaries and exposure
Discoverable memorization is all or nothing, while an auditor wants a graded answer. Carlini et al. (2019) plant canaries, random secrets of a fixed format such as “my pin is” followed by five random digits. After training, you order all the values the secret could have taken from the most to the least likely under the model. The planted value’s rank in that order is the number of guesses an attacker trying them in turn needs.
Write \(\hat r\) for the planted value and \(|\mathcal R|\) for the number of values in the set \(\mathcal R\) it could have taken. The exposure is the number of bits of search the model saves an attacker, \[\mathrm{exposure}(\hat r) = \log_2|\mathcal R| - \log_2\operatorname{rank}(\hat r). \tag{13.2}\] Each bit halves the guesses the attacker needs. At rank 1 the exposure reaches its maximum, \(\log_2|\mathcal R|\), and the secret can be extracted. For five digits, \(10^5\) values, the maximum is 16.61 bits.
Exposure works as an audit because its behaviour is known when nothing was memorized. A canary’s value is drawn uniformly at random, so a model that never saw it puts it at a uniformly random rank. So for any threshold of \(t\) bits, \[\Pr\big[\mathrm{exposure}(\hat r) \ge t\big] \le 2^{-t}. \tag{13.3}\] So \(2^{-\text{exposure}}\) bounds the p-value, the chance that an uninserted canary would look at least this memorized. The same uniform rank gives an uninserted canary an average exposure of \(\log_2 e\), about 1.44 bits, which the controls should match.
To run the audit, draw canaries in the format of the secrets your data could contain, since a format unlike your data measures how the model treats unfamiliar text. Insert each one a chosen number of times, from once to many, keep some never inserted as controls, and fine-tune as usual. Then score each canary’s value, and many random values of the same format, by the model’s log-probability after the prefix. The share of random values that score at least as high estimates the rank fraction, the rank divided by \(|\mathcal R|\), and minus its base-2 logarithm is the exposure.
Scoring is where audits most often go wrong. A candidate’s log-probability is the sum over its tokens, but the mean loss that Hugging Face models return divides that sum by the number of tokens. Values of different token lengths then get scores on different scales, and the ranking is wrong. So score every candidate by its summed log-probability, in a format where every candidate has the same number of tokens. The script practitioner_lora.py fine-tunes the small language model Pythia-14m with low-rank adapters (LoRA) from peft. It spaces the digits of each pin, as in “the pin of Alice is 8 6 5 2 3”, so that each digit is one token. The exposure functions come from the book’s module practitioner_privacy_tests.py, which follows TensorFlow Privacy.
@torch.no_grad()
def secret_scores(model: PeftModel, tokenizer: PreTrainedTokenizerBase, prefix: str, secrets: list[str]) -> Scores:
    """Summed log-probability of each secret's five digit tokens after the prefix."""
    prefix_ids = tokenizer(prefix)["input_ids"]
    rows = [prefix_ids + tokenizer(" " + s)["input_ids"] for s in secrets]
    ids = torch.tensor(rows)  # every secret is five tokens, so the rows have equal length
    logits = model(input_ids=ids[:, :-1], logits_to_keep=5).logits  # the predictions of the five digits
    logprobs = logits.log_softmax(dim=-1).gather(-1, ids[:, -5:, None])
    return logprobs.sum(dim=(1, 2)).double().numpy()


def canary_exposure(
    model: PeftModel, tokenizer: PreTrainedTokenizerBase, canary: Canary, candidates: list[str]
) -> tuple[float, float]:
    """The exposure of the canary's secret among the candidates, measured and extrapolated past the cap."""
    candidate_scores = scores_batched(model, tokenizer, canary.prefix, candidates)
    score = float(scores_batched(model, tokenizer, canary.prefix, [canary.secret])[0])
    return exposure(score, candidate_scores), extrapolated_exposure(score, candidate_scores, SECRET_SPACE)
The model trains on 1,024 sequences of Tiny Shakespeare, a public extract of Shakespeare’s plays. The script inserts three canaries at each copy count from 1 to 64, keeps three as controls, and ranks each value among 2,000 random candidates. The command uv run python code/part05-dp-ml/practitioner_lora.py runs it in about two and a half minutes. Each line gives a group’s mean exposure, that exposure extrapolated past the cap the candidates set (explained below), and how many of its secrets greedy decoding wrote out.
non-private 1 copies: mean exposure 2.0 bits  extrapolated 2.0  extracted 0/3
non-private 4 copies: mean exposure 5.9 bits  extrapolated 5.7  extracted 0/3
non-private 16 copies: mean exposure 10.0 bits  extrapolated 13.0  extracted 0/3
non-private 64 copies: mean exposure 11.0 bits  extrapolated 16.3  extracted 3/3
non-private controls: mean exposure 1.4 bits  extrapolated 1.5  extracted 0/3
Exposure rises with the copies, and the controls sit at 1.4 bits, as the 1.44 expected for them predicts. Greedy decoding extracts only the three canaries seen 64 times. Yet two of the canaries seen 4 times reach 6.9 and 8.2 bits, which no extraction test notices, so an audit measures exposure and not only extraction. The canaries fill a quarter of the training set here, which lets so small a model memorize them in a short run. In the same script, fine-tuning with differential privacy at a privacy level \(\varepsilon = 8\) extracts nothing (Fine-tune a language model privately).
The cap comes from sampling the candidates. A canary that beats all 2,000 shows only that its rank fraction is below about 1 in 2,000. So its exposure stops at \(\log_2 2000 = 10.97\) bits, which the 64-copy canaries reach. Past the cap, the script fits a skew-normal distribution to the candidates’ scores and reads the canary’s rank off its tail, as Carlini et al. (2019) do. Ties hide memorization too, because when every candidate gets the same score, every exposure is 0.
A canary repeated 16 or more times is the positive control: if it does not reach a high exposure without privacy, the run is too short to tell you anything. Pre-release privacy risk assessment sets the exposure that blocks a release.

title: 13  Memorization and training-data extraction
section: 13.5 Extraction without the prefix: generate, rank, verify
text:
13.5 Extraction without the prefix: generate, rank, verify
A real attacker has only the model. Carlini et al. (2021) extracted data from GPT-2 by generating many samples, ranking them by how likely each was to be memorized, and checking the top ones. Ranking is the hard step, because a model finds a string likely either because it is ordinary text or because it memorized it. A reference model, trained on similar data but not on the target’s training set, stands in for ordinary text. Write \(p_\theta(x)\) for the target model’s probability of a string \(x\), and \(p_{\mathrm{ref}}(x)\) for the reference’s. Rank by the log-likelihood ratio \[\Lambda(x) = \ln p_\theta(x) - \ln p_{\mathrm{ref}}(x). \tag{13.4}\]
The ratio cancels the strings that any model finds likely, such as software licences and boilerplate, which raw likelihood would put first and which reveal nothing. A crude reference, such as a smaller model of the same family, works, and to audit your own fine-tuned model, the base model before fine-tuning is a natural one.
Without the prefix, an attacker extracts less than the discoverable rate suggests, but aligned production models are not safe. Nasr et al. (2023) asked ChatGPT to repeat one word forever, until it left its aligned behaviour and wrote memorized text. For about 200 US dollars of queries, they extracted over 10,000 records.

title: 13  Memorization and training-data extraction
text:
13.6 Cheat sheet



Table 13.2: The results of this chapter.









Question
Answer




Exposure of a canary
\(\log_2\lvert\mathcal R\rvert - \log_2\operatorname{rank}\), at most 16.61 bits for five digits; p-value at most \(2^{-\text{exposure}}\); controls average 1.44 bits


How to score a candidate
Summed log-probability, in a format where all candidates have the same token count


Ranking generations
\(\ln p_\theta(x) - \ln p_{\mathrm{ref}}(x)\), never raw likelihood


Defences, in order
Deduplicate (deduplicate-text-datasets, datasketch), scrub PII, then differential privacy for singletons






Rules of thumb

A verbatim rate is a lower bound on the leak, not a measure of it.

text:

title: 14  Gradient inversion
text:
14.1 Why this matters
A phone keyboard learns from what its users type without the text leaving the phones. A server sends the current model to each phone, which computes the gradient of the loss on its own few records and sends back only that gradient. The server averages the gradients and takes a training step. This is federated learning (FL), often called private because “the data stay on the device”.
Yet one client’s gradient can give back all of that client’s data, because it holds one derivative for every parameter, and many of them are simple functions of the input. Averaging over a batch protects much less than people expect (Section 14.6), so treat a per-client update as being as sensitive as the data it came from.

title: 14  Gradient inversion
section: 14.2 The attacker and what it sees
text:
14.2 The attacker and what it sees
The attacker is the server, which knows every parameter because it sent the model out. Since it also sees each client’s own update, its access is the transcript of Threat models and privacy games, everything training exposes. Assume first that it is honest-but-curious, so it only analyses what it receives. Each client holds a batch of \(B\) records and sends the average of their gradients. Write \(\ell_i\) for the loss on record \(i\), which depends on all the parameters \(\theta\). The client then sends \[g = \frac1B\sum_{i=1}^B\nabla_\theta\ell_i. \tag{14.1}\]

title: 14  Gradient inversion
section: 14.3 Exact recovery from a fully connected layer
text:
14.3 Exact recovery from a fully connected layer
The most common first layer, a fully connected layer with a bias, gives its input back by one division. Write \(W_1\) and \(b_1\) for its weights and bias. Each unit \(j\) multiplies the input \(x\) by its row of weights and adds its bias. Its backward signal \(u_j\) is how fast the loss responds to the unit’s output, and the chain rule turns it into the weight and bias gradients \[\nabla_{W_1}\ell = u\,x^\top, \qquad \nabla_{b_1}\ell = u. \tag{14.2}\] So row \(j\) of the weight gradient is the input scaled by \(u_j\), and the bias gradient of unit \(j\) is that same scale. For a single record, dividing one by the other gives the input exactly, for every unit whose bias gradient is not zero: \[x = \frac{(\nabla_{W_1}\ell)_{j,:}}{(\nabla_{b_1}\ell)_j}. \tag{14.3}\]
Everything above the layer, including the network’s depth, the loss and the label, sits inside \(u_j\) and cancels. So the attack needs no optimization and no knowledge of the data. The snippet plays one client with one image of scikit-learn’s digits in PyTorch, and its last line reads the label (Section 14.4).
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F
from sklearn.datasets import load_digits

torch.manual_seed(0)
images, labels = load_digits(return_X_y=True)
x = torch.tensor(images[[7]] / 16, dtype=torch.float32)  # one client's image, pixels in [0, 1]
y = torch.tensor(labels[[7]])
first, last = torch.nn.Linear(64, 32), torch.nn.Linear(32, 10)
F.cross_entropy(last(torch.relu(first(x))), y).backward()  # the gradient the client sends
# Row j of the weight gradient is the input times the bias gradient of unit j: divide them.
j = int(first.bias.grad.abs().argmax())
recovered = first.weight.grad[j] / first.bias.grad[j]
print(f"image recovered: {torch.allclose(recovered, x[0], atol=1e-6)}")  # image recovered: True
# Only the true label's logit has a negative gradient (softmax minus one-hot).
print(f"recovered label {int(last.bias.grad.argmin())}, true label {int(y)}")  # recovered label 7, true label 7
The snippet divides at the unit whose bias gradient is largest, because a switched-off ReLU unit has a zero gradient, and one active unit is enough. A convolutional first layer stops the division. Its filter is reused at every position of the image, so its gradient sums one such product per image patch, which no division can separate. The attacker then has to search (Section 14.5).

title: 14  Gradient inversion
section: 14.4 Label recovery from the last layer
text:
14.4 Label recovery from the last layer
The label is often the most sensitive part of an example, such as a diagnosis. It can be read off the last layer without search if that layer has a bias and feeds the softmax and cross-entropy loss (Zhao, Mopuri & Bilen 2020). Write \(p\) for the predicted probabilities and \(e_y\) for the vector with a 1 at the position of the label \(y\). The gradient of the last layer’s bias \(b_2\) is then \(p - e_y\). Every entry of \(p\) lies between 0 and 1, so only the entry at the true label is negative, and for a single record \[y = \arg\min_k(\nabla_{b_2}\ell)_k, \tag{14.4}\] which is the snippet’s argmin. It fails only for a very confident model: if the true label’s probability \(p_y\) rounds to 1 in floating point, that entry becomes zero, and no entry is negative.
A batch hides which record has which label, but not how many records each class has. Each entry of the bias gradient is then the class’s average predicted probability minus its share of the batch. So a server that estimates the average prediction on data of its own can read off each class’s count. In the full edition’s experiment, this gave every count exactly in all batches of 4, and in 52.5% of batches of 64.

title: 14  Gradient inversion
text:
14.5 Deep Leakage from Gradients
When the division does not apply, the attacker searches. Deep Leakage from Gradients (DLG), from Zhu, Liu & Han (2019), guesses inputs and computes the gradient they would produce. It then moves the guesses until that gradient matches the observed gradient \(g\). Write \(x_i'\) for the guessed inputs, \(y_i\) for their labels, read first from the last layer, and \(\ell(\theta; x', y)\) for the loss of one guess. The attack minimizes the matching loss \(R\), the squared distance between the guesses’ average gradient and \(g\): \[\hat x_1, \dots, \hat x_B = \arg\min_{x_1', \dots, x_B'}R(x'), \qquad R(x') = \Big\|\frac1B\sum_{i=1}^B\nabla_\theta\ell(\theta; x_i', y_i) - g\Big\|^2. \tag{14.5}\] In PyTorch, create_graph=True in torch.autograd.grad makes the guess’s gradient differentiable, so an optimizer such as Adam can follow the slope of \(R\) back to the input.
Two things decide whether the search works. The activation’s slope must vary, because the search differentiates a gradient, and the ReLU’s slope is constant on each side of zero. So Zhu et al. used the sigmoid. And because \(R\) is not convex, the search can get stuck. So run it until \(R\) stops falling, and judge the final value against the squared size \(\|g\|^2\) of the observed gradient. In double precision, a successful run in the full edition ends near \(10^{-27}\) and a stuck one near \(10^{-5}\). Another input can also give a small \(R\), so restart from several random guesses, and trust an image only when the restarts agree on it.

title: 14  Gradient inversion
text:
14.6 Batches and averaging
Clients usually send the average over a batch, or the change in their parameters after several training steps on the device (local steps). Averaging breaks the division and slows the search, but much of the structure survives. Each record adds one outer product to the first-layer gradient, so every row of that gradient is a combination of the \(B\) inputs. The server therefore learns their span, the set of all such combinations, which contains every record.
The division still recovers a record exactly when some ReLU unit is switched on for that record only, because the other records then add nothing to that unit’s row. Such a unit isolates the record. If units switched on like independent fair coins, a unit would isolate a given record with probability \(2^{-B}\), so isolation would become rare as the batch grows. But on images that resemble one another, a unit fires on many records or on few, so far more units fire on just one. In the full edition’s network with 1,024 hidden units and batches of 16 synthetic \(8\times8\) images, the coin model predicts that 1.6% of the batch is exposed, but 69.1% was.
Table 14.1 gives the share exposed in the same experiment. It falls with a larger batch and rises with a wider first layer, so measure at your own width and batch size, report both, and treat any isolated record as a breach.

DLG suffers more from batching: on the full edition’s sigmoid network with 32 hidden units, the median run on a batch of 4 gets stuck. That is a harder search, not less information, since the isolation attack recovered all four images of such a batch. Local steps do not protect a single record either. Each step’s first-layer gradient is an outer product with the same input, and only the backward signal changes, so the division still works on the total change. And a malicious server that chooses the weights can plant units that fire only on rare inputs, each isolating one record. It then recovers most records of a batch of any size (Boenisch et al. 2023; Fowl et al. 2022).

section: 14.7 What to do as a deployer
text:
14.7 What to do as a deployer
Table 14.2 reads off the risk of an FL deployment from who can see one client’s update.



Table 14.2: Gradient leakage by FL setting, and the response.










Setting

What to do

Updates protected by differential privacy (DP)

The only protection with a guarantee






Secure aggregation is a cryptographic protocol that lets the server see only the sum over many clients, which removes the per-client view every attack here uses. But a sum over very few clients is close to a single update, so set a minimum cohort size, and make sure that clients dropping out mid-round cannot shrink a sum below it.
Secure aggregation alone is not enough. The sum is still a batch average that the attacks above can read, the final model still leaks like any model, and a malicious server can still choose its weights. For a guarantee, add DP with the client as the unit of privacy. Clipping each client’s update to a fixed maximum norm and adding noise to the sum bounds what any one client’s data can change (User-level privacy). Flower and TensorFlow Federated offer both protections. Heuristic defences such as gradient pruning raise the cost of the search but carry no guarantee.
To assess your deployment, find out whether the server sees single updates or only sums, and with what minimum cohort. Then run the attacks on your own architecture, batch size and number of local steps, for example with Geiping’s open-source breaching framework for PyTorch. If any client’s update is visible on its own, block the deployment until secure aggregation or client-level DP is in place, and record the verdict in the Pre-release privacy risk assessment.

title: 15  Linkage and re-identification
text:
15.1 Why this matters
A hospital shares its discharge records with researchers after deleting the names, but keeps the postcode, the date of birth, the sex and the diagnosis. Anyone with a voter roll, which lists names next to those same three columns, can join the two tables and put a name back on most rows. This is a linkage attack, and putting a name back on a “de-identified” record is re-identification.
Whether a table can be linked is judged by counting identifying information in bits. Each bit halves the candidates, so singling out one person in a population of \(n\) people takes \(\log_2 n\) bits, 27.9 bits for the United States of 1990. Almost everyone is unique once the attributes an adversary knows carry a few bits more than that, and a unique record can be linked.

title: 15  Linkage and re-identification
text:
15.2 Quasi-identifiers and the linkage attack
Direct identifiers, like a name or an email address, name a person on their own. Sensitive attributes, such as a diagnosis, are what the release is about. Quasi-identifiers sit in between: none of them names anyone alone, but together they often single out one person, and they appear next to names in other datasets.
To score a release you hold, group its \(n\) records into equivalence classes, the sets of records with identical quasi-identifiers, and write \(J\) for the number of classes. Suppose an adversary knows the target’s quasi-identifiers and that the target is in the release. If the target is alone in its class, the adversary names its record for sure, and if the class holds \(k\) look-alikes, one time in \(k\). A class of \(k\) records holds \(k\) targets, each named with probability \(1/k\), so every class adds one win whatever its size. Averaged over all \(n\) targets, the chance of naming the right record is therefore \[\Pr[\text{win}] = \frac{J}{n}, \tag{15.1}\] and no adversary that sees only the quasi-identifiers can do better. This is the prosecutor model, the worst case, because it assumes the adversary knows the target is in the data.
The script practitioner_table_risk.py shows how fast uniqueness grows on a real table, Adult, the 48,842 people of the 1994 US Current Population Survey in the UCI repository. Adult has no ZIP code or birth date, so the script starts from age, sex and race. It adds one quasi-identifier at a time, with native country as the only geography. For each set it prints the share of unique records, the share in classes smaller than 5, the smallest class size and \(J/n\).
n = df.height
for qis in QI_SETS:
    # One row per equivalence class (records that agree on every quasi-identifier), with its size.
    sizes = df.group_by(qis).len()
    unique = sizes.filter(pl.col("len") == 1).height / n  # share of records alone in their class
    small = sizes.filter(pl.col("len") < 5)["len"].sum() / n  # share in classes smaller than 5
    min_k = sizes["len"].min()  # the table is k-anonymous for this k
    print(
        f"{' + '.join(qis)}: unique={unique:.2%}  in classes <5={small:.2%}  "
        f"min k={min_k}  J/n={sizes.height / n:.3f}"
    )
Run it with uv run python code/part02-attacks/practitioner_table_risk.py, which prints:
age + sex + race: unique=0.12%  in classes <5=0.75%  min k=1  J/n=0.012
age + sex + race + native-country: unique=3.07%  in classes <5=7.83%  min k=1  J/n=0.060
age + sex + race + native-country + marital-status: unique=5.88%  in classes <5=11.99%  min k=1  J/n=0.100
age + sex + race + native-country + marital-status + education: unique=14.64%  in classes <5=26.83%  min k=1  J/n=0.227
age + sex + race + native-country + marital-status + education + hours-per-week: unique=36.55%  in classes <5=57.05%  min k=1  J/n=0.480
Three columns that look harmless leave 0.12% of the records unique, and six leave 14.64%. Adding the hours worked per week, which nobody would list as an identifier, makes 36.55% unique and puts more than half the records in classes smaller than 5. So add every column an adversary could know to the test, one at a time, because the one that breaks the table may be one nobody suspected. A minimum class size of 5 is a common convention, yet every set here has classes of a single record.

title: 15  Linkage and re-identification
text:
15.3 Pseudonyms and hashed identifiers
Many releases replace each identifier by a pseudonym, a code that stays the same across a person’s records, and such codes fail in two ways. First, a hash without a secret key, such as plain MD5, can be reversed whenever the possible identifiers can be listed, because the adversary can hash every candidate and look each pseudonym up. New York City hashed its taxi drivers’ licences this way in its 2013 trip release. There were only about 2 million possible licences, so in 2014 Vijay Pandurangan hashed them all in minutes, and public lists of licence holders then named each driver.
The second failure survives any key. The pseudonym ties a person’s records together, so linking any one of them reveals all the others. In the taxi data, a pickup minute and place single out one trip, which a passenger who knows who drove it can find. The driver’s pseudonym, even a random one, then reveals every trip that driver made. This is why the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) still counts pseudonymized data as personal data.
If you must keep a join key, derive it with a keyed hash, a hash-based message authentication code (HMAC), and keep the key away from the data.
import hashlib
import hmac
import secrets

licence = "482913"  # a six-digit licence number, the identifier being pseudonymized
pseudonym = hashlib.md5(licence.encode()).hexdigest()  # what an unkeyed release prints

# Dictionary attack: hash all 10**6 possible licences once, then look the pseudonym up.
lookup = {hashlib.md5(f"{i:06d}".encode()).hexdigest(): f"{i:06d}" for i in range(10**6)}
print(lookup[pseudonym])  # 482913

# A keyed hash still gives one code per person, but without the key nobody can build the table.
key = secrets.token_bytes(32)  # store it apart from the data; draw a new one for each release
keyed = hmac.new(key, licence.encode(), hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()
print(keyed in lookup)  # False
The key stops the dictionary attack but not the second failure, since each person’s records still form an identifying history. Reusing the key would join that history across releases, so draw a fresh key for each release.

title: 15  Linkage and re-identification
text:
15.4 How many people are unique?
For a release still being designed, there is no table to count, so estimate uniqueness by adding bits. An attribute with \(v\) equally likely values carries \(\log_2 v\) bits, and the bits of independent attributes add. Attributes that carry \(b\) bits in total split people into \(2^b\) cells. If each person lands in a cell at random, every cell equally likely, the expected share of the \(n\) people who are alone in their cell is about \[\frac{\text{unique people}}{n} \approx \exp\big(-2^{\log_2 n - b}\big). \tag{15.2}\] The share depends only on the bits beyond \(\log_2 n\), and it rises steeply with them. Half the people are unique at 0.53 bits beyond \(\log_2 n\), and 99% at 6.64 bits.
For example, ZIP code, birth date and sex carry 31.1 bits, a few more than the 27.9 bits that single out one American. The formula then predicts that 0.899 of Americans are unique, close to the 87% that Latanya Sweeney estimated from the 1990 census. Real attributes are skewed and correlated, which usually lowers uniqueness, so the estimate errs on the side of caution.

title: 15  Linkage and re-identification
text:
15.5 Sparse data: the Netflix attack
Ratings, purchases and locations have no quasi-identifier columns, yet they identify people even better. Netflix released about 100 million movie ratings in 2006, with the subscribers’ names replaced by random numbers. Narayanan and Shmatikov (2008) matched its records to public reviews with a score that adds up the items on which a record agrees with what the adversary knows. Each item is weighted by its rarity, because agreeing on an obscure film says more than agreeing on a hit. With this score, eight ratings with dates known to within 14 days identified 99% of the records, even when two of them were wrong.
The best score always points at some record, even when the target is not in the release. So the eccentricity test declares a match only if the best score beats the second best by a margin, counted in standard deviations of all the scores. Calibrate that margin on people known not to be in the data: on the full edition’s simulated ratings, the original attack’s margin also matched 26.3% of such outsiders. So report the attack’s success at a stated false positive rate (Hypothesis testing).

title: 15  Linkage and re-identification
text:
15.6 Does releasing a sample protect?
Agencies often release a sample, as Adult is, arguing that a record unique in the sample may share its attributes with someone left out. The argument is weaker than it sounds. Suppose the adversary knows a person and finds exactly one matching record in a release that holds a share \(q\) of the population, the sampling rate. Write \(\lambda\) for the expected number of other people in the population who share the target’s cell. The record found can be a look-alike’s only if the target was left out, which happens with probability \(1 - q\). So for a rare cell, the probability \(\kappa\) that the match is right is about \[\kappa \approx \frac{1}{1 + \lambda(1 - q)}. \tag{15.3}\]
Take a rare cell, one expected to hold \(\lambda = 0.1\) other people. Even a 1% sample leaves a match right with probability 0.910. Sampling enters only through \(1 - q\), which can never exceed 1, so the chance of a right match never falls below \(1/(1 + \lambda)\), and shrinking the sample barely helps. Sampling protects only people whose cells are crowded anyway.
So the Adult figures above are sample uniqueness, exact when the target is known to be in the release. The population uniqueness behind them is lower, but not by much for rare cells, so estimate it with a model rather than assume the risk away. ARX and sdcMicro offer such estimates, and Rocher, Hendrickx and de Montjoye (2019) model correlated attributes for it.

title: 15  Linkage and re-identification
text:
15.7 A pre-release risk check
A quasi-identifier is any column an adversary could find next to a name elsewhere, such as a date, a location or a rare event, so list them all. No tool can do this for you, because no tool knows what auxiliary data exist. To lower the risk, coarsen geography and dates first, since they carry the most bits. Then suppress the records that remain unique (Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks). If the analysis needs fine-grained or sparse data, release a differentially private output instead (Release statistics with a library). Pre-release privacy risk assessment runs this check with thresholds fixed before the counts are seen.

title: 16  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks
text:
16.1 Why this matters
Linkage and re-identification showed that deleting names does not anonymize a table, because quasi-identifiers such as age, postcode and sex single out many people. The classic answer is to coarsen the table until every person hides in a crowd. The definitions that make this precise are called syntactic, because you check each one by reading the published table. Statistics offices and tools such as ARX and sdcMicro still use them, so you will meet them in audits. But each holds for one table against an adversary whose knowledge is fixed in advance, so one unanticipated fact, or a second release of the same people, voids it.
crumbs: 16  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks

title: 16  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks
section: 16.2 What the adversary believes about a class
text:
16.2 What the adversary believes about a class
To anonymize a table, the custodian, the organization that holds the data, applies a generalization, which turns an age into a range or a postcode into a prefix. Records with the same generalized quasi-identifiers form an equivalence class. An adversary who knows the target’s quasi-identifiers finds the target’s class \(E\) but cannot tell its records apart. So its belief about the target’s sensitive value, its posterior, is the share of the class with that value. Write \(\lvert E\rvert\) for the size of the class and \(n_E(v)\) for the number of its records with a sensitive value \(v\). The posterior that the target’s sensitive value, written \(S_{\text{target}}\), equals \(v\) is
\[\Pr[S_{\text{target}} = v \mid \text{release}] = \frac{n_E(v)}{\lvert E\rvert}. \tag{16.1}\] Background knowledge works by elimination: ruling out a value crosses out its records, and the posterior is recomputed over those that remain. Every attack in this chapter is this calculation.
crumbs: 16  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks

title: 16  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks
text:
16.3 k-anonymity and what it costs
k-anonymity (Sweeney and Samarati, 1998) asks that every class hold at least \(k\) records, for a crowd size \(k\) the custodian chooses. Generalization gets there, together with suppression, which deletes the records that still stand out. In the previous chapter, an adversary who knows the target is in the release links it with probability \(J/n\), the number of classes \(J\) over the number of records \(n\). At least \(k\) records per class means at most \(n/k\) classes, so \[\Pr[\text{win}] = \frac{J}{n} \le \frac1k. \tag{16.2}\] The guarantee covers names only, and only against an adversary who knows nothing beyond the quasi-identifiers. The choice of \(k\) is a policy: a minimum of 5 is common, and some health-data rules ask for more.
Anonymizers such as Mondrian search for a generalization that loses little, but you can also generalize by hand and recheck. The script practitioner_table_risk.py takes the previous chapter’s Adult census extract and its six quasi-identifiers. It puts age into 10-year bands, native country into US or other, and education into four levels. Then it counts the records alone in their class, and the different occupations in each class, with occupation standing in for a sensitive attribute. Both are Polars counts, since no maintained Python package computes k-anonymity or distinct \(\ell\).
general = df.with_columns(
    (pl.col("age") // 10 * 10).alias("age"),  # 10-year bands: 30 stands for 30-39
    pl.when(pl.col("native-country") == "United-States")
    .then(pl.lit("US"))
    .otherwise(pl.lit("other"))
    .alias("native-country"),
    # education-num runs from 1 (preschool) to 16 (doctorate); 9 is high-school graduate.
    pl.col("education-num")
    .cut([8, 9, 12], labels=["no diploma", "HS-grad", "some college", "bachelor+"])
    .alias("education"),
)
# Recheck, and count the occupations in each class (distinct l).
classes = general.group_by(QIS).agg(pl.len(), pl.col("occupation").n_unique().alias("l"))
unique = classes.filter(pl.col("len") == 1).height / general.height
one_job = classes.filter(pl.col("l") == 1)["len"].sum() / general.height
print(f"after generalizing: unique={unique:.2%}  in a class with one occupation={one_job:.2%}")
Run it with uv run python code/part02-attacks/practitioner_table_risk.py. Its first two output lines use the six generalized quasi-identifiers, and the third adds the raw hours worked per week.
after generalizing: unique=0.94%  in a class with one occupation=1.20%
age + sex + race + native-country + marital-status + education: unique=0.94%  in classes <5=3.31%  min k=1  J/n=0.032
age + sex + race + native-country + marital-status + education + hours-per-week: unique=10.09%  in classes <5=21.78%  min k=1  J/n=0.175
  records in classes of size >=5 with l=1: 0.03%
Generalizing cut the unique share to 0.94%, from 14.64% before. Yet the smallest class still holds one record, so the 3.31% of records in classes smaller than 5 must be suppressed, or the bands made coarser. And the result is fragile, because an adversary who also knows the hours worked finds 10.09% of the records unique again.
crumbs: 16  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks

title: 16  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks
text:
16.4 Homogeneity, background knowledge and l-diversity
k-anonymity hides who a record belongs to, but not what it says (Machanavajjhala and colleagues, 2006). If all three records of Alice’s class say heart disease, her posterior is 1 without anyone finding her record, which is the homogeneity attack. If Bob’s class says cancer, cancer and flu, a neighbour who knows he did not have flu crosses out that record. The neighbour learns that Bob has cancer, which is the background knowledge attack.
l-diversity asks each class to hold enough different sensitive values. The distinct version asks for at least \(\ell\) different values. It does not cap the most common value’s share, so a class can be 3-diverse with one value in most of its records. The recursive version adds that cap, with a constant \(c\) the custodian picks, so that an adversary who rules out \(\ell - 2\) values keeps a posterior below \(c/(1 + c)\). That cap is already one half at \(c = 1\), so even this version protects against certainty, not likelihood.
Suppressing the small classes also removes most homogeneous ones. On Adult, 1.20% of the generalized records sit in a class where everyone has the same occupation, but only 0.03% sit in such a class of 5 or more. On a synthetic hospital table of the full edition, distinct 3-diversity removed the certain disclosures at little cost, while the recursive version forced some classes to grow to 641 patients.
crumbs: 16  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks

title: 16  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks
text:
16.5 Measuring what a release teaches
Compare every posterior with the imputation baseline of Attribute inference and model inversion, the best guess of a sensitive value from the population alone. Only the success beyond it is about the individual. On the hospital table, guessing each patient’s diagnosis from age alone is right for 53.6% of patients, and a 5-anonymous release raises that to 59.3%. Most of what the release teaches is the link between age and diagnosis, which any useful study would report. Only the excess of 5.7 percentage points is a leak.
crumbs: 16  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks

title: 16  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks
text:
16.6 Skewness, similarity and t-closeness
l-diversity misses two attacks (Li, Li and Venkatasubramanian, 2007). In the skewness attack, a class that is half HIV is 2-diverse, yet in a table where 1% have HIV it raises its members’ posterior fifty-fold. In the similarity attack, a class of three different stomach diseases is 3-diverse but still reveals a stomach disease.
t-closeness answers both, by asking that the distribution of values in every class \(E\) be within a distance \(t\) of the whole table’s. Write \(P_E(A)\) and \(P(A)\) for the chance that a value drawn from the class, or from the table, lands in a set \(A\) of values. With the total variation (TV) distance, no such chance, and so no belief, moves by more than \(t\), \[\lvert P_E(A) - P(A)\rvert \le t. \tag{16.3}\] The bound is a difference, not a ratio, so it protects rare values badly. At \(t = 0.15\), a value held by 1% of the table may rise to 16%. Against the similarity attack, Li and colleagues used the earth mover’s distance (EMD) instead, which counts similar values as close.
t-closeness costs a lot. At \(t = 0.15\), guessing diagnoses from the hospital release was right for only 22.2% of patients, below the 53.6% of imputation from age alone. The release told less about the population than no release.
crumbs: 16  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks

title: 16  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks
text:
16.7 The composition attack
Ganta, Kasiviswanathan and Smith (2008) asked what happens when two hospitals each publish a k-anonymous or l-diverse table. A patient treated at both sits in a class \(E_A\) of one release and a class \(E_B\) of the other. The adversary keeps only the diagnoses that appear in both classes, \[\{v : n_{E_A}(v) > 0\} \cap \{v : n_{E_B}(v) > 0\}. \tag{16.4}\] When one candidate is left, the diagnosis is pinned down.
In the full edition’s simulation, two hospitals share 6,649 patients. Their two 5-anonymous releases together pin down the diagnosis of 9.9% of them, over three times what either pins alone. With distinct 3-diversity neither release pins anyone, yet together they pin 18.
No single-table definition can stop this, because the intersection of two tables is a table that neither custodian checked. A definition that survives must compose across releases, hold whatever the adversary knows, and bound the ratio of beliefs, so that rare values are protected. The definition of differential privacy starts from these requirements, which is why statistics offices such as the US Census Bureau have moved towards it (Reconstruction attacks).
crumbs: 16  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks

title: 16  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks
text:
16.8 Choosing and running an anonymization
Start from the quasi-identifiers of Linkage and re-identification, since a list that is too short is the commonest failure. Use k-anonymity against linkage, and add distinct l-diversity when a class with one sensitive value would be a disclosure. Use t-closeness, the costliest, only when the sensitive attribute is skewed or has similar values.
Then audit the anonymizer’s output yourself, in Polars as the excerpt does, or with pycanon, which reports the crowd size \(k\), \(\ell\) and \(t\) for a pandas table. Pre-release privacy risk assessment turns these checks into a release decision. Move to differential privacy when other releases of the same people exist, when the sensitive attribute is rare, or when the data are sparse. For tables of counts and sums, Release statistics with a library does the job end to end.

title: 17  Reconstruction attacks
text:
17.1 What it is
A reconstruction attack rebuilds the records behind published aggregates, because every count is a linear equation in the secret values of the people counted. Suppose each of \(n\) people has one secret bit, listed in \(d\). A subset-sum query asks how many people in a set have bit 1. The attacker’s \(m\) queries are the rows of a matrix \(A\) of zeros and ones, and the curator who answers publishes the true answers plus an error vector \(e\), \[a = Ad + e. \tag{17.1}\]
Least squares finds the real numbers whose answers come closest to the published ones, then clips and rounds each to 0 or 1. Let each query include every person with probability one half, and let the noise be normal with standard deviation \(\sigma\). Then least squares recovers about a fraction \[\Phi\left(\frac{\sqrt{m - n}}{4\sigma}\right) \tag{17.2}\] of the bits, where \(\Phi\) is the standard normal distribution function. The baseline is the majority guess, which gives everyone the commoner value: one half for balanced bits. With a few times more queries than people, noise well below \(\sqrt n\) therefore reveals the data. Answering all \(2^n\) subset sums needs error of order \(n\) to stop reconstruction (Dinur and Nissim 2003).
These results are the Fundamental Law of Information Recovery: answering too many questions too accurately destroys privacy. But stopping reconstruction is not privacy. A curator that answers from a secret random half of the people stops it, yet gives that half away exactly. And learning only whether someone took part needs far fewer statistics (Homer et al. 2008, Lower bounds).

title: 17  Reconstruction attacks
text:
17.2 When you meet it
Every published count, cross-tabulation, dashboard cell or query answer is such an equation. The Census Bureau attacked its own 2010 publications and rebuilt a record for every person. About 46% of them matched a real person exactly on block, sex, age, race and ethnicity. Linked to commercial data, they confirmed the identity of about 17% of the population, so the 2020 Census moved to differential privacy. Query systems fall too: the noise of the commercial system Diffix did not grow with the number of queries, so Cohen and Nissim (2020) averaged it away.

title: 17  Reconstruction attacks
text:
17.3 How to use it
To audit an aggregate release, first count the equations. If the cells or allowed queries outnumber the people, only the noise protects them. Put your noise level and number of queries into Equation 17.2, and if the prediction is far above the majority guess, run the attack. The snippet draws the noise from OpenDP’s Gaussian mechanism, as a release would, and runs least squares. OpenDP’s noise cannot be seeded, so it checks the share recovered against the prediction instead of printing it.
from statistics import NormalDist

import numpy as np
import opendp.prelude as dp

dp.enable_features("contrib")
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n, m = 500, 2000  # people with a secret bit each, and random subset-sum queries
sigma = 0.25 * np.sqrt(n)  # noise sd added to each answer
secret = rng.integers(0, 2, n)
queries = rng.integers(0, 2, (m, n))
space = dp.vector_domain(dp.atom_domain(T=float, nan=False)), dp.l2_distance(T=float)
gaussian = dp.m.make_gaussian(*space, scale=sigma)  # OpenDP's Gaussian mechanism on all m answers
answers = np.array(gaussian((queries @ secret).astype(float).tolist()))
estimate = np.linalg.lstsq(queries, answers, rcond=None)[0]  # the textbook attack: least squares
recovered = np.mean(np.clip(estimate, 0, 1).round() == secret)
predicted = NormalDist().cdf(np.sqrt(m - n) / (4 * sigma))
print(f"predicted {predicted:.4f}")  # predicted 0.9584
print(f"recovered within 0.04 of it: {abs(recovered - predicted) < 0.04}")  # recovered within 0.04 of it: True
The number of queries matters as much as the noise. In the full edition’s simulation, with noise of twice \(\sqrt n\), four queries per person recovered only 0.5875 of the bits. Yet solving Equation 17.2 at that noise shows that 106.1 queries per person recover 90%. So fixed noise falls to enough queries, and the noise must grow with the number of answers, as differential privacy makes it.
For queries that are not random, the linear-programming decoder of Dinur and Nissim fits unknowns between 0 and 1 with scipy.optimize.linprog. For published tables, write each cell as a constraint on whole-number unknowns, solve with scipy.optimize.milp, and count the solutions, since a single one rebuilds the records. The release fails when either decoder beats the majority guess.

title: 17  Reconstruction attacks
text:
17.4 What goes wrong
Rounding, household swapping and small-cell suppression are not noise. Rounding hides nothing, because the attacker can round the answers of each candidate dataset too. Swapping leaves most constraints exact, and a suppressed cell adds one, that the count is below the threshold. Sticky noise, which repeats the same answer to a repeated query, only stops repeats, which the attack never needs.
Test the union of all releases, not one table at a time. And do not trust least squares alone, since errors chosen against it hurt it more than random noise. Reconstruct your own release with both decoders before publishing it, and record the result in Pre-release privacy risk assessment.

title: 18  Pre-release privacy risk assessment
text:
18.1 Why this matters
Before a model or a table leaves your hands, someone has to decide whether it leaks too much about the people in it. This chapter runs the attacks of this part as the assessment a privacy reviewer would ask for. Its three releases are a classifier behind a scoring API, a language model whose weights go to a partner, and a record-level census extract.
The order matters as much as the attacks. The results that block the release are written down before anything runs, because a threshold chosen after seeing the numbers can be bent to fit them. And a failed attack shows only that this attack failed, so the assessment reports how strong its attacks were.
practitioner_lira.py and practitioner_table_risk.py run in seconds on public data. The language-model step reuses the output of practitioner_lora.py, from Fine-tune a language model privately with LoRA, which takes a few minutes on an idle CPU.

title: 18  Pre-release privacy risk assessment
section: 18.2 Fix the threat model and the thresholds first
text:
18.2 Fix the threat model and the thresholds first
Fill in the worksheet of Threat models and privacy games once per artefact, because each release can expose the same data differently. By default the privacy unit is the person, and the adversary sees scores, the confidences a model returns, since many services return them.
Then write the blocking rules of Table 18.1 into the plan. The membership rule uses the true positive rate (TPR), the share of members an attack flags, and the false positive rate (FPR), the share of non-members it wrongly flags. At an FPR of \(10^{-3}\), it blocks when the lower end of the TPR’s 95% confidence interval exceeds ten times the FPR. Reading the lower end means a lucky run cannot trigger it, and the factor of ten is a policy choice: an attack may beat chance, but not tenfold.
Several remedies use differential privacy (DP), Part 3’s guarantee that caps what any attack learns about one person by a privacy level \(\varepsilon\). One is stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with each record’s gradient clipped and noise added, called DP-SGD.
