The four middle rows block on any leak beyond the attack’s own baseline, which the chapters on attribute, property and reconstruction attacks and gradient inversion define. In the last row, an audit with independent trials certifies a lower bound on a DP model’s \(\varepsilon\), and a bound above the claim proves a bug (Auditing private training).

title: 18  Pre-release privacy risk assessment
text:
18.3 Classifier: the free check
Compare the model’s accuracy on its training data and on held-out data. Then run the loss attack, which says “member” whenever the loss on the true label is low (Membership inference). The model is a logistic regression on scikit-learn’s digits, 1,797 small images of handwritten digits. The script trains 64 copies, each on a random half of the images. Each copy in turn plays the target, the model under assessment, while the others serve as shadow models in the next step.
target 0: train accuracy=1.0000  test accuracy=0.9650
train-test gap, mean over 64 targets=0.0422
ART rule-based attack on target 0: TPR=1.0000  FPR=0.9650  advantage=0.0350
loss attack at FPR 0.001: TPR=0.0009
loss attack at FPR 0.01: TPR=0.0105
The first target gets every training image right, but only 0.9650 of its test images. So even the rule “member if correctly classified” beats chance, by the mean gap of 0.0422. That is a free lower bound on the leak, though it does not say who is exposed. The Adversarial Robustness Toolbox (ART), a Python library of attacks, runs that rule as MembershipInferenceBlackBoxRuleBased, and its advantage of 0.0350 on the first target is that model’s gap. The loss attack, at an FPR of \(10^{-3}\), flags no more members than non-members. A weak attack’s failure proves little, so this check can never clear a model. A large gap says regularize first, and a small one only that you need the next step.

title: 18  Pre-release privacy risk assessment
text:
18.4 Classifier: LiRA with shadow models
The likelihood ratio attack (LiRA) of Membership inference compares the target’s output on a record with the outputs of shadow models. These are trained like the target on random halves of the data, some with that record and some without. LiRA works with the logit \(\phi\) of the confidence \(p\) in the true label, \[\phi = \ln\frac{p}{1 - p}, \tag{18.1}\] which is close to normal across retrainings. For each image, it fits a normal to \(\phi\) over the shadows that trained on it (IN) and another over those that did not (OUT). Online LiRA scores the target’s \(\phi\) by its log-likelihood ratio between the two fits. Offline LiRA uses only the OUT fit, and counts how many OUT standard deviations \(\phi\) lies above the OUT mean. ART’s SklearnClassifier trains every model, and the helper practitioner_privacy_tests.py computes the LiRA scores.
Four decisions set the attack’s strength. Use online LiRA, the strongest, for a release decision. Train 64 shadows when training is cheap; with 16 or fewer, fit one variance shared by all images, because per-image variances from so few models are too noisy. Put each record in each model by a fair coin, so that every record has IN and OUT shadows. And let each model serve once as the target, with the other 63 as its shadows. That gives 57,704 member and 57,304 non-member pairs of a model and an image.
At an FPR of \(10^{-3}\), the 57,304 non-member pairs allow only about 57 false positives, so the script reads the rate with care. It takes the best TPR among thresholds whose FPR stays at or below the target. Then it puts a Clopper–Pearson interval, the exact binomial interval of Hypothesis testing, on each rate.
# Every (target model, image) pair is one trial; members are the positives.
fpr, tpr, thresholds = roc_curve(member.ravel(), scores.ravel())
# The best TPR among thresholds whose FPR does not exceed the target.
i = int(np.flatnonzero(fpr <= target_fpr)[-1])
n_members, n_nonmembers = int(member.sum()), int((~member).sum())
true_pos = round(tpr[i] * n_members)
false_pos = round(fpr[i] * n_nonmembers)
# Exact 95% intervals (Clopper-Pearson) for both rates.
tpr_ci = clopper_pearson(true_pos, n_members)
fpr_ci = clopper_pearson(false_pos, n_nonmembers)
  loss attack: AUC=0.518  TPR@0.001=0.0009  TPR@0.01=0.0105
  ART shadow-model attack: AUC=0.570  TPR@0.001=0.0014  TPR@0.01=0.0146
  LiRA offline: AUC=0.577  TPR@0.001=0.0087  TPR@0.01=0.0345
  LiRA online: AUC=0.623  TPR@0.001=0.0318  TPR@0.01=0.0790
[At FPR 0.001: counts, exact 95% intervals, ln(TPR/FPR) as a point estimate, not a certified bound; step 1 blocks if the TPR's lower end > 0.01]
  loss attack: TP=53/57704  TPR=0.0009 [0.0007, 0.0012]  FP=57/57304  FPR=0.00099 [0.00075, 0.00129]  ln(TPR/FPR)=-0.08  pass
  ART shadow-model attack: TP=82/57704  TPR=0.0014 [0.0011, 0.0018]  FP=57/57304  FPR=0.00099 [0.00075, 0.00129]  ln(TPR/FPR)=0.36  pass
  LiRA offline: TP=502/57704  TPR=0.0087 [0.0080, 0.0095]  FP=56/57304  FPR=0.00098 [0.00074, 0.00127]  ln(TPR/FPR)=2.19  pass
  LiRA online: TP=1833/57704  TPR=0.0318 [0.0303, 0.0332]  FP=57/57304  FPR=0.00099 [0.00075, 0.00129]  ln(TPR/FPR)=3.46  block
By area under the curve (AUC) the four attacks look alike, but at an FPR of \(10^{-3}\) they differ sharply. Online LiRA flags 1,833 members, a TPR of 0.0318. The lower end of its interval, 0.0303, is above 0.01, so the model fails Table 18.1. Offline LiRA would have passed it, and so would ART’s attack of Shokri et al. (2017), which learns one rule for all images from four shadow models of its own. So a release decision rests on the strongest attack you can afford.
A model with privacy level \(\varepsilon\) keeps the TPR within about \(e^{\varepsilon}\) times the FPR. So the last column, ln(TPR/FPR), estimates the \(\varepsilon\) each attack implies. It is not a certified lower bound, because pairs that share a model are not independent trials (Auditing private training).
The script also prints the ten images an attacker exposes first, those whose IN and OUT fits lie furthest apart. Inspect them, since such records are usually rare or mislabelled.
Three things go wrong here. Shadows trained with another recipe describe another model, which weakens the attack. Too few non-members leave the FPR uncertain, and even here its interval runs from 0.00075 to 0.00129. The script also sets thresholds and measures on the same pairs, which flatters the attack slightly, where Hypothesis testing uses two splits. And a confidence of 1 makes \(\phi\) infinite, so compute \(\phi\) from the logits, the model’s raw outputs. Clipping the confidence instead hides a confident model’s most exposed records (Membership inference).

title: 18  Pre-release privacy risk assessment
section: 18.5 Fine-tuned language model: canaries and extraction
text:
18.5 Fine-tuned language model: canaries and extraction
A language model can repeat a secret word for word, which a membership test does not measure. So the assessment plants canaries, random secrets of a fixed format, and checks how well the trained model knows them (Memorization and training-data extraction). The run adapts Pythia-14m with low-rank adaptation (LoRA) to 1,024 sequences of Tiny Shakespeare, once without privacy and once with DP at \(\varepsilon = 8\) per sequence.
The canaries should look like the secrets you fear. Each reads “the pin of”, a name such as Alice, “is”, and five random digits, spaced so that every possible secret is exactly five tokens. Three are inserted once, and three more at each of 4, 16 and 64 copies. Three controls are drawn the same way and never inserted. The canaries make up a quarter of the training set, far denser than real secrets, so even this small model memorizes them. The non-private model is then a positive control, one known to leak.
Each canary is scored in two ways, with the functions of Fine-tune a language model privately with LoRA. Exposure ranks the secret among random secrets of the same format by the summed log-probability of its five digit tokens. It turns the rank into bits, as \(\log_2\) of the number of candidates minus \(\log_2\) of the rank. Sum rather than average, since the mean loss that transformers returns misranks secrets of different token counts. Extraction gives the model the prefix and lets it write the likeliest token five times, which is greedy decoding. Run it with the partner’s decoding settings, and check whether it wrote the secret.
non-private 1 copies: mean exposure 2.0 bits  extrapolated 2.0  extracted 0/3
non-private 4 copies: mean exposure 5.9 bits  extrapolated 5.7  extracted 0/3
non-private 16 copies: mean exposure 10.0 bits  extrapolated 13.0  extracted 0/3
non-private 64 copies: mean exposure 11.0 bits  extrapolated 16.3  extracted 3/3
non-private controls: mean exposure 1.4 bits  extrapolated 1.5  extracted 0/3
Ranking among 2,000 random candidates caps the measured exposure at 10.97 bits, below the 16.61 the whole space of secrets allows. So the measured column can never reach the blocking line 3 bits below that maximum. Only the extrapolated column can, by fitting a skew-normal distribution to the candidates’ scores and reading how far into its tail each secret lies. A random rank is worth \(\log_2 e = 1.44\) bits on average, and the controls’ 1.4 bits match it, so the measurement is sound. The one-copy canaries stay far below the line, at 2.0 bits. But greedy decoding writes out all three 64-copy secrets, so the non-private model fails Table 18.1 and must not be shared.
The 4-copy canaries show why you measure both, since two reach 6.9 and 8.2 bits yet neither is extracted. The DP run extracts nothing, but its most repeated canaries still average about 4 bits, against 2.2 for its controls. That is because \(\varepsilon\) protects one sequence, and a repeated secret is many sequences. So deduplicate before training, whatever else you do.
The usual failures are a canary format unlike your data, no controls, and ranking by a mean loss. For a release, also measure the share of training sequences that greedy decoding completes from their start, the discoverable rate, which the script skips (Memorization and training-data extraction).

title: 18  Pre-release privacy risk assessment
text:
18.6 Table: re-identification on quasi-identifiers
Quasi-identifiers are the columns an adversary can find elsewhere, such as age, sex and country in a register (Linkage and re-identification). Records that agree on all of them form an equivalence class, and a record alone in its class can be linked to a name. The table is Adult, a census extract from the UCI Machine Learning Repository, with 48,842 records and an agreed set of six columns, from age to education.
For each set of columns, the script prints the share of unique records and the share in classes smaller than 5. It also prints the smallest class size \(k\), and J/n, the number of classes per record (Linkage and re-identification shows the loop).
age + sex + race: unique=0.12%  in classes <5=0.75%  min k=1  J/n=0.012
age + sex + race + native-country: unique=3.07%  in classes <5=7.83%  min k=1  J/n=0.060
age + sex + race + native-country + marital-status + education: unique=14.64%  in classes <5=26.83%  min k=1  J/n=0.227
age + sex + race + native-country + marital-status + education + hours-per-week: unique=36.55%  in classes <5=57.05%  min k=1  J/n=0.480
On the agreed six, 14.64% of the records are unique, and hours per week, a column that looks harmless, raises that to 36.55%. So the list must include every column an adversary might hold, and when in doubt, test with the column added.
The standard remedy is to generalize: age into 10-year bands, country into United States or other, and education into four levels. The script then rechecks the classes and counts the distinct occupations in each, the distinct \(\ell\) of Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks, with occupation as the sensitive column.
after generalizing: unique=0.94%  in a class with one occupation=1.20%
age + sex + race + native-country + marital-status + education: unique=0.94%  in classes <5=3.31%  min k=1  J/n=0.032
age + sex + race + native-country + marital-status + education + hours-per-week: unique=10.09%  in classes <5=21.78%  min k=1  J/n=0.175
Generalizing cuts the unique share from 14.64% to 0.94%, but the smallest class still has one record, so the table still fails Table 18.1. Suppressing the classes smaller than 5 would remove 3.31% of the records. That would hold only for these columns, since raw hours per week makes 10.09% unique again. And 1.20% of the records sit in a class with a single occupation, which reveals it without any unique match.
These shares count uniqueness in the sample, which fits the prosecutor model, where the adversary knows the target is in the table. Otherwise, estimate population uniqueness (Linkage and re-identification).
Even a table that passes after suppression can be intersected with a second release of the same people (Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks). And k-anonymity says nothing against richer side information. So when a table cannot pass without losing its use, release statistics with DP, as Release statistics with a library does. Plain aggregates are no fallback, because many accurate counts let an attacker rebuild records (Reconstruction attacks).

title: 18  Pre-release privacy risk assessment
text:
18.7 Write the decision
The last step compares each result with its threshold and writes a release memo, Table 18.2. A reviewer who did not run the attacks must be able to check it, so it gives each estimated rate with its interval.



Table 18.2: A release memo for the three artefacts.

The residual-risk entry, the one most often left out, names the attacks that were not run. For a DP model the memo carries that guarantee and its evidence, which Release and governance assembles into the release package.

title: Differential privacy foundations
text:
Part 2 showed that anonymization and access control do not stop releases from leaking. This part introduces differential privacy (DP), the defence the rest of the book builds on. It is a property of the release process, not of a dataset. Changing one person’s data may change the probability of any output by at most a factor \(e^\varepsilon\), set by a privacy level \(\varepsilon\), plus a small slack \(\delta\). That one condition caps every attack of Part 2. So a DP claim must state \(\varepsilon\), \(\delta\) and what counts as one person’s data, the unit of privacy, such as a record or a user.



Table 1: Notation used throughout Part 3.









Symbol
Meaning




\(\varepsilon\), \(\delta\)

\(\Delta_1f\), \(\Delta_2f\)

The part teaches one workflow. First fix the unit of privacy and the neighbouring relation (the definition of differential privacy). Then bound each person’s contribution and calibrate a mechanism to it (The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms). Finally, account for every release, since only post-processing is free (Post-processing, group privacy and composition). The last page, Release statistics with a library, runs this workflow with OpenDP on a real shop’s invoices, from bounding each customer’s lines to the written guarantee.
The full chapters in between cover common tasks. Selection picks the best of many options or a private median, and Query release publishes many counts at once. Trust models apply when nobody can be trusted with the raw data, and Private mean estimation says how many records a private mean needs.
Four short reference pages cover the rest. Advanced composition and Beyond global sensitivity matter when the simple rules are too loose. Read Discrete mechanisms before you sample noise yourself, and Lower bounds before you promise an accuracy.
Part 4 then replaces hand composition with accountants, and Part 5 applies all of it to training models. The code here runs OpenDP and diffprivlib on the Adult census data and the UCI Online Retail invoices, and every number comes from a snippet or script you can run. By the end, you can release a count, a sum, a median or a table with error bars and a guarantee you can defend.

title: 19  The definition of differential privacy
text:
19.1 Why this matters
Every attack in Threat models and attacks runs an algorithm on one of two datasets that differ in one person, and guesses from the output which one was used. Differential privacy (DP) makes the two outputs look alike against every test, including tests nobody has invented yet. It is a property of the algorithm, not of the data, so you can check it before any data are touched, and read any claim of it for what it protects and what it leaves out.
crumbs: 19  The definition of differential privacy

title: 19  The definition of differential privacy
text:
19.2 Neighbouring datasets
The first question about any claim is what “differ in one record” means, and the neighbouring relation answers it. Under add/remove, two datasets are neighbours when one has a record the other lacks, so the guarantee hides whether a person is in the data at all. Under replace, they have the same size and differ in the value of one record, so only what the record says is hidden. A replacement is a removal followed by an addition, two steps that each cost the privacy level \(\varepsilon\) of Section 19.3, so \[\varepsilon\text{-DP under add/remove} \implies 2\varepsilon\text{-DP under replace}. \tag{19.1}\] The reverse fails, because replace never compares datasets of different sizes.
You also choose the unit of privacy, what one record is. At the example level, it is one training record or one event, and at the user level, all the data of one person. Under example-level DP, a user who wrote 200 messages is a group of 200 records, protected only at \(200\varepsilon\) (Post-processing, group privacy and composition). So check that the claim protects the person. The guarantee must also hide every record the data format allows, even a person aged 900, whose record could move an average a long way. So private algorithms clip each input to a fixed range before they add noise.
crumbs: 19  The definition of differential privacy

title: 19  The definition of differential privacy
text:
19.3 The definition
Call a randomized algorithm that takes a dataset and returns an output a mechanism, written \(M\), and write \(D\) for a dataset and \(D'\) for one of its neighbours. The definition asks that no set of outputs become more than a factor \(e^\varepsilon\) more likely when one record changes, up to a small additive slack \(\delta\). Here \(\varepsilon\) is a non-negative privacy parameter. A mechanism is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-differentially private if every pair of neighbours and every set \(S\) of outputs satisfy \[\Pr[M(D) \in S] \le e^\varepsilon\,\Pr[M(D') \in S] + \delta. \tag{19.2}\] The probabilities come only from the mechanism’s own randomness, with the data held fixed.
When \(\delta = 0\) the guarantee is called pure DP, and otherwise approximate DP. Either way, a private mechanism must be random. A deterministic one that answers differently on two neighbours gives that answer probability 1 on one and 0 on the other, which no factor \(e^\varepsilon\) covers. So rounding, aggregating or hiding small table cells gives no guarantee by itself.
crumbs: 19  The definition of differential privacy

title: 19  The definition of differential privacy
text:
19.4 The privacy loss and δ
For an output \(y\), write \(p_{M(D)}(y)\) for its probability, or its density, when the mechanism runs on \(D\). The privacy loss of \(y\) is the logarithm of how much more likely the output is on \(D\) than on \(D'\), \[L(y) = \ln\frac{p_{M(D)}(y)}{p_{M(D')}(y)}. \tag{19.3}\] Independent outputs multiply their likelihood ratios, so their losses add, which is why Part 4’s accountants work with the loss. Pure \(\varepsilon\)-DP holds exactly when every output has a loss between \(-\varepsilon\) and \(\varepsilon\). Laplace noise meets that, while the loss of Gaussian noise grows without limit in the far tail (The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms).
Under approximate DP, \(\delta\) pays for the outputs whose loss exceeds \(\varepsilon\). It counts only the part of each one’s probability on \(D\) above \(e^\varepsilon\) times its probability on \(D'\). So \(\delta\) is not the chance that the loss exceeds \(\varepsilon\), and the total is the hockey-stick divergence (Divergences). Each \(\varepsilon\) has its own smallest \(\delta\), and the function \(\delta(\varepsilon)\) is the mechanism’s privacy curve, of which a quoted pair is one point. The noise parameters fix the whole curve, so report them with the pair and others can recompute it (Numerical accounting).
crumbs: 19  The definition of differential privacy

title: 19  The definition of differential privacy
text:
19.5 Randomized response
In randomized response, a survey design, each person tells the truth with some probability \(t\) and lies otherwise, so a single answer proves nothing about them. A person who tosses a coin, answers truthfully on heads and answers by a second toss on tails tells the truth with probability \(\frac34\). The true answer is then three times as likely as the false one, which gives pure DP at \(\varepsilon = \ln 3\). In general, randomized response at level \(\varepsilon\) tells the truth with probability \[t = \frac{e^\varepsilon}{1 + e^\varepsilon}. \tag{19.4}\]
If the coins are independent, the guarantee is \(\varepsilon\) per person however many people answer, but only under replace, since under add/remove the number of reports reveals who answered. Write \(\bar y\) for the share of “yes” reports among the \(n\) people. Undoing the lies with \(t\) gives the estimate of the true fraction \(\pi\) and its standard deviation, \[\hat\pi = \frac{\bar y - (1 - t)}{2t - 1}, \qquad \operatorname{sd}(\hat\pi) = \frac{e^{\varepsilon/2}}{(e^\varepsilon - 1)\sqrt n}. \tag{19.5}\] For 1,000 people the two-coin scheme has a standard deviation of 0.0274. When the true fraction is 0.3, that is about twice the sampling error of 0.0145 the survey already has. This doubling is the price of the local model, in which nobody sees a true answer (Local, shuffle and distributed trust models).
OpenDP builds the mechanism from its truth probability, here the two-coin 0.75, and map turns one changed answer into its \(\varepsilon\), \(\ln 3\). The contrib feature switches on mechanisms not yet formally vetted.
import opendp.prelude as dp

dp.enable_features("contrib")
rr = dp.m.make_randomized_response_bool(prob=0.75)
print(f"{rr.map(1):.4f}")  # 1.0986
crumbs: 19  The definition of differential privacy

title: 19  The definition of differential privacy
section: 19.6 What ε means for an attacker
text:
19.6 What ε means for an attacker
A membership attacker looks at the output and decides whether to accuse the target of being in the data, so it has two error rates (Hypothesis testing). Its false positive rate (FPR) is how often it accuses a target who is out, and its true positive rate (TPR) how often it accuses one who is in. The outputs on which it accuses form a set, which the definition bounds, so under add/remove every attack satisfies \[\mathrm{TPR} \le e^\varepsilon\,\mathrm{FPR} + \delta. \tag{19.6}\]
This is the form to use, because Part 2 judged attacks by their TPR at a low FPR. Take \(\varepsilon = 1\) and the \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) that Section 19.7 recommends for 10,000 people. At an FPR of \(10^{-3}\), no attack reaches a TPR above \(e \cdot 10^{-3} + 10^{-5} = 0.002728\). As the FPR falls towards 0, the first term vanishes, so at a very low FPR the guarantee rests almost entirely on \(\delta\).
Read backwards, the cap turns a measured attack into a lower bound on \(\varepsilon\), \[\varepsilon \ge \ln\frac{\mathrm{TPR} - \delta}{\mathrm{FPR}}. \tag{19.7}\] Suppose a model is claimed to be \((2, 10^{-5})\)-DP, and an attack reaches a TPR of 0.05 at an FPR of 0.001. If those rates were exact, \(\varepsilon\) would be at least about \(\ln 50 = 3.91\), and the claim false. A real audit puts confidence bounds on the rates and plants a canary, a record built to be as easy to detect as possible (Auditing).
Two summaries are easier to explain to a lawyer. The first, the membership advantage, is the TPR minus the FPR, how much better than a coin flip an attacker does. Under \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP it is at most \[\mathrm{TPR} - \mathrm{FPR} \le \frac{e^\varepsilon - 1 + 2\delta}{e^\varepsilon + 1}. \tag{19.8}\]
The second, the posterior bound, speaks about beliefs. Under pure DP, one output can multiply an adversary’s odds between two neighbours by at most \(e^\varepsilon\). So a prior belief \(p\) that the data are \(D\) rises at most to \[\Pr[D \mid y] \le \frac{e^\varepsilon p}{e^\varepsilon p + 1 - p}. \tag{19.9}\] Table 19.1 turns a claimed \(\varepsilon\) into both numbers.

Between 1 and 10 a claim needs the mechanism’s privacy curve as justification, and above 10, where the bounds promise almost nothing, an audit as well (Choosing ε). For statistics, start from the error you can accept and solve it for \(\varepsilon\) (The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms). The table is for pure DP, so for an \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) claim quote the advantage bound and the cap on the TPR, which both include \(\delta\).
crumbs: 19  The definition of differential privacy

title: 19  The definition of differential privacy
text:
19.7 How small δ must be
A small \(\delta\) barely moves the advantage bound, but the advantage averages over everyone, so it can hide total harm to a few people. Take a mechanism that publishes each record in full, independently with probability \(\delta\). Under add/remove it is \((0, \delta)\)-DP, because a record changes the output only when its own coin publishes it. Yet over \(n\) records it publishes at least one with probability \[1 - (1 - \delta)^n \approx 1 - e^{-n\delta}. \tag{19.10}\] With 10,000 records and \(\delta = 1/n\), that is \(1 - e^{-1} = 0.6321\).
So treat \(\delta\) as a per-person budget for catastrophe, which may be spent on total failures like these. This book’s default keeps \(n\delta\), the expected number of people exposed this way, well below 1. Let \(n\) count people rather than records, and choose \[\delta \le \frac{1}{n^{1.1}}, \tag{19.11}\] rounded down to a power of ten. For 10,000 people the rule gives \(10^{-5}\). The publishing mechanism then has \(n\delta = 0.1\) and exposes someone with probability only 0.0952.
crumbs: 19  The definition of differential privacy

title: 19  The definition of differential privacy
section: 19.8 What differential privacy does not protect
text:
19.8 What differential privacy does not protect
DP compares a world with your record and a world without it, so anything that can be learned in both worlds is outside the guarantee. A study that never used Alice’s record may show that smokers get cancer at a high rate, which changes what anyone believes about Alice, a smoker, yet the study is 0-DP with respect to her. So a reported harm is a DP violation only if the inference would differ materially without the person’s record. Correlated records are a second gap: a household of five that always answers alike is a group of five, unless the household is the unit of privacy. The third gap is the implementation, which needs its own review (Discrete and floating-point-safe mechanisms).
crumbs: 19  The definition of differential privacy

title: 19  The definition of differential privacy
text:
19.9 Writing the guarantee down
A reviewer can check only what a claim writes down. So a guarantee names the unit of privacy with its neighbouring relation, and \(\varepsilon\) and \(\delta\) for the whole release rather than per query. It also names the mechanism, the library version, the trust model and what was treated as public, since public information is not protected. This example uses the central model, in which a trusted curator holds the raw data and adds the noise:

This release satisfies \((1, 10^{-5})\)-DP for adding or removing one customer and all their invoice lines, at most 100 per customer, under the central model, with Gaussian noise from OpenDP 0.16.0. The market list was fixed in advance.

Release statistics with a library and Release and governance print such statements from the code that made the release.

title: 20  Post-processing, group privacy and composition
text:
20.1 Why this matters
A private mechanism is never the whole system. Its output gets rounded or fed into a model, people own many records each, and an analyst rarely asks only one question. Three properties of differential privacy (DP) say what guarantee then holds, without a new proof for every pipeline. Post-processing makes anything computed from a private output free, group privacy covers a person with several records, and composition adds up the budgets of several mechanisms. Together they turn privacy into bookkeeping: you prove each building block once, then keep a ledger of what you spend.
crumbs: 20  Post-processing, group privacy and composition

title: 20  Post-processing, group privacy and composition
text:
20.2 Post-processing
Take an \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP mechanism \(M\), with privacy level \(\varepsilon\) and slack \(\delta\). Apply to its output any function \(f\), which may use randomness of its own but never reads the data. Then the processed release is just as private, \[f(M(D)) \text{ is } (\varepsilon, \delta)\text{-DP}. \tag{20.1}\] Processing can blur the evidence that an output carries about the data, but it can never sharpen it.
So rounding a noisy count, clamping it at zero, or adjusting noisy subtotals to match their noisy total costs nothing. A private system therefore adds noise at one narrow point, such as counts or gradients, and treats everything after it as public. The rule covers attackers too, because a membership-inference attack is a function of the output. So the definition’s cap on how often any attack succeeds holds even for attacks invented after the release.
The condition is that \(f\) never reads the data. “Take the noisy top category, then report its exact count” breaks it, because the second step is a new and non-private mechanism.
crumbs: 20  Post-processing, group privacy and composition

title: 20  Post-processing, group privacy and composition
text:
20.3 Group privacy
The definition protects one record, but a customer of an online shop has dozens of invoice lines. For a person who owns \(k\) records, you need a guarantee for datasets that differ in \(k\) records. You can walk from one such dataset to the other by changing one record at a time, at a cost of \(\varepsilon\) per step. So under pure DP, where \(\delta = 0\), \(\varepsilon\)-DP per record becomes \(k\varepsilon\)-DP for the group. The slack grows much faster than \(k\). For a group of \(k\) records, an \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP mechanism is \[\Big(k\varepsilon,\ \delta_k\Big)\text{-DP}, \qquad \delta_k = \delta\,\frac{e^{k\varepsilon} - 1}{e^\varepsilon - 1} \le k\,e^{(k-1)\varepsilon}\delta. \tag{20.2}\]
The form on the right is a simpler, looser bound. With \(\varepsilon = 0.5\) and \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) per record, a person with 10 records gets a slack of \(2.272\times10^{-3}\). That hurts, because \(\delta\) was chosen far below one over the number of people (How small δ must be).
OpenDP computes group guarantees from the mechanism itself. A measurement’s map(d_in=k) is its guarantee when neighbouring datasets differ in \(k\) records, here for a count with Laplace noise and one with Gaussian noise.
count = dp.t.make_count(dp.vector_domain(dp.atom_domain(T=int)), dp.symmetric_distance())
laplace = count >> dp.m.then_laplace(scale=2.0)  # epsilon = 0.5 per record
print(f"Laplace count: epsilon {laplace.map(d_in=1):.1f} per record, {laplace.map(d_in=10):.1f} for 10")

def gaussian(scale: float) -> dp.Measurement:  # a Gaussian count, as a privacy curve
    return dp.c.make_zCDP_to_approxDP(count >> dp.m.then_gaussian(scale=scale))

def at_1e5(scale: float) -> dp.Measurement:
    return dp.c.make_fix_delta(gaussian(scale), delta=1e-5)

scale = dp.binary_search_param(at_1e5, d_in=1, d_out=(0.5, 1e-5))  # (0.5, 1e-5) per record
curve = gaussian(scale).map(d_in=10)  # the privacy curve for a group of 10 records
print(f"Gaussian count, group of 10: epsilon {curve.epsilon(1e-5):.2f} at delta 1e-5")
# delta_k is the slack that the group-privacy formula gives the group
print(f"Gaussian count, group of 10: epsilon {curve.epsilon(delta_k):.2f} at delta {delta_k:.3e}")
Laplace count: epsilon 0.5 per record, 5.0 for 10
Gaussian count, group of 10: epsilon 6.43 at delta 1e-5
Gaussian count, group of 10: epsilon 4.57 at delta 2.272e-03
For the Laplace count, map(d_in=10) gives \(k\varepsilon = 5.0\), as the formula does. The Gaussian count, calibrated to \((0.5, 10^{-5})\) per record, does better, because OpenDP reads the group’s guarantee off the mechanism’s whole privacy curve. At the formula’s slack of \(2.272\times10^{-3}\) the group gets \(\varepsilon = 4.57\), below the formula’s 5.0. So read a group guarantee off the library’s map, and fall back on the formula only for a mechanism the library cannot map.
Better still, if you care about people, make the person the unit of privacy, so that neighbouring datasets differ in all of one person’s records. Then bound how many records each person may contribute before any noise is added, as Release statistics with a library does on real data. Group privacy is the fallback when you cannot, and for records of different people that reveal each other, such as a household that shares an address and an income.
crumbs: 20  Post-processing, group privacy and composition

title: 20  Post-processing, group privacy and composition
text:
20.4 Sequential composition
An analyst asks several queries of the same data, each answered with fresh noise, and an adversary sees all the answers together. Say there are \(k\) mechanisms, and write \((\varepsilon_i, \delta_i)\) for the budget of the \(i\)-th. Releasing all their outputs is then \[\Big(\sum_{i=1}^k\varepsilon_i,\ \sum_{i=1}^k\delta_i\Big)\text{-DP}. \tag{20.3}\] This is basic composition. It needs every mechanism to draw fresh noise and to use the same neighbouring relation, add/remove or replace.
The rule also covers adaptive composition, where each query is chosen after reading the earlier answers, as long as each budget is fixed in advance. A budget chosen from the answers (“keep going until the estimate looks good”) needs a privacy filter, a rule that decides when to stop (Adaptive composition).
Basic composition is loose for many releases. Ten Gaussian counts, each calibrated to \((0.5, 10^{-5})\), are charged \((5, 10^{-4})\), but at that slack their exact \(\varepsilon\) is only 1.504. So beyond a handful of releases, use an accountant, which computes the total from the mechanisms themselves (Advanced and optimal composition, Part 4).
crumbs: 20  Post-processing, group privacy and composition

title: 20  Post-processing, group privacy and composition
text:
20.5 Parallel composition
Per-region statistics use disjoint subsets of the data. When each person has one record, that record falls in one region only, so each region can spend the full budget. To use this, fix in advance a public rule that sends every possible record to exactly one part. Then run a mechanism \(M_i\) with independent noise on the \(i\)-th part. If each \(M_i\) is \((\varepsilon_i, \delta_i)\)-DP under add/remove, the whole release is \[\big(\max_i\varepsilon_i,\ \max_i\delta_i\big)\text{-DP under add/remove}. \tag{20.4}\]
So a histogram with Laplace noise of scale \(1/\varepsilon\) on every bin is \(\varepsilon\)-DP however many bins it has. Under replace, a record can move from one bin to another, so two bins change and the cost doubles to \(2\varepsilon\). A person with records in several bins breaks the rule too. Then either charge each bin as a separate query, or first bound the number of bins a person may touch.
The rule fixed in advance is the condition that is easiest to break. A split into “the top 10% of earners and the rest” moves its boundary when one high earner is added, so both parts change. Partitioning on the keys that appear in the data fails too, because a key present only through one person’s record reveals that person. So use fixed bins or a public key list. When the keys are not public, release only the keys whose noisy count clears a threshold, a step called partition selection (Release statistics with a library).
crumbs: 20  Post-processing, group privacy and composition

title: 20  Post-processing, group privacy and composition
text:
20.6 Keeping a budget
Fix a total budget for a dataset before the first release, and charge every release against it. In the Python library diffprivlib, a BudgetAccountant holds the total, and each function you hand it charges its own \(\varepsilon\) and \(\delta\). A call that would exceed the total raises a BudgetError instead of answering. The script practitioner_adult_statistics.py runs it on the Adult census data, 48,842 people with one row each, for which the default slack is \(10^{-6}\). It spends half the budget on the mean age and half on the number of people over 50, then asks for one more count.
age = adult["age"].to_numpy()
acc = BudgetAccountant(epsilon=1.0, delta=1e-6)  # the total, fixed in advance
mean_age = tools.mean(age, epsilon=0.5, bounds=(17, 90), accountant=acc, random_state=seed)
over_50 = tools.count_nonzero(age > 50, epsilon=0.5, accountant=acc, random_state=seed)
print(f"private mean age: {mean_age:.2f}  private count over 50: {over_50:,}")
print(f"spent: {acc.total()}")
try:
    tools.count_nonzero(age > 60, epsilon=0.1, accountant=acc, random_state=seed)
except BudgetError as err:
    print(f"refused: {err}")
Run it with uv run python code/part03-dp-foundations/practitioner_adult_statistics.py. With random_state=0 it prints the following.
private mean age: 38.64  private count over 50: 9,813
spent: (epsilon=1.0, delta=0.0)
refused: Privacy spend of (0.1,0) not permissible; will exceed remaining privacy budget. Use BudgetAccountant.remaining() to check remaining budget.
The true values are 38.64 and 9,808. Both calls add Laplace noise, so no \(\delta\) was spent and the \(10^{-6}\) stays available for a Gaussian query. The ledger has two limits. It applies basic composition to every call, so it overcharges calls on disjoint parts of the data. And it trusts each call’s own guarantee: diffprivlib’s mean divides by the exact number of rows, treating it as public. That number is public only when neighbours have the same size, so this ledger holds under replace neighbours.
Most real failures break a condition of the three properties, and the damage is usually total rather than a small loss. Table 20.1 lists the common cases.



Table 20.1: What composes and what doesn’t.










Situation
Composes?
What to do




A function of the output, with its own coins
Yes, for free
Process as much as you like


Another query on the same data, fresh noise
Yes, budgets add
Charge it to the ledger


A query chosen from earlier answers
Yes, budgets add
Fix its budget in advance


Two releases that share one noise draw
No
Draw fresh noise for every query


“Post-processing” that reads the data again
No
Charge it as a new mechanism


A DP release beside an exact statistic of the same data
No, the exact one has no guarantee
Release the statistic privately too


A split whose boundaries depend on the data
No, not in parallel
Fix the bins in advance


Guarantees under add/remove and replace in one ledger
Only after conversion
Convert to replace: \(2\varepsilon\) and \((1 + e^\varepsilon)\delta\)






Shared noise is the clearest case. Release the number of smokers and the number of smokers aged 40 or over, adding the same Laplace draw of scale 1 to both. Each release alone is 1-DP, but their difference cancels the noise and gives the exact number of smokers under 40, so the pair is not DP at all. In code, the bug hides in two mechanisms with the same random seed, a cached noise value re-added to a related query, or noise reused across shards. A fixed seed such as random_state=0 above reproduces a book’s numbers, but in production it makes the noise reproducible and so removable. Returning the same noisy answer to a repeated identical query is fine, because that is post-processing of one release.

Never share a random seed between mechanisms, and never fix one in production.

title: 21  The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms
text:
21.1 Why this matters
Suppose a hospital wants to publish how many of its patients have diabetes, with a differential privacy (DP) guarantee. Almost every such release, and every noisy gradient of private training, is built with one of the two mechanisms of this chapter. Both compute the exact answer of a query \(f\) on the dataset \(D\), then add fresh random noise, written \(Z\), and publish \[M(D) = f(D) + Z. \tag{21.1}\] Three decisions fix such a mechanism. The sensitivity, how far one record can move the answer, is what the noise must hide. The noise distribution sets the kind of guarantee: Laplace noise gives pure DP, while Gaussian noise needs a small slack \(\delta\). And a calibration formula sets the amount of noise for a target \(\varepsilon\), through the privacy loss of the definition of differential privacy.
crumbs: 21  The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms

title: 21  The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms
text:
21.2 Sensitivity
The noise must cover the largest change one record can make to the answer. A query often returns a vector of \(d\) numbers, such as the bins of a histogram, so the change needs a size. Laplace noise uses the \(\ell_1\) norm, the sum of the absolute changes, and Gaussian noise the \(\ell_2\) norm, the square root of the sum of the squared changes. Writing \(D \sim D'\) for a pair of neighbours, the \(\ell_p\) sensitivity of the query is the largest change between their answers, \[\Delta_pf = \max_{D \sim D'}\big\|f(D) - f(D')\big\|_p, \qquad p \in \{1, 2\}. \tag{21.2}\] The two are equal when one record moves a single coordinate, but when it moves all \(d\) of them, \(\Delta_1f\) can be \(\sqrt d\) times \(\Delta_2f\).
The sensitivity also depends on the neighbouring relation. Under add/remove one dataset has one record more than the other, while under replace one record is swapped for another, so the size \(n\) is public. Write \(B\) for the largest value a record may take after clipping. Then Table 21.1 gives the standard queries.

Unbounded data have infinite sensitivity, so clip every value to a fixed range first. With ages clipped to at most 100, the mean age of 1,000 patients has sensitivity \(B/n = 0.1\) under replace.
crumbs: 21  The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms

title: 21  The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms
text:
21.3 The Laplace mechanism
The Laplace mechanism adds independent noise from the Laplace distribution, a two-sided exponential peaked at 0, to each coordinate. Its scale \(b\) sets its typical size, and \(\mathrm{Lap}(b)\) denotes it. For an \(\varepsilon\)-DP guarantee, the scale is the sensitivity divided by \(\varepsilon\), \[b = \frac{\Delta_1f}{\varepsilon}. \tag{21.3}\]
The error of the mechanism is the noise itself. Each coordinate of the noise is off by \(b\) on average, and exceeds a distance \(t\) with probability \(e^{-t/b}\). Allow a small failure probability \(\beta\) for all \(d\) coordinates together, and give each coordinate a share \(\beta/d\) of it. The width that holds for all of them is then \[\Pr\Big[\max_i|Z_i| > b\ln\frac d\beta\Big] \le \beta. \tag{21.4}\] Publish this width with the release. Read backwards, it is an error budget: for a single number, fix a target width \(t\) and solve for the privacy level, \[\varepsilon = \frac{\Delta_1f\,\ln(1/\beta)}{t}. \tag{21.5}\] So a count that must be within 10 of the truth with probability 0.95 needs \(\varepsilon = \ln(20)/10 = 0.2996\). For \(d\) numbers, solve each with the failure probability \(\beta/d\), and add up their \(\varepsilon\) by composition.
At the hospital, 1,234 of the 10,000 patients have diabetes. A count has sensitivity 1 under add/remove, so at \(\varepsilon = 0.1\) the noise is \(\mathrm{Lap}(10)\). Its 95% error bar is \(10\ln 20 = 29.96\), or 2.43% of the count.
The scale does not depend on the size of the data, so the relative error of a count of size \(n\) is about \(1/(n\varepsilon)\). But the sensitivity must include every number one record can move. If one record can change all of 10 released counts, noise calibrated for one count makes the release \(10\varepsilon\)-DP, not \(\varepsilon\)-DP.
crumbs: 21  The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms

title: 21  The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms
text:
21.4 The Gaussian mechanism
The Gaussian mechanism adds independent normal noise with mean 0 and standard deviation \(\sigma\) to each coordinate. Its privacy loss is unbounded in the far tail, so it always carries a \(\delta\). In exchange, it is calibrated to the \(\ell_2\) sensitivity, which can be much smaller than the \(\ell_1\) one. Only the ratio of the sensitivity to the noise matters, so write \(\mu = \Delta_2f/\sigma\) for the number of noise standard deviations between the answers on two neighbours. Write \(\Phi\) for the cumulative distribution function (CDF) of the standard normal distribution. The mechanism is then \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP exactly when \(\delta\) is at least \[\delta_\mu(\varepsilon) = \Phi\Big(\frac\mu2 - \frac\varepsilon\mu\Big) - e^\varepsilon\,\Phi\Big(-\frac\mu2 - \frac\varepsilon\mu\Big). \tag{21.6}\]
This formula is how you calibrate. As \(\mu\) grows, the exact \(\delta\) rises steadily from 0 to 1, so exactly one value \(\mu^*\) hits your target. The smallest noise that works is then \[\sigma^* = \frac{\Delta_2f}{\mu^*}, \qquad \text{where } \delta_{\mu^*}(\varepsilon) = \delta, \tag{21.7}\] and libraries solve for \(\mu^*\) for you (Section 21.7). For 10,000 patients the book’s default slack is \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) (The definition of differential privacy). At \(\varepsilon = 1\) this analytic calibration then gives \(\sigma^* = 3.7306\,\Delta_2f\).
Many papers and libraries still use the classic calibration of Dwork and Roth (2014), proved only for \(\varepsilon\) and \(\delta\) both between 0 and 1, \[\sigma = \frac{\Delta_2f\sqrt{2\ln(1.25/\delta)}}{\varepsilon}. \tag{21.8}\] At \(\varepsilon = 1\) and \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) it gives \(4.8448\,\Delta_2f\), 30% more noise than the analytic \(3.7306\,\Delta_2f\). Above \(\varepsilon = 1\) it has no proof behind it, and beyond \(\varepsilon = 8.42\) it gives too little noise for the claimed guarantee. So use the analytic calibration.
A Gaussian mechanism satisfies a whole curve of guarantees, one \(\delta\) for each \(\varepsilon\), and the accountants of Part 4 compose whole curves. So report \(\sigma/\Delta_2f\) with every Gaussian release, as well as the pair you chose.
Back at the hospital, Gaussian noise for the diabetes count at \(\varepsilon = 0.1\) and \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) gives a 95% error bar of 60.27, which is 1.96 standard deviations. Laplace noise gave 29.96 with no \(\delta\) at all, so for a single count it wins on both error and guarantee.
crumbs: 21  The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms

title: 21  The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms
text:
21.5 Laplace or Gaussian?
The choice depends on how one record spreads its change across the coordinates. To see why, compare the root-mean-square error (RMSE) of each released number at the same \(\varepsilon\). Laplace noise of scale \(b = \Delta_1f/\varepsilon\) has standard deviation \(\sqrt2\,b\). Write \(\sigma_1\) for the analytic Gaussian noise level at unit \(\ell_2\) sensitivity. The errors per coordinate are then \[\text{Laplace: } \frac{\sqrt2\,\Delta_1f}{\varepsilon}, \qquad \text{Gaussian: } \Delta_2f\,\sigma_1. \tag{21.9}\]
In a sparse query, such as a histogram under add/remove, one record moves one coordinate, so the two sensitivities are equal. At \(\varepsilon = 1\) and the default \(\delta\), \(\sigma_1 = 3.7306\), so Laplace noise wins at every \(d\), since \(\sqrt2 = 1.4142\) is smaller. In a dense query, such as the threshold counts, one record moves every coordinate, so the Laplace error grows like \(d\) and the Gaussian error only like \(\sqrt d\). Laplace noise is then more accurate only while \[d < \frac{(\varepsilon\sigma_1)^2}2, \tag{21.10}\] so with \(\sigma_1 = 3.7306\), Gaussian noise wins for threshold counts from 7 counts on.
Gaussian noise also wins under heavy composition, because several Gaussian releases compose exactly into one Gaussian mechanism, with the root of the summed squared sensitivities. Private training has both, since one record’s gradient moves every coordinate of a model at every step. So it clips each gradient’s \(\ell_2\) norm and calibrates Gaussian noise to that clip.
crumbs: 21  The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms

title: 21  The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms
text:
21.6 Calibrating a release
Every noisy release takes five steps.

Fix the neighbouring relation and the unit of privacy, usually one person under add/remove.
Clip every value to a range fixed in advance, and read the sensitivity off Table 21.1 or work it out from the worst record.
Choose Laplace noise for one number or a sparse vector, and Gaussian noise for a dense vector.
Set the scale with Equation 21.3 or Equation 21.6, and charge it to your budget (Post-processing, group privacy and composition).
Draw the noise with a vetted library, and publish the error bar and the noise parameters with the result.

A mean under add/remove has no simple sensitivity, because its denominator moves too. So release a noisy sum and a noisy count, each with half of the budget, and divide one by the other, which as post-processing costs nothing more. For the mean’s error bar, take each one’s bar at 97.5%, so that both hold together 95% of the time. The mean then lies above the sum’s lower end divided by the count’s upper end. It lies below the sum’s upper end divided by the count’s lower end, provided both lower ends are positive. OpenDP’s .dp.mean makes the same split, and summarize(alpha=0.025) reports the two bars at 97.5%. When you do not know the range to clip to, Private mean estimation finds it privately.
Plain numpy.random.laplace is for prototypes only, because textbook floating-point samplers can leak through the low-order bits of their output (Discrete and floating-point-safe mechanisms). For a whole release with clipping, grouping and one budget, follow Release statistics with a library.
crumbs: 21  The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms

title: 21  The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms
text:
21.7 Code
The snippet checks the hospital’s numbers and the analytic \(\sigma^*\) at \(\varepsilon = 1\). In OpenDP, a mechanism’s map takes the sensitivity and returns the \(\varepsilon\) it costs, and the accuracy helpers turn a scale into a 95% error bar or back. For a count, with sensitivity 1, one over that scale is the \(\varepsilon\) of the error budget. IBM’s diffprivlib calibrates the analytic Gaussian.
import math

import opendp.prelude as dp
from diffprivlib.mechanisms import GaussianAnalytic

dp.enable_features("contrib")
laplace = dp.m.make_laplace(dp.atom_domain(T=float, nan=False), dp.absolute_distance(T=float), scale=10.0)
print(laplace.map(1.0))  # 0.1
print(f"{dp.laplacian_scale_to_accuracy(10.0, alpha=0.05):.2f}")  # 29.96
print(f"{1 / dp.accuracy_to_laplacian_scale(10.0, alpha=0.05):.4f}")  # 0.2996
gauss = GaussianAnalytic(epsilon=1.0, delta=1e-5, sensitivity=1.0)
print(f"{math.sqrt(gauss.variance(0.0)):.4f}")  # 3.7306
To add the noise, call the mechanism on the value, as in laplace(1234.0).

title: 22  Advanced and optimal composition
text:
22.1 What it is
A dashboard refreshes a hundred counts, and a training run takes thousands of noisy steps, yet you report one differential privacy (DP) guarantee for the whole run. Each step has its own privacy level \(\varepsilon\) and slack \(\delta\) (The definition of differential privacy). Basic composition adds them, so a run of \(k\) steps costs \(k\varepsilon\) and \(k\delta\) (Post-processing, group privacy and composition). That is correct but pessimistic. The steps’ privacy losses add up, but each depends on the noise drawn and is often negative, so their sum almost never reaches \(k\varepsilon\).
Advanced composition (Dwork, Rothblum & Vadhan 2010) uses this cancellation. For an extra slack \(\delta'\) that you pick for the whole run, the steps are together \((\varepsilon_{\mathrm{total}}, k\delta + \delta')\)-DP, with \[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{total}} = \varepsilon\sqrt{2k\ln(1/\delta')} + k\varepsilon\tanh(\varepsilon/2). \tag{22.1}\] The first term is the spread of the total loss, which grows only like \(\sqrt k\). The second is its average, the drift.
Optimal composition (Kairouz, Oh & Viswanath 2015) is the exact best bound for steps known only by their \((\varepsilon, \delta)\). Take a hundred counts at \(\varepsilon = 0.1\) each, with no slack, on 10,000 people. Basic composition gives a total of 10, still with no slack. The other two rules spend the book’s default slack for 10,000 people, \(\delta' = 10^{-5}\), and give 5.30 and 4.31.

title: 22  Advanced and optimal composition
text:
22.2 When you meet it
You meet these rules in papers, privacy reviews and any library that quotes a total \(\varepsilon\) for many steps. They decide which number you plan with and which you report (Table 22.1).

“Optimal” means optimal for steps described by one pair each. A real mechanism has a whole privacy curve, one \(\delta\) for every \(\varepsilon\), and a single pair forgets the rest of it. A thousand Gaussian steps with noise standard deviation 20 on a query of sensitivity 1 are exactly \((7.51, 10^{-5})\)-DP when composed as curves. Summarizing each step by its best single pair and composing optimally gives 62.7, about eight times worse. So whenever you know the mechanism, compose its curve with an accountant (Privacy accounting).

title: 22  Advanced and optimal composition
text:
22.3 How to use it
Composition does two jobs. The first is planning: to split a total budget \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{total}}\) over \(k\) steps, run advanced composition backwards. When \(\varepsilon\sqrt k\) is small the second term, the drift, is negligible, so each step can have about \[\varepsilon \approx \frac{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{total}}}{\sqrt{2k\ln(1/\delta')}}. \tag{22.2}\] Once \(\varepsilon\sqrt k\) nears 1, the drift takes over and this shortcut gives each step too much.
The second job is reporting. When you know the mechanism, report the accountant’s number at the run’s total \(\delta\), and otherwise report optimal composition. This snippet plans the hundred counts within a total of \((1, 10^{-5})\), giving the whole slack to \(\delta'\). It then reports the thousand Gaussian steps with two accountants of Google’s dp_accounting, based on the privacy loss distribution (PLD) and on Rényi differential privacy (RDP).
import math

import dp_accounting

print(f"{1.0 / math.sqrt(2 * 100 * math.log(1e5)):.4f}")  # 0.0208
step = dp_accounting.GaussianDpEvent(noise_multiplier=20.0)
run = dp_accounting.SelfComposedDpEvent(step, 1000)
pld = dp_accounting.pld.PLDAccountant()
pld.compose(run)
print(f"{pld.get_epsilon(target_delta=1e-5):.2f}")  # 7.51
rdp = dp_accounting.rdp.RdpAccountant()
rdp.compose(run)
print(f"{rdp.get_epsilon(target_delta=1e-5):.2f}")  # 8.08
Each count gets 0.0208, twice basic composition’s \(1/100\). The PLD accountant matches the exact 7.51 quoted above, and the RDP accountant gives a valid but looser 8.08 (Choosing an accountant).

title: 22  Advanced and optimal composition
text:
22.4 What goes wrong
For a few steps, advanced composition can lose to basic composition, so always take the smaller of the two. Every rule also adds up the steps’ slacks, so count each \(\delta\). And when the steps have different privacy levels, optimal composition is computationally hard, one more reason to use an accountant.
All these rules hold when each query depends on earlier answers, provided each step’s budget is fixed in advance. Choosing the budgets from the answers needs a privacy filter (Adaptive composition), and stopping early needs care. A stopping rule that reads only the noisy answers is post-processing, so the run costs no more than its planned length. But a run that stops when the true count of some group crosses a threshold reveals that count through its length. Every answer can then be \(\varepsilon\)-DP while the whole run is not DP for any finite \(\varepsilon\).
So, for a reviewer, a total below optimal composition is a red flag unless an accountant computed it from the mechanism’s curve.
Derivations. Every result here is derived step by step in the full edition’s chapter.

title: 23  Selection: exponential mechanism, report-noisy-max, sparse vector
text:
23.1 Why this matters
Many questions ask you to pick something rather than compute a number, such as the best model on a validation set, a median, or the first alarm among many statistics. Publishing every candidate’s score with Laplace noise would charge the budget once per candidate, because the budgets of separate releases add. The mechanisms of this chapter instead release the position, not the values. One record can change which candidate wins only a little, however many candidates there are. So under differential privacy (DP), a selection costs as much as a single query, and the number of candidates enters only the accuracy, through its logarithm.

title: 23  Selection: exponential mechanism, report-noisy-max, sparse vector
text:
23.3 The exponential mechanism
The candidates form a fixed set, written \(\mathcal R\). Each candidate \(r\) has a score on the dataset \(D\), written \(u(D, r)\), such as the number of validation records a model gets right. The exponential mechanism of McSherry and Talwar (2007) picks each candidate with probability proportional to an exponential of its score. With a privacy budget \(\varepsilon\), it outputs candidate \(r\) with probability \[\Pr[M_E(D) = r] = \frac{\exp\big(\varepsilon\,u(D, r)/(2\Delta u)\big)}{\sum_s\exp\big(\varepsilon\,u(D, s)/(2\Delta u)\big)}. \tag{23.1}\] It is \(\varepsilon\)-DP because one record changes each weight, and also their sum, by at most a factor \(e^{\varepsilon/2}\), which makes \(e^\varepsilon\) for their ratio.
Two conditions decide whether a use is correct. First, fix the list of candidates before you look at the data, because a list built from the data reveals records by itself, as a word in a corpus’s vocabulary does when only one person used it. Second, drop the 2 in the exponent only when the scores are monotone, meaning that one record pushes all of them the same way. Counts under add/remove neighbours are monotone. A histogram under replace neighbours is not, because moving one record lowers one count and raises another, so dropping the 2 there doubles the real cost.
crumbs: 23  Selection: exponential mechanism, report-noisy-max, sparse vector

title: 23  Selection: exponential mechanism, report-noisy-max, sparse vector
section: 23.4 Accuracy, and the cost of many candidates
text:
23.4 Accuracy, and the cost of many candidates
The number of candidates \(|\mathcal R|\) is free for privacy but not for accuracy, because more candidates means more bad ones to pick. Call the best score minus the chosen candidate’s score the gap. On average it is at most \[\frac{2\Delta u}{\varepsilon}(\ln|\mathcal R| + 1), \tag{23.2}\] so doubling the candidates adds only \(\ln 2\) to the bracket.
Suppose you trained 50 models and want to release the best one, judged on a private validation set of 1,000 records. Model \(r\), numbered from 1, gets \(900 - r\) records right, so model 1 is the best. The score is that count, which one record moves by at most 1, so \(\Delta u = 1\). At \(\varepsilon = 1\) the mechanism picks the best model only 39% of the time. Yet it loses just 1.54 correct predictions on average, or 0.15% accuracy, because its mistakes are mostly near-ties. Hyperparameter tuning picks models this way.
crumbs: 23  Selection: exponential mechanism, report-noisy-max, sparse vector

title: 23  Selection: exponential mechanism, report-noisy-max, sparse vector
section: 23.5 A private quantile or clipping norm
text:
23.5 A private quantile or clipping norm
Reading a median or a clipping norm off the data leaks it, so pick it with the exponential mechanism. First fix a range before looking at the data, and clip every record into it. The mechanism then scores each point of the range by how close the share of records below it is to the quantile you want, such as one half for the median, and one added or removed record moves any score by at most 1. The score stays the same between consecutive sorted records. So the mechanism picks one of these intervals, called pieces, favouring long pieces near the quantile, and returns a uniform point inside it.
diffprivlib’s tools.quantile and tools.median take an epsilon and the range as bounds. OpenDP’s .dp.quantile and .dp.median, which work on Polars data frames, pick one value from a finite list of candidates instead. The script practitioner_adult_statistics.py takes the median age of the Adult census data, 48,842 people with one row each, at \(\varepsilon = 1\). The range of 17 to 90 comes from the survey’s documentation.
age = adult["age"].to_numpy()
private = tools.median(age, epsilon=1.0, bounds=(17, 90), random_state=seed)
print(f"true median age: {np.median(age):.1f}  diffprivlib median: {private:.2f}")
With random_state=0 it prints a true median of 37.0 and a private one of 37.72. Ages are whole numbers, so every point between 37 and 38 has the same score, and the mechanism picked that piece and a point in it at random. OpenDP refuses to run the median without a public upper bound on the number of rows, declared as a Margin. Choose it generously from public facts, since it must be at least the true number of rows and a larger one costs almost nothing.
context = dp.Context.compositor(
    data=adult.lazy(),
    privacy_unit=dp.unit_of(contributions=1),  # one row per person
    privacy_loss=dp.loss_of(epsilon=1.0),
    split_evenly_over=1,
    margins=[dp.polars.Margin(max_length=100_000)],  # a public bound on the number of rows
)
age_col: Any = pl.col("age")  # OpenDP adds .dp to Polars expressions when it is imported
query = context.query().select(age_col.dp.median(candidates=list(range(17, 91))))
print(query.summarize(alpha=0.05))
released = query.release().collect()  # changes on every run: OpenDP's noise has no seed
Its summary reports ExponentialMin with a scale of 2.0, because OpenDP 0.16 adds exponential noise to every candidate’s score and reports the best. That is permute-and-flip (McKenna & Sheldon 2020), with the exponential mechanism’s guarantee and never a worse expected error. The accuracy is null, because OpenDP gives no error bar for a quantile. Its noise has no seed, so the released value changes from run to run, and uv run python code/part03-dp-foundations/practitioner_adult_statistics.py prints one at the end.
The error bar you can state is about rank, not value. With probability \(1 - \beta\), the exponential mechanism’s gap is at most \((2\Delta u/\varepsilon)(\ln|\mathcal R| + \ln(1/\beta))\), the tail form of Equation 23.2. For a median, with \(\Delta u = 1\), the gap is the number of records by which the output misses the middle rank, so \(\beta = 0.05\) gives its 95% bar in ranks. A bar in value would need the number of records near the median, which the release does not reveal. If a dashboard needs values, spend budget on a few noisy counts below candidate values.
A generous range is cheap, because its width enters the gap only through the logarithm of the number of candidates.
Two things go wrong in practice. Where the data near the quantile are sparse, the best piece is long and the output can land anywhere in it. A small error in rank is then a large error in value. And the range or the candidates must not come from the data, since setting the upper end to the observed maximum reintroduces the leak. diffprivlib warns with a PrivacyLeakWarning when you leave out bounds (Sensitivity).
crumbs: 23  Selection: exponential mechanism, report-noisy-max, sparse vector

title: 23  Selection: exponential mechanism, report-noisy-max, sparse vector
text:
23.6 Report-noisy-max and Gumbel noise
Report-noisy-max adds independent Laplace noise to each candidate’s score and outputs the candidate with the largest noisy score. It is \(\varepsilon\)-DP for any number of candidates when the noise has scale \(2\Delta u/\varepsilon\), or \(\Delta u/\varepsilon\) when one record pushes all scores the same way. Release only the winner’s index, and pay for a fresh noisy answer if you need its score. Its accuracy is close to the exponential mechanism’s, and neither is always better.
Gumbel noise of scale \(2\Delta u/\varepsilon\) in place of the Laplace noise gives exactly the exponential mechanism. Libraries sample it with this Gumbel-max trick, because the exponential of a score in the thousands overflows, while noisy scores do not. Keeping the \(c\) largest Gumbel-noised scores picks the top \(c\) at once (Durfee & Rogers 2019).
crumbs: 23  Selection: exponential mechanism, report-noisy-max, sparse vector

title: 23  Selection: exponential mechanism, report-noisy-max, sparse vector
text:
23.7 The sparse vector technique
Sometimes queries arrive one at a time, and you want the first one that is high enough. The sparse vector technique (Dwork et al. 2009) compares each with one noisy threshold and pays only for the one that fires. Its basic form, AboveThreshold, takes a threshold \(\tau\) and a stream of queries \(f\), all with the same sensitivity \(\Delta f\). It splits the budget into \(\varepsilon_1\) for the threshold and \(\varepsilon_2\) for the queries.

Draw one threshold noise, written \(\nu\), from \(\mathrm{Lap}(\Delta f/\varepsilon_1)\) for the whole run.
For each query, draw a fresh noise from \(\mathrm{Lap}(2\Delta f/\varepsilon_2)\) and add it to the query’s answer. If the result is at least \(\tau + \nu\), output “above” and halt. Otherwise output “below” and go on.

AboveThreshold is \((\varepsilon_1 + \varepsilon_2)\)-DP for any number of “below” answers, even when each query is chosen after the earlier answers. All the “below” answers together pay \(\varepsilon_1\), through the one threshold noise, and the single “above” pays \(\varepsilon_2\).
The accuracy, unlike the privacy, depends on the stream length \(k\), which must be fixed before the run. Write \(\beta\) for the chance that the accuracy guarantee fails. With an equal split, \(\varepsilon_1 = \varepsilon_2 = \varepsilon/2\), every query is classified correctly unless its true value is within a margin \[\alpha = \frac{8\Delta f\big(\ln k + \ln(2/\beta)\big)}{\varepsilon} \tag{23.3}\] of the threshold. Monitor 1,000 counts, each with \(\Delta f = 1\), against a threshold of 500 at \(\varepsilon = 1\). At \(\beta = 0.05\) the margin is 84.77, so with probability 0.95 only a count that close to the threshold can be misclassified.
To find the first \(c\) queries above the threshold, restart AboveThreshold with fresh threshold noise after each “above”, at \(\varepsilon/c\) per run, and halt after the \(c\)-th. The margin then grows with \(c\), so ask for as few alarms as you can. Lyu, Su and Li instead keep one threshold for all \(c\) alarms and multiply the query noise by \(c\).

23.8 When the sparse vector technique goes wrong
Several published variants do not have the privacy they claim (Table 23.2).



Table 23.2: Variants of the sparse vector technique and their actual privacy, from Lyu, Su & Li (2017).










Variant (as numbered by Lyu, Su & Li)
What it changes
Actual privacy




Algorithm 3
Outputs the noisy value of each “above”
\(\infty\)


Algorithm 4
Query noise does not grow with \(c\)
\(\frac{1 + 6c}{4}\varepsilon\)


Algorithm 5
No noise on the queries
\(\infty\)


Algorithm 6
Never halts
\(\infty\)






The no-halt variant is the one to remember. It adds exactly as much noise per query as AboveThreshold, so a reviewer who checks noise scales will miss it. Yet at \(\varepsilon = 1\) its privacy loss reaches 18.1246 on 80 queries.
So review the accounting, not just the noise. An implementation must draw one threshold noise per run, since a threshold redrawn for each query makes every “below” answer cost budget that nobody counted. It must draw fresh noise for every query, since one query-noise draw reused for all of them amounts to Algorithm 5. And it must halt after the allowed number of “above” answers and never publish the noisy values it compared.

title: 24  Query release and private multiplicative weights
text:
24.1 Why this matters
Analysts rarely want one statistic. They ask for every two-way table over a handful of columns, or for a synthetic file they can query as often as they like, and both must satisfy differential privacy (DP). Such tables are marginal tables: each counts the records for every combination of values of a few attributes, and each count is a cell.
These releases work by adding noise to whole tables rather than to single cells, scaled to how much one person can change the table. One person sits in one cell of a table, so a whole table costs about as much as one count. Everything computed from the noisy tables afterwards is free, including repairs that make the cells add up to the total. When the queries are too many for noise on every cell, synthetic data fitted to a few noisy tables takes over.
crumbs: 24  Query release and private multiplicative weights

title: 24  Query release and private multiplicative weights
text:
24.2 Which method to use
The choice depends on how many queries you have, compared with the number of records, and on how many attributes a record has (Table 24.1).



Table 24.1: Which query-release method to use.





Situation
Use




A few marginal tables, with a public list of cells
Noisy counts on every cell, one budget share per table


Hundreds of tables or thousands of cells
Gaussian noise on every cell, scaled to the whole set of tables


A table whose list of values is not public
Noisy counts, keeping only cells that clear a noisy threshold (Release statistics with a library)


Far more queries than records, or queries not known in advance
Synthetic data from AIM or MST


Queries that arrive one at a time, perhaps adaptively
Online private multiplicative weights






Where “a few” tables end follows from the dense-query rule of the Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms. One person sits in every table, so the tables form a dense query, and at a privacy level \(\varepsilon\) of 1 and a slack \(\delta\) of \(10^{-5}\), Gaussian noise wins from 7 tables on.
crumbs: 24  Query release and private multiplicative weights

title: 24  Query release and private multiplicative weights
text:
24.3 Noise on every cell
Under add/remove neighbours, a person with one record changes one cell of a marginal table by 1, so the whole table has sensitivity 1, whatever its number of cells. Laplace noise of scale \(1/\varepsilon\) on every cell then makes the table \(\varepsilon\)-DP, by parallel composition. Under replace neighbours a person can move from one cell to another, so two cells change and the sensitivity doubles.
Several tables of the same people do compose, because one person sits in one cell of every table. With Laplace noise the budget is split among the tables, so the error per cell grows in proportion to their number. Gaussian noise is calibrated to the square root of the sum of squared changes, which for one person in \(m\) tables is \(\sqrt m\), so its error grows only like \(\sqrt m\).
An example from the full edition shows the gap. A table of 10,000 records has eight yes/no attributes, so \(2^8 = 256\) possible records. The release is every cell of the marginal table of every set of attributes, 6,560 cells in all, each as a fraction of the records, under replace neighbours. A uniform guess, which ignores the data, has a largest error of 0.232 over these cells. At \(\varepsilon = 1\), Laplace noise on every cell does worse than that, with 0.497. Gaussian noise does much better, with 0.037, at a slack \(\delta\) of \(10^{-6}\), stricter than the book’s default.
Two mistakes are common. Scaling each cell’s noise to its own sensitivity, as if it were the only query, silently spends \(\varepsilon\) once for every table. And splitting \(\varepsilon\) evenly over thousands of separately noised cells with basic composition wastes most of the budget. Calibrate to the whole set of tables instead.
crumbs: 24  Query release and private multiplicative weights

title: 24  Query release and private multiplicative weights
text:
24.4 Releasing a marginal with OpenDP
The script practitioner_adult_statistics.py releases the education-by-income table of the Adult census data, 48,842 people with one row each, at \(\varepsilon = 1\). The survey’s documentation lists 16 levels of education and two income classes, so the keys are public and the table has 32 cells. Empty cells are released too, since omitting one would reveal that nobody has those values. Map a missing value to a listed key such as “Unknown”, because a row whose key is not in the list is dropped. In OpenDP, a Margin (a setting, not a marginal table) with invariant="keys" declares the list of cells public, and with_keys pins the release to exactly those cells.
keys = pl.LazyFrame({"education": EDUCATION}).join(pl.LazyFrame({"income": INCOME}), how="cross")
context = dp.Context.compositor(
    data=adult.lazy(),
    privacy_unit=dp.unit_of(contributions=1),
    privacy_loss=dp.loss_of(epsilon=1.0),
    split_evenly_over=1,
    margins=[dp.polars.Margin(by=["education", "income"], invariant="keys")],  # the cells are public
)
query = context.query().group_by("education", "income").agg(dp.len(signed=True)).with_keys(keys)
print(query.summarize(alpha=0.05))
released = query.release().collect()  # all 32 cells, zeros included; changes on every run
Run it with uv run python code/part03-dp-foundations/practitioner_adult_statistics.py. The summary is deterministic.
shape: (1, 5)
┌────────┬──────────────┬─────────────────┬───────┬──────────┐
│ column ┆ aggregate    ┆ distribution    ┆ scale ┆ accuracy │
│ ---    ┆ ---          ┆ ---             ┆ ---   ┆ ---      │
│ str    ┆ str          ┆ str             ┆ f64   ┆ f64      │
╞════════╪══════════════╪═════════════════╪═══════╪══════════╡
│ len    ┆ Frame Length ┆ Integer Laplace ┆ 1.0   ┆ 3.375618 │
└────────┴──────────────┴─────────────────┴───────┴──────────┘
Each cell gets integer Laplace noise of scale 1 (Discrete and floating-point-safe mechanisms). The 95% accuracy of 3.38 means each noisy count lands that close to the truth 95% of the time. Print that error bar beside every cell, and remember that it covers the noise only, not sampling error or mistakes in the data. OpenDP’s noise has no seed, so these four cells come from one run, beside the true counts.
  Doctorate >50K: 432  true 431  accuracy 3.38
  HS-grad <=50K: 13281  true 13281  accuracy 3.38
  Preschool <=50K: 82  true 82  accuracy 3.38
  Preschool >50K: 0  true 1  accuracy 3.38
The large cells barely move, but the smallest true cell, one person with a preschool education and a high income, is smaller than the noise. Noise of a fixed size is large only next to small counts, so if small cells matter, merge rare categories in advance. With signed=True a count may come out negative, which keeps it unbiased. Clamping it at zero, rounding, and scaling the cells to add up to a total already released are post-processing, so they cost nothing.
Three things go wrong. Taking the list of cells from the data, as unique() on a private column does, reveals rare values by itself. Without a codebook, use partition selection (Release statistics with a library). A second table of the same people needs its own share of the budget, so set split_evenly_over to the number of tables. And for many tables, give the budget as dp.loss_of(rho=...), with the \(\rho\) that converts to your \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) (Release statistics with a library shows how). OpenDP then uses Gaussian noise, which composes far better, and accounts in zero-concentrated differential privacy (zCDP) (Concentrated differential privacy).
