title: 24  Query release and private multiplicative weights
text:
24.5 Synthetic data
When the queries far outnumber what noise on every cell can bear, or nobody knows them in advance, release synthetic data instead. The practical tools follow four steps.

Select a set of marginal tables to measure, from domain knowledge or privately with the exponential mechanism, scoring each table by how badly the current model fits it.
Measure each whole table with Gaussian noise, scaled to the whole set.
Generate a compact graphical model that fits the noisy tables.
Sample synthetic rows from the model.

Everything after the measurements is post-processing, so the synthetic rows can be queried and shared at no further privacy cost. The standard methods are MST and AIM, both by McKenna and coauthors, and AIM chooses which tables to measure as it goes. SmartNoise Synth, the snsynth package, wraps both behind one interface. It is not installed in this book’s environment, so the call below was not run; install it in an environment of its own.
# smartnoise-synth 1.0.8: not installed in this book's environment, not run
from snsynth import Synthesizer

synth = Synthesizer.create("aim", epsilon=1.0, delta=1e-6)
synth.fit(adult_pandas, categorical_columns=["education", "sex", "race", "occupation", "income"])
rows = synth.sample(48_842)
A synthetic table is accurate on the tables it measured, by construction, so evaluate it on other queries, but not freely against the private data. Keeping the best of several runs, judged against the private data, is a selection on that data, and each extra run spends the generator’s budget again. So score candidate settings on a public dataset of the same shape, or charge the comparisons to the budget. And a generator trained without DP is not anonymised, however synthetic its rows look.
crumbs: 24  Query release and private multiplicative weights

title: 24  Query release and private multiplicative weights
text:
24.6 Private multiplicative weights
The synthetic-data tools keep the select, measure and update loop of the multiplicative weights exponential mechanism (MWEM) of Hardt, Ligett and McSherry (2012). MWEM is the practical form of private multiplicative weights. It keeps a guessed histogram with one weight for every possible record, 256 in the eight-attribute example, starting from uniform, and runs a fixed number of rounds. Each round selects a query that the guess answers badly, with the exponential mechanism, measures it with fresh Laplace noise, and moves the guess toward the measurement. An online-learning bound caps the number of corrections ever needed, whatever the number of queries. So the budget pays for corrections rather than queries, and the error grows only with the logarithm of the number of queries.
That pays off only for very large sets of queries. On the eight-attribute example at privacy level 1, with 38 rounds, its largest error is 0.078. That beats Laplace noise but loses to Gaussian noise by a factor of about two. Its running time also grows with the number of possible records, which limits it to a few attributes.
Three rules make an implementation correct. Fix the number of rounds before seeing the data, by minimizing the error bound, which uses only public quantities. Measure with fresh noise, because the selection step’s scores are exact and never released, so reusing one would use the data without paying for it. And release the average of the guesses, not the last one, because the accuracy guarantee covers only the average. For queries that arrive one at a time, an online form answers from the guess and pays only for its corrections (Adaptive data analysis).

title: 25  Beyond global sensitivity
text:
25.1 What it is
The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms set their noise by the global sensitivity, the most one record can move the answer over every pair of neighbouring datasets that could exist. The median of ages between 0 and 100 has global sensitivity 100. So under differential privacy (DP) at a privacy level of \(\varepsilon = 1\), the Laplace mechanism’s median error is \(100\ln 2 = 69.31\) years. Yet on a simulated sample of 1,001 ages, one person moves the median by only 0.1386 years. That smaller number is the local sensitivity, the most one record can move the answer \(f\) starting from the dataset \(D\) you hold: \[\mathrm{LS}_f(D) = \max_{D' \text{ a neighbour of } D}|f(D) - f(D')|. \tag{25.1}\]
The techniques of this page add noise on the scale of the data you hold, under one rule. A noise scale, bound or threshold computed from the data is itself a statistic of the data, so it must be private too. Throughout, datasets have a fixed size \(n\), and neighbours replace one record.

title: 25  Beyond global sensitivity
text:
25.2 When you meet it
You meet these techniques whenever a statistic has no useful worst case (Table 25.1).



Table 25.1: Which technique releases what, and where you meet it.










You release
Technique
Where you meet it




A sum, mean or gradient of unbounded values
Clipping to a bound fixed in advance
Every library’s bounds, and the clipping norm of private training


A median or quantile
Inverse sensitivity
diffprivlib.tools.quantile, OpenDP’s dp.quantile


A discrete answer with a clear winner
Stability-based release
The threshold of private partition selection


A black-box model or estimator
Subsample-and-aggregate
Teacher ensembles for private prediction






A stability-based release publishes a discrete answer, such as the most common value, exactly, but only when a noisy test shows that it leads the runner-up by about \(2\ln(1/\delta)/\varepsilon\) records, for a slack \(\delta\). Otherwise it refuses, so plan for refusals downstream. The same test decides which keys found in the data a group-by may release (Release statistics with a library).
Subsample-and-aggregate runs any estimator on disjoint blocks fixed in advance, clips each block’s answer and averages them with noise. Private aggregation of teacher ensembles (PATE) is its voting form (Private prediction).
Propose-test-release proposes a bound on the local sensitivity, checks with noise that the data are many records away from breaking it, and refuses otherwise. Smooth sensitivity scales heavy-tailed noise to a bound that cannot jump between neighbours. PATE uses it to publish the \(\varepsilon\) of its votes, but on the 1,001 ages it is about twelve times less accurate than inverse sensitivity (below).

title: 25  Beyond global sensitivity
text:
25.3 How to use it
Most of the time you bound the inputs. Clipping replaces each value \(x\) by \(\min(x, C)\), for a clip bound \(C\) fixed before seeing the data. For values that cannot be negative, one record then moves the sum by at most \(C\) and the mean of \(n\) records by at most \(C/n\). Laplace noise of scale \(C/(n\varepsilon)\) on the clipped mean gives \(\varepsilon\)-DP, and raising \(C\) shrinks the bias but grows the noise.
Choose \(C\) from domain knowledge, such as a legal maximum or a sensor range. Failing that, assume a distribution in advance and take the \(C\) that minimizes bias plus noise under it, or spend a small slice of the budget, charged by composition, on a private high quantile and clip there. If you omit the bound, diffprivlib computes it from the data and issues a PrivacyLeakWarning. So turn that warning into an error with warnings.simplefilter("error", PrivacyLeakWarning), as practitioner_adult_statistics.py does. Bounding the rows each person contributes is the same move for a whole person (Release statistics with a library).
For a median or quantile, use inverse sensitivity, which favours each candidate output by how few records must change before the median equals it. That is the exponential mechanism, with pure \(\varepsilon\)-DP, so pass it bounds or a candidate grid fixed in advance. On the 1,001 ages at \(\varepsilon = 1\), its median error is 0.0783 years, below even the local sensitivity of 0.1386.

title: 25  Beyond global sensitivity
text:
25.4 What goes wrong
Noise scaled to the local sensitivity is not private. The five ages \((0, 0, 0, 0, 100)\) have median 0, and no single change moves it, so they get no noise. Their neighbour \((0, 0, 0, 100, 100)\) has a positive local sensitivity, so it gets continuous noise and its output is never exactly 0. An output of exactly 0 therefore names the first dataset. The same leak hides in a clip bound set to the observed maximum, a candidate grid built from the data’s values, or keys read off the data. In review, look for a max(), quantile() or unique() on the private data that feeds a parameter.
Clipping from above always biases a mean downward, and a two-sided clip cancels the bias only when the range is centred on the data (Private mean estimation). If neighbours add or remove a record, \(n\) is not public, so release a noisy clipped sum and a noisy count and divide them.
Derivations. Every result here is derived step by step in the full edition’s chapter.

title: 26  Discrete and floating-point-safe mechanisms
text:
26.1 What it is
The proof of the Laplace mechanism is about densities on the real line, but a computer samples floating-point numbers, a finite set with uneven gaps. The textbook sampler adds \(\pm b\ln(1/U)\) to the true answer, for a noise scale \(b\) and a uniform draw \(U\). Mironov (2012) showed that in double precision it leaks the true answer through the last bits of its output. Floats are dense near 0 and sparse far from it, so many outputs can come from a true answer of 0 or of 1, but not from both, and such an output names its input with certainty.
Differential privacy (DP) cannot cover that. It caps how much one record can change the chance of any output, through a privacy level \(\varepsilon\) and a slack \(\delta\) (The definition of differential privacy). Take a set \(S\) of outputs that a dataset \(D\) can reach but its neighbour never can. No factor \(e^\varepsilon\) can lift the neighbour’s probability of \(S\) above 0, so for a mechanism \(M\) the slack must cover \[\delta \ge \Pr[M(D) \in S]. \tag{26.1}\] In a toy sampler with 12-bit floats, such outputs carry probability 0.4791, and more bits do not shrink it.
So DP is a property of the distribution the code actually produces. There are two repairs. The snapping mechanism keeps floats, but clamps the answer, adds noise, rounds to a coarse power-of-two grid and clamps again. The other makes the query integer-valued and adds exact discrete Laplace or discrete Gaussian noise.

title: 26  Discrete and floating-point-safe mechanisms
text:
26.2 When you meet it
You meet this when you review code that adds noise itself, such as the unsafe x + np.random.laplace(0, b), and when you choose a library. OpenDP’s samplers are exact, and on integer data they give discrete Laplace and discrete Gaussian noise. diffprivlib offers mechanisms.Geometric, its name for the discrete Laplace, mechanisms.GaussianDiscrete and mechanisms.Snapping. Its continuous Laplace, used by its tools functions, resists this attack by drawing four uniform variates (Holohan & Braghin 2021), a mitigation rather than an exact sampler. Secure aggregation needs integer noise too (Local, shuffle and distributed trust models).
In private training, Opacus adds continuous Gaussian noise in floating point, so the proof of Private stochastic gradient descent covers only idealized code. Its secure_mode=True draws the noise from a cryptographic generator to blunt these attacks. Check that a released model used it and states its guarantee for the idealized mechanism.

title: 26  Discrete and floating-point-safe mechanisms
text:
26.3 How to use it
Use a library on integer data. Its discrete Laplace noise gives each integer \(z\) a probability proportional to \(e^{-|z|/b}\), and you calibrate it like continuous noise. For an integer query whose sensitivity is \(\Delta f\), it gives \(\varepsilon = \Delta f/b\), and at \(b = 1\) a count comes out exact with probability 0.4621.
The discrete Gaussian gives each integer \(x\) a probability proportional to \(e^{-x^2/(2\sigma^2)}\), for a width \(\sigma\). Its exact privacy curve differs slightly from the continuous one: at sensitivity 1 and \(\sigma = 1\), its \(\delta\) at \(\varepsilon = 1\) is 0.1414, against 0.1269. So either report the discrete curve, or account as OpenDP does in zero-concentrated DP. There the discrete Gaussian keeps the continuous one’s privacy parameter, \(\rho = (\Delta f)^2/(2\sigma^2)\). In the snippet, map(1) gives each guarantee at sensitivity 1.
import opendp.prelude as dp

dp.enable_features("contrib")
integers, distance = dp.atom_domain(T=int), dp.absolute_distance(T=int)
laplace = dp.m.make_laplace(integers, distance, scale=1.0)
print(laplace.map(1))  # 1.0
gauss = dp.m.make_gaussian(integers, distance, scale=2.0)
print(gauss.map(1))  # 0.125
print(gauss.output_measure)  # ZeroConcentratedDivergence
A real-valued query, such as a sum of clipped values, becomes integer in three steps. Divide by a step much smaller than the noise and round randomly, up with probability equal to the fractional part, so that the result stays unbiased. Recompute the sensitivity in those units, since rounding can push neighbours slightly apart. Then add discrete noise and multiply back.

title: 26  Discrete and floating-point-safe mechanisms
text:
26.4 What goes wrong
Ask these questions of any implementation.

Is every sensitivity computed from bounds fixed in advance, with no max(), quantile() or unique() on the private data (Beyond global sensitivity)?
Under add/remove, is a mean a noisy sum over a noisy count, not over the true \(n\) (The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms)?
Do all releases about the same people draw on one budget (Post-processing, group privacy and composition)?
Is an exact statistic of the same data, such as a maximum, published beside the private ones, with no guarantee?
Is the noise drawn by a vetted library, or by an exact sampler with no floating-point exp, log or random() inside? Search for np.random, random., scipy.stats, default_rng, .laplace( and .normal(.
Does integer data get integer noise, and is every floating-point output snapped and clamped to a fixed range?
Does each release draw fresh noise from a cryptographic source, such as secrets.SystemRandom(), rather than a fixed seed that makes it removable?
Is the running time fixed or padded? A rejection sampler’s rounds depend on the value drawn, which Jin et al. (2022) exploit.
Does the stated guarantee match the mechanism, including the discrete Gaussian’s own curve and the sensitivity after rounding?

Derivations. Every result here is derived step by step in the full edition’s chapter.

title: 27  Local, shuffle and distributed trust models
text:
27.1 Why this matters
Every mechanism so far in this part assumed a trusted curator, which holds the raw data and releases only the mechanism’s output. In this central model, the differential privacy (DP) guarantee protects what the curator publishes, but not against a breach of its database, a curious engineer or a court order. A browser vendor that collects usage statistics is often not trusted that far.
Three other models trust less. In the local model nobody is trusted, and each person randomizes their own record before it leaves their device. The shuffle model trusts a shuffler only to cut the link between each report and its sender. The distributed model trusts cryptography that reveals only a sum, run by enough honest participants. The closer to each person the noise is added, the fewer parties you trust, and the more noise reaches the answer.
crumbs: 27  Local, shuffle and distributed trust models

title: 27  Local, shuffle and distributed trust models
text:
27.2 Choosing a trust model
That extra noise is the price of trusting less. As the population grows, the noise on a private count stays fixed in the central model but grows with its square root in the local model. On the full edition’s eight-value histogram over a hundred thousand people, the local model’s squared error is about 42,000 times the central one at the same guarantee. The shuffle and distributed models close most of that gap.
So use the central model whenever a curator can be trusted with the raw data, as Release statistics with a library does end to end. Choose local only when nobody may see a raw record and the population is large enough, which you check by solving the standard deviation of Section 27.3 for the number of people. Either way, state the trust model next to the privacy parameters, because the same \(\varepsilon\) protects against a different adversary in each model.
crumbs: 27  Local, shuffle and distributed trust models

title: 27  Local, shuffle and distributed trust models
text:
27.3 Central and local differential privacy
In the local model, each person sends only a report, the output of a local randomizer \(R\) run on their own record. Write \(\varepsilon_0\) for the privacy level of one report. The randomizer is \(\varepsilon_0\)-DP when no set of possible reports becomes more than \(e^{\varepsilon_0}\) times as likely when the record changes. In symbols, every set of reports \(S\) and every two records \(x\) and \(x'\) satisfy \[\Pr[R(x) \in S] \le e^{\varepsilon_0}\Pr[R(x') \in S]. \tag{27.1}\] Changing one person’s record changes only their own report, so the whole collection is then \(\varepsilon_0\)-DP in the central sense, with neighbours that differ in one replaced record. The guarantee covers only the randomized value, so a network address stored with a report links it back to the person.
The basic local randomizer is randomized response on one bit: each person reports their true bit with a probability \(p = e^{\varepsilon_0}/(1 + e^{\varepsilon_0})\), and the flipped bit otherwise. The analyst undoes the expected flips by subtracting \(1 - p\) from the share of reported ones and dividing by \(2p - 1\). The estimate’s standard deviation then depends only on the level and the number of people \(n\): \[\operatorname{sd}(\hat\pi) = \frac{e^{\varepsilon_0/2}}{(e^{\varepsilon_0} - 1)\sqrt n}. \tag{27.2}\]
The script practitioner_adult_statistics.py runs both models at \(\varepsilon_0 = \ln 3\) on the 48,842 people of the Adult census data, where each bit says whether a person’s income is over $50K. In the local model, each bit goes through diffprivlib’s Binary mechanism, and the analyst sees only the reports.
answers = (adult["income"] == ">50K").cast(pl.Int8).cast(pl.String).to_list()  # "1" or "0"
n, eps = len(answers), log(3)
coin = Binary(epsilon=eps, value0="0", value1="1", random_state=seed)
reports = [coin.randomise(a) for a in answers]  # each person randomizes their own answer
p = exp(eps) / (1 + exp(eps))  # chance a report is truthful: 0.75
reported = reports.count("1") / n
local = (reported - (1 - p)) / (2 * p - 1)  # undo the expected flips
local_sd = math.sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n) / (2 * p - 1)  # the randomization noise alone
print(f"true share over 50K: {answers.count('1') / n:.4f}")
print(f"local estimate: {local:.4f}  sd {local_sd:.4f}")
In the central model, a trusted curator counts the true bits with diffprivlib’s tools.count_nonzero at the same level, which adds Laplace noise with standard deviation \(\sqrt2/\varepsilon\) to the count.
rich = (adult["income"] == ">50K").to_numpy()
central = tools.count_nonzero(rich, epsilon=log(3), random_state=seed) / len(rich)
central_sd = math.sqrt(Laplace(epsilon=log(3), sensitivity=1).variance(0)) / len(rich)  # the count's noise
print(f"central estimate: {central:.4f}  sd {central_sd:.6f}")
Its seed-0 run, uv run python code/part03-dp-foundations/practitioner_adult_statistics.py, prints this.
true share over 50K: 0.2393
local estimate: 0.2359  sd 0.0039
central estimate: 0.2393  sd 0.000026
local sd / central sd: 149
So at the same guarantee, the local estimate is 149 times noisier, and the factor grows like the square root of the population. It belongs to the model, not to randomized response: no local protocol can estimate a fraction with an error below order \(1/((e^{\varepsilon_0} - 1)\sqrt n)\), and randomized response reaches that order. That is why Apple, Google and Microsoft use local DP only for the most frequent items in very large populations.

title: 27  Local, shuffle and distributed trust models
section: 27.4 Frequency estimation: \(k\)-ary randomized response and unary encoding
text:
27.4 Frequency estimation: \(k\)-ary randomized response and unary encoding
The workhorse of deployed local DP is frequency estimation. Each person holds one value from a known list, such as an emoji, and the analyst wants the share holding each one. A report votes for a value with some probability \(p_1\) if the person holds it, and with a smaller probability \(p_0\) otherwise. If \(c_v\) of the \(n\) reports vote for a value \(v\), removing the false votes on average gives the unbiased estimate \[\hat f_v = \frac{c_v/n - p_0}{p_1 - p_0}. \tag{27.3}\]
Two designs set \(p_1\) and \(p_0\) for a list of \(k\) values. In \(k\)-ary randomized response, each person reports their true value with probability \(e^{\varepsilon_0}/(e^{\varepsilon_0} + k - 1)\), and another value otherwise. Optimized unary encoding sends one bit per value, keeping the 1 of the value held only half the time but almost never turning a 0 into a 1. Most values of a long list are rare, and a rare value’s variance sets the smallest share that can be seen. Comparing those variances, use \(k\)-ary randomized response when \(k < 3e^{\varepsilon_0} + 2\), and unary encoding otherwise, at the price of a \(k\)-bit report. The pure-ldp Python package implements both.
Take a keyboard app that wants the share of each of 128 emoji from a million users at \(\varepsilon_0 = 1\). A rare emoji’s estimate has a standard deviation of 0.0019 under unary encoding, against 0.0066 under \(k\)-ary randomized response. By convention, an estimate must stand three standard deviations above zero to be told from noise. So even the better design loses every emoji used by fewer than about \(3 \times 0.0019\), or 0.6%, of users. Size the population from that floor before collecting. For domains too large to list, local hashing and heavy-hitter protocols send a few bits per report instead of one per value (Wang et al. 2017; Bassily et al. 2017).
crumbs: 27  Local, shuffle and distributed trust models

title: 27  Local, shuffle and distributed trust models
section: 27.5 Numbers in one bit: local mean estimation
text:
27.5 Numbers in one bit: local mean estimation
For numbers between 0 and a known bound, such as minutes in an app, one bit per person is enough (Ding, Kulkarni & Yekhanin 2017). The chance of sending a 1 rises in a straight line with the value, so the analyst can invert that line to get an unbiased mean. For a million users, a bound of 1,440 minutes and \(\varepsilon_0 = 1\), the mean has a standard deviation of 1.420 minutes. Fix the bound before collection and clip to it on the device, because a bound computed from the reports would let one person’s value change everyone’s randomizer.
crumbs: 27  Local, shuffle and distributed trust models

title: 27  Local, shuffle and distributed trust models
text:
27.6 Collecting every day: memoization
Telemetry asks the same question every day. An analyst who averages the daily reports of an unchanged value averages away their fresh noise, and composition counts that leak by adding each report’s \(\varepsilon_0\). The fix is memoization: the device draws one permanent randomized response per value and reuses it, so an unchanged value costs only that response’s level, written \(\varepsilon_\infty\). RAPPOR, Google’s collection of Chrome users’ homepages, has \(\varepsilon_\infty = 2.043\).
Memoization fails when the value changes, since each new value costs another \(\varepsilon_\infty\). A user who changes their homepage every month reaches \(12 \times 2.043 = 24.5\) in a year.
crumbs: 27  Local, shuffle and distributed trust models

title: 27  Local, shuffle and distributed trust models
section: 27.7 The shuffle model and amplification by shuffling
text:
27.7 The shuffle model and amplification by shuffling
In the shuffle model (Cheu et al. 2019), each person sends a local report to a shuffler, which strips identifiers and timing and forwards the reports in random order. Each report then hides among the others, so the collection meets central \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP at an \(\varepsilon\) far below \(\varepsilon_0\) (Amplification by shuffling and by iteration). The closed-form bound of Feldman, McMillan & Talwar (2021) gives that \(\varepsilon\) only when there are enough people to hide among: \[\varepsilon_0 \le \ln\frac{n}{16\ln(2/\delta)}. \tag{27.4}\]
In practice you fix the central target and solve for the largest \(\varepsilon_0\) it allows. For a central \((1, 10^{-6})\), ten thousand people may each randomize at \(\varepsilon_0 = 3.504\), while at a thousand people the condition above binds first and caps it at 1.460. Both use a \(\delta\) below the book’s default \(1/n^{1.1}\). The closed form overstates \(\varepsilon\) by a factor of 2.6 to 4.6 at ten thousand people, so plan with it, and deploy with the paper’s published numerical bound.
Three things undo the amplification. A shuffler that colludes with the analyst leaves each report at \(\varepsilon_0\), so choose an \(\varepsilon_0\) you could defend on its own, within the tiers of the definition. Fake senders give no cover, so count only honest ones in \(n\). And real shufflers batch and pad their traffic, so that timing and sizes do not leak.
crumbs: 27  Local, shuffle and distributed trust models

title: 27  Local, shuffle and distributed trust models
text:
27.8 Distributed DP: splitting the noise
In the distributed model, each client adds a small share of the central noise, and secure aggregation reveals only the sum to the server (Cryptography basics). Gaussian noise splits cleanly, because variances of independent shares add. If each of \(n\) clients adds normal noise of variance \(\sigma^2/n\), the shares sum to central noise with standard deviation \(\sigma\), as private as the central Gaussian mechanism.
The small shares are also the weakness. A client that colludes with the server can reveal its share, and one that drops out adds none. With \(t\) such clients, only the honest clients’ noise is left, with standard deviation \[\sigma\sqrt{\frac{n - t}{n}}. \tag{27.5}\] So fix in advance the largest fraction \(\rho\) of clients that may collude or drop out, and have each client add variance \(\sigma^2/(n(1 - \rho))\). The honest clients alone then supply the full noise.
For example, a server sums a histogram of about a hundred thousand users through 100 clients and targets \((1, 10^{-6})\), the default \(\delta\) for that many users. A user who changes value moves one count down and another up, so the \(\ell_2\) sensitivity is \(\sqrt 2\). The analytic Gaussian calibration of the Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms gives a total \(\sigma\) of 5.975, or \(5.975/\sqrt{100} = 0.597\) per client. Without over-provisioning, a fifth of the clients colluding weakens the guarantee to \(\varepsilon = 1.128\) at the same \(\delta\), and nine-tenths to 3.525.
Secure aggregation works on integers, so clients add integer noise, Skellam or the distributed discrete Gaussian of Discrete mechanisms, as TensorFlow Federated’s tff.aggregators.DistributedDpSumFactory does. And it does not check inputs, so a malicious client can still send any vector.

title: 28  Lower bounds: what privacy costs
text:
28.1 What it is
A lower bound says that no mechanism satisfying differential privacy (DP) can be more accurate than some floor. It holds for every mechanism at once, so it works as a feasibility check. Accuracy has two numbers here. The error \(\alpha\) is how far the output may land from the true answer, and the failure probability \(\beta\) is the chance that it lands further away.
The floor you meet most is for a histogram over \(N\) bins under pure DP, with a privacy level \(\varepsilon\) and no slack. If such a histogram is within \(\alpha\) records of every count with probability at least \(1 - \beta\), then \[\alpha \ge \frac12\left(\frac{\ln\big(N(1 - \beta)\big)}{\varepsilon} - 1\right). \tag{28.1}\] The floor grows only with the logarithm of the number of bins, but under pure DP it keeps growing. Under approximate DP, which allows a small slack \(\delta\), it stops at about \(\ln(1/\delta)/\varepsilon\) records, however many bins there are.
crumbs: 28  Lower bounds: what privacy costs

title: 28  Lower bounds: what privacy costs
text:
28.2 When you meet it
You meet a lower bound when a design looks too good. Take a request for a histogram over a million locations at \(\varepsilon = 1\) with no slack, accurate to five records in every bin with 95% probability. First ask whether one person moves one of the statistics, as in the disjoint cells of a histogram, or all of them, as in the means of many attributes. The histogram floor governs the first case, and the fingerprinting and reconstruction floors below the second. The floor then decides whether to keep tuning. A target below it needs more data, a coarser answer or a weaker guarantee. A mechanism within a small factor of it is done, because no algorithm gains more than that factor.
crumbs: 28  Lower bounds: what privacy costs

title: 28  Lower bounds: what privacy costs
text:
28.3 How to use it
For the million locations, every pure-DP histogram has an error of at least 6.38 records in some bin, so the five-record promise is impossible. The Laplace histogram of the Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms has an error of 16.79, about 2.6 times the floor, so it is already near the best. With \(\delta = 10^{-6}\), the floor never passes about \(\ln(10^6) = 13.82\) records. A stability-based histogram, which releases only non-empty bins, has an error that does not grow with \(N\) at all (Beyond global sensitivity). So when a huge, mostly empty universe puts the floor too high, switch to approximate DP.
The same floor sizes a dataset, because dividing an error in records by the number of records \(n\) gives an error in frequencies. A pure-DP histogram whose frequencies must all be within \(\alpha\) needs \[n \ge \frac{\ln\big(N(1 - \beta)\big) - \varepsilon}{2\alpha\varepsilon}. \tag{28.2}\] If the data are a sample from a population, sampling costs records too, about \(\ln(2N/\beta)/(2\alpha^2)\) by Hoeffding’s inequality, and you need the larger of the two. At \(\varepsilon = 1\) and 95% probability, a million cells at an error of 0.1 need at least 64 records for privacy and at most 875 for sampling. At an error of 0.01, privacy needs 638 and sampling 87,522. So at \(\varepsilon = 1\) it is sampling, which no mechanism fixes, that makes fine answers short of records.
When one person moves many statistics, the rate changes. Releasing the means of \(d\) yes/no attributes costs records in proportion to \(d\) under pure DP. Under approximate DP, the fingerprinting bound puts the cost at about \(\sqrt{d\ln(1/\delta)}/(\alpha\varepsilon)\) records, and the Gaussian mechanism matches it to within \(\sqrt{\ln d}\). So use approximate DP for outputs with many coordinates, such as a gradient, and once the Gaussian noise is calibrated, look for more records, not a better mechanism. For about \(n\) counting queries on \(n\) records, the reconstruction attack of Dinur and Nissim sets the floor at an error of order \(\sqrt n\) per answer (Reconstruction attacks). With far more queries than records, answer them from one private synthetic dataset, whose error grows only slowly with their number (Query release).
crumbs: 28  Lower bounds: what privacy costs

title: 28  Lower bounds: what privacy costs
text:
28.4 What goes wrong
Aggregates are not a defence. The attack behind the fingerprinting bound, from Homer and colleagues (2008), found from a genome study’s published frequencies of genetic variants whether a given person took part. It scores how far the released means lean, attribute by attribute, towards the target’s record and away from the population means. Members score higher, because each pulls the means toward their own record. On the means of 50 people over 2,000 attributes, it reaches a true positive rate (TPR) of 0.242 at a false positive rate (FPR) of 1%. A \((1, 10^{-5})\)-DP Gaussian mechanism cuts that TPR to 0.014.
So use the score, with population means from a separate sample, to audit any release of many averages. Compare its TPR at a low FPR with the cap \(\mathrm{TPR} \le e^\varepsilon\,\mathrm{FPR} + \delta\) from the definition. An audit that beats the cap has found a bug in the mechanism or its accounting. Passing proves nothing, because an attack only bounds \(\varepsilon\) from below (Auditing private training).
Every approximate-DP floor here assumes a meaningful \(\delta\), such as the book’s default \(\delta \le 1/n^{1.1}\) (How small δ must be). Otherwise they mean little: a mechanism that publishes each record outright with probability \(\delta\) is \((0, \delta)\)-DP, so a claim with \(\delta\) near \(1/n\) allows publishing about one record.

title: 29  Private mean estimation
text:
29.1 Why this matters
The mean is the statistic that private machine learning computes most often. Each step of private stochastic gradient descent averages clipped per-example gradients, and even a survey share is a mean of 0/1 answers. The planning questions are how many records a private estimate needs, and how to choose a clipping range without looking at the data.
Differential privacy (DP) must hold for every dataset, including datasets your assumptions say cannot happen (The definition of differential privacy). So an assumption such as “the records are normal” may make a mechanism more accurate, but it must never enter the privacy argument. Every mechanism below therefore clips each record to a range, which caps one record’s influence whatever the data are. Its noise grows with the width of that range, and a narrow range must not be read off the data. So spend a small part of the budget finding where the data are, then clip there and spend the rest on the mean.

title: 29  Private mean estimation
section: 29.2 Bounded data: privacy adds a lower-order term
text:
29.2 Bounded data: privacy adds a lower-order term
Throughout the chapter, datasets have a fixed size \(n\), and neighbours differ in one replaced record. An estimate is judged by its root-mean-square error (RMSE), the typical distance between the estimate and the mean of the population the records came from.
Start with records in a known interval of width \(w\), such as yes/no answers coded 0 and 1, and write \(\sigma^2\) for the variance of a record. Release the average plus Laplace noise with scale \(w/(n\varepsilon)\), which is \(\varepsilon\)-DP because one record moves the average by at most \(w/n\) (The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms). Laplace noise has variance twice its scale squared, and it is independent of the sampling error, so the two variances add: \[\mathrm{RMSE} = \sqrt{\frac{\sigma^2}{n} + \frac{2w^2}{n^2\varepsilon^2}}. \tag{29.1}\] To plan a study, set the RMSE equal to a target error \(\alpha\) and solve for \(n\), as the snippet in the Code section does. The number of records needed is at most \[\frac{\sigma^2}{\alpha^2} + \frac{\sqrt2\,w}{\alpha\varepsilon}. \tag{29.2}\]
So sampling needs about \(\sigma^2/\alpha^2\) records whatever you do, and privacy adds at most about \(w/(\alpha\varepsilon)\) more. For a yes/no survey of a population that is half yes, the worst case for sampling, an RMSE of 0.05 needs 100 people. Privacy at \(\varepsilon = 1\) raises that to 108. The privacy term grows only like \(1/\alpha\), against \(1/\alpha^2\) for sampling, so it matters most at a coarse target and a small \(\varepsilon\). It also grows with the width \(w\), so the rest of the chapter is about narrowing the range.
Libraries make you state the range. In diffprivlib, tools.mean(x, epsilon=..., bounds=(lower, upper)) clips to the bounds and adds noise. Without bounds, it computes them from the observed minimum and maximum, which leaks them, and raises a PrivacyLeakWarning. OpenDP likewise needs clamping bounds, its word for clipping bounds (Release statistics with a library).
Bounds that are too tight fail in another way, because they clip real records. The script practitioner_adult_statistics.py releases the mean hours worked per week by the 48,842 people of the Adult census data at \(\varepsilon = 1\), once with loose bounds and once with tight ones.
hours = adult["hours-per-week"].to_numpy()
loose = tools.mean(hours, epsilon=1.0, bounds=(1, 99), random_state=seed)
tight = tools.mean(hours, epsilon=1.0, bounds=(20, 60), random_state=seed)
clipped = np.clip(hours, 20, 60).mean()  # what the tight bounds can at best recover
print(f"true mean hours: {hours.mean():.3f}")
print(f"bounds (1, 99): {loose:.3f}  bounds (20, 60): {tight:.3f}")
print(f"bias of (20, 60): {clipped - hours.mean():+.3f}")
Its seed-0 run, uv run python code/part03-dp-foundations/practitioner_adult_statistics.py, prints these lines, the last two from code next to the excerpt.
true mean hours: 40.422
bounds (1, 99): 40.421  bounds (20, 60): 40.361
bias of (20, 60): -0.061
people outside (20, 60): 8.7%
noise scale (1, 99): 0.0020  (20, 60): 0.0008
The tight bounds shrink the noise scale from 0.0020 to 0.0008 hours. But they clip the 8.7% of people outside them, which moves the mean by 0.061 hours, far more than the noise they save. No budget removes that bias, so report the error in three parts: sampling, clipping bias and noise. Choose the bounds from the schema or public data, and check the share they clip on data you may look at.
The formulas also treat \(n\) as public, which holds only because neighbours replace a record. If the size is itself private, divide a noisy sum by a noisy count, with the budget split between the two.

title: 29  Private mean estimation
section: 29.3 The cost of an unknown range
text:
29.3 The cost of an unknown range
Now let the records be normal with variance 1, and suppose you know only that their mean lies within some distance \(R\) of zero. Normal records rarely stray far from their mean, so write \(\tau\) for a distance from the mean that holds them all, except with a small failure probability \(\beta\). For 1,000 records at \(\beta = 0.05\), it is 4.604.
The naive estimator clips every record to the widest place the data could be, \(R + \tau\) on either side of zero, and adds Laplace noise for that width. So its error grows in step with \(R\). With 1,000 records at \(\varepsilon = 1\), its RMSE reaches 2828.44 when \(R\) is a million. Yet Lower bounds shows that an unknown range need cost only about \(\ln R/\varepsilon\) extra records.
Coarse then fine (Karwa & Vadhan 2018) comes close to that floor in two steps. The coarse step cuts the range into bins of width \(2\tau\) and picks the fullest bin with the exponential mechanism, spending a part \(\varepsilon_1\) of the budget. The records it needs grow only with the logarithm of the number of bins. The fine step clips every record to the chosen bin and its two neighbours, since the data can straddle two bins. It releases their average with Laplace noise for that window. It spends the rest of the budget, so by composition the two steps together are \(\varepsilon\)-DP.
With a quarter of the budget on the coarse step, the same 1,000 records give an RMSE of 0.0609 for every \(R\) from 10 to a million. The fine step has only three quarters of the budget and a window three bins wide, though, so for small ranges the naive estimator wins, here up to \(R = 13.81\). Beyond that, use coarse then fine, or locate the data with a private quantile such as diffprivlib’s tools.quantile. Under approximate DP, with its slack \(\delta\), a stability-based histogram does the coarse step with about \(\ln(1/\delta)/\varepsilon\) records whatever the number of bins, so \(R\) drops out (Beyond global sensitivity).
Two things go wrong. A budget split, bin width or \(\beta\) chosen after looking at the data leaks it. And a coarse step with too few records can pick an empty bin and clip everything to the wrong place.

title: 29  Private mean estimation
text:
29.4 Many dimensions: clip the norm
Vectors in \(d\) dimensions, such as embeddings or gradients, follow the same recipe with a different measure of size. Clip each record’s \(\ell_2\) norm, its length, to a radius \(C\), so that one replaced record moves the average by at most \(2C/n\). Then add Gaussian noise calibrated to that sensitivity (The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms). This is exactly the step of private gradient descent, and private training gives the rules for choosing the clipping norm there. With unit variance per coordinate, records lie about \(\sqrt d\) from their mean, so the radius must grow like \(\sqrt d\). Noise at that scale in every coordinate then grows like \(d\) in total, against \(\sqrt d\) for the sampling error. So in high dimension privacy is the larger cost, and the fingerprinting lower bound shows that no mechanism avoids it.
When you do not know where the mean is, the range problem returns, and a grid of bins would pay for the range once per dimension. The shrinking balls of CoinPress (Biswas, Dong, Kamath & Ullman 2020) avoid the grid: each round clips to a ball around a noisy guess of the mean and then shrinks it, so fix the number of rounds and their budget split in advance.

title: 29  Private mean estimation
section: 29.5 Heavy tails: clip into the data
text:
29.5 Heavy tails: clip into the data
Incomes, session lengths and per-example gradient norms have heavy tails. When all you know is that the variance is at most \(\sigma^2\), a range wide enough to touch no record is enormous. So clip into the data on purpose, and accept a bias.
Now let \(\tau\) be a clipping half-width: clip every record to within \(\tau\) of a centre near the mean, found by a coarse step. Only the rare records beyond \(\tau\) move, so with the centre at the mean the bias is at most \(\sigma^2/\tau\), while the noise grows in proportion to \(\tau\). The bound on the total error is smallest at \[\tau_b = \sigma\sqrt{\frac{n\varepsilon}{2\sqrt2}}, \tag{29.3}\] which uses only \(n\), \(\varepsilon\) and the variance bound. There, an error \(\alpha\) needs about \(\sigma^2/\alpha^2 + 8\sqrt2\,\sigma^2/(\alpha^2\varepsilon)\) records. So privacy is no longer a lower-order cost, since both terms grow like \(1/\alpha^2\). No \(\varepsilon\)-DP mechanism does better for every distribution with that variance, though a bound on a higher moment lowers the cost.
Table 29.1 shows the trade-off on Pareto records, a heavy-tailed distribution scaled to variance 1. Its first width clips no record except with probability 0.05, and its noise dominates. The worst-case width \(\tau_b\) cuts the error to 0.0607, and the best width for this distribution does better still.

title: 29  Private mean estimation
text:
29.6 Code
The snippet computes the records a bounded mean needs, checks its noise with OpenDP, and computes the default clipping width for heavy tails. Setting the RMSE equal to \(\alpha\) and multiplying by \(n^2\) gives a quadratic in \(n\), whose positive root the first function rounds up.
from math import ceil, sqrt

import opendp.prelude as dp


def records_for_bounded_mean(alpha: float, sd: float, width: float, eps: float) -> int:
    """Smallest n with sd^2/n + 2 (width/(n eps))^2 <= alpha^2."""
    a, c = sd**2, 2 * (width / eps) ** 2
    return ceil((a + sqrt(a * a + 4 * c * alpha**2)) / (2 * alpha**2))


def heavy_tail_width(n: int, eps: float, sd: float) -> float:
    """The clipping half-width that balances the bias bound sd^2/tau against the noise."""
    return sd * sqrt(n * eps / (2 * sqrt(2)))


n = records_for_bounded_mean(0.05, 0.5, 1.0, 1.0)
print(n)  # 108
print(f"{dp.laplacian_scale_to_accuracy(1.0 / (n * 1.0), alpha=0.05):.4f}")  # 0.0277
print(f"{heavy_tail_width(1000, 1.0, 1.0):.2f}")  # 18.80
OpenDP states accuracy as a half-width that the noise stays within with a chosen probability. Its laplacian_scale_to_accuracy turns the scale \(w/(n\varepsilon)\) at the planned 108 records into that half-width at 95%.

title: 30  Release statistics with a library
text:
30.1 Why this matters
Suppose you are the analytics engineer of an online shop. The business wants a dashboard of purchase lines, revenue and the typical sale, overall and per country, and of how many customers bought each product. The figures describe customers, so they should come with a differential privacy (DP) guarantee. The difficulty is that one customer appears in many rows, and a guarantee for one row would protect a single purchase, not the person behind a hundred. This chapter does the whole job with OpenDP, from the unit and the budget to the written guarantee.
The data are the Online Retail set from the University of California, Irvine (UCI) Machine Learning Repository, with 541,909 invoice lines of a British online shop. Each line records one product on one invoice, with its quantity, unit price, customer and country. The script practitioner_release_statistics.py runs every step in under a minute, with OpenDP 0.16.0 and Polars 1.36.1.
OpenDP draws its noise from a cryptographic generator, which cannot be seeded, so the released values change on every run. This page therefore quotes scales, error bars and thresholds, which involve no noise, and shows released values only in a block marked as one run.

title: 30  Release statistics with a library
section: 30.3 Decide the unit and the budget
text:
30.3 Decide the unit and the budget
The unit of privacy is what the guarantee protects, and for this dashboard it is a customer. The neighbouring datasets therefore differ by adding or removing one customer with all their lines (The definition of differential privacy). The script drops lines with no customer identifier, which belong to nobody, as well as returns and lines with a zero price. Each filter judges a line by that line alone, so adding or removing a customer still changes only that customer’s lines.
raw = practitioner_datasets.online_retail()
lines, stats = clean(raw)
n_customers = stats.customers
delta = delta_for(n_customers)  # 1/n^1.1, rounded down to a power of ten
per_line = per_customer(lines)
print(f"customers: {n_customers:,}  purchase lines: {lines.height:,}")
print(f"delta: {delta:.0e}")
p50, p90, p99, top = quantiles(per_line, [0.5, 0.9, 0.99, 1.0])
print(f"lines per customer: p50={p50} p90={p90} p99={p99} max={top}")
customers: 4,372  purchase lines: 397,884
delta: 1e-05
lines per customer: p50=41 p90=208 p99=662 max=7847
The slack \(\delta\) follows the book’s default for \(n\) people, \(\delta \le 1/n^{1.1}\) rounded down to a power of ten, which gives \(10^{-5}\). The 4,372 customers are counted before returns are dropped, which leaves 4,338, but both counts give the same slack. OpenDP logs a general warning that \(\delta\) should be at most \(10^{-6}\), while this book ties \(\delta\) to the number of people. The privacy level is \(\varepsilon = 1\) for the whole release, because all its tables describe the same customers and their costs add up (Post-processing, group privacy and composition).
The median customer has 41 lines, but under a guarantee per line the largest customer would be a group of 7,847 records. Group privacy multiplies \(\varepsilon\) by the size of the group. Printing that maximum is fine only because this set is public, since a bound read off private data leaks.
crumbs: 30  Release statistics with a library

title: 30  Release statistics with a library
text:
30.4 Bound each customer’s contribution
Write \(k\) for the largest number of lines a customer may contribute, so that every query keeps at most \(k\) lines of each customer. A small \(k\) means little noise but throws data away, while a large \(k\) keeps the data but needs more noise, as the script measures on this public set.
k=10: lines kept 10.2%  customers truncated 84.8%
k=25: lines kept 22.4%  customers truncated 64.6%
k=50: lines kept 36.9%  customers truncated 44.0%
k=100: lines kept 55.1%  customers truncated 24.9%
k=200: lines kept 72.7%  customers truncated 10.4%
k=500: lines kept 88.2%  customers truncated 1.8%
The default is a high percentile of lines per customer, read from public or historical data, never from the data you release. With neither, spend a small share of the budget on a private high quantile of the lines per customer, over candidates fixed in advance (Selection). This chapter takes \(k = 100\), below the 90th percentile of 208 because the noise grows with \(k\). It keeps 55.1% of the lines and truncates a quarter of the customers.
Keeping the first \(k\) lines by date would bias every statistic towards each customer’s early purchases, so the script keeps a random sample of \(k\) lines per customer. The filter below does what OpenDP’s truncate_per_group(k, keep="sample") does, but with a seed, so that the true values of the check stay fixed.
def sample_per_customer(k: int, seed: int, *by: str) -> pl.Expr:
    """True for at most k randomly chosen lines of each customer (within each value of `by`)."""
    return pl.int_range(pl.len()).shuffle(seed=seed).over("CustomerID", *by) < k
Values need bounds as well. A line’s value is its quantity times its unit price, which the script clips to between £0 and £200. The lower end holds because returns were dropped, and the upper end is a bound the business sets, which clips 1.02% of the lines. So one customer can move the revenue by at most 100 lines of £200 each. Take value bounds from the domain, never from the data’s minimum or maximum (Beyond global sensitivity).
A group-by needs two more bounds: \(L_0\), the number of groups one customer may touch, and \(L_\infty\), the lines a customer may put in any one group. Countries need neither, because however a customer spreads their \(k\) lines over countries, the country counts change by at most \(k\) in all, which the noise already covers. When customers spread over many groups, as with country by month, bounding \(L_0\) and \(L_\infty\) can beat a total \(k\). The noise then scales with \(L_0L_\infty\) for Laplace and \(\sqrt{L_0}\,L_\infty\) for Gaussian. Products need both bounds for partition selection (Section 30.8).
crumbs: 30  Release statistics with a library

title: 30  Release statistics with a library
text:
30.5 Set up the context
OpenDP keeps the whole release in a context, which holds the data, the unit, the total budget and its split between queries. Contexts need dp.enable_features("contrib"), which switches on components not yet formally vetted, so a reviewer who needs vetted code must check each call in OpenDP’s documentation.
context = dp.Context.compositor(
    data=lines.lazy(),
    privacy_unit=dp.unit_of(contributions=1, identifier="CustomerID"),
    privacy_loss=dp.loss_of(rho=rho, delta=delta / 2),  # Gaussian noise; delta/2 for thresholds
    split_by_weights=WEIGHTS,  # scalars, countries, products
    margins=[dp.polars.Margin(by=[], max_length=MAX_LINES)],
)
The identifier column makes the unit a customer, so contributions=1 means adding or removing one customer with all their lines, which the truncation filters then bound. For replace, OpenDP takes changes= instead. The budget is in zero-concentrated differential privacy (zCDP) (Concentrated differential privacy). It states privacy as one number, written \(\rho\), that adds up across queries and converts to \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) at the end.
With a zCDP budget, the context adds Gaussian noise to every count and sum. That suits the product counts, where one customer touches many groups (The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms). The script’s rho_for finds \(\rho = 0.0284\), the largest value that OpenDP’s own conversion turns into \(\varepsilon \le 1\) with half of \(\delta\). The other half pays for the threshold of Section 30.8. Finally, the margin states a public upper bound on the number of lines, which OpenDP needs before it sums floating-point values.
The weights give a quarter of the budget to the overall statistics, a quarter to the countries and half to the products, which need it most. The script prints the split and converts the whole release back to the \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) the statement will claim.
budget scalars: rho=0.0071 delta=1.25e-06
budget countries: rho=0.0071 delta=1.25e-06
budget products: rho=0.0142 delta=2.50e-06
whole release as (epsilon, delta): (1.0000, 1e-05)
A query takes its share of the budget when it is built, but spends it only when it is released. Each new query is built with the next unspent share. So if you build all the queries first, every one gets the first share, and the product query gets a quarter’s noise but is charged half. So build, check and release each query in turn, as the script does.
crumbs: 30  Release statistics with a library

title: 30  Release statistics with a library
section: 30.6 Release overall statistics with error bars
text:
30.6 Release overall statistics with error bars
The first query releases the count of lines, the revenue and the median line value. The context holds the raw lines, so each query truncates them itself.
value = clipped_value()  # the line value, clipped to [low, high]
scalars = (
    context.query()
    .filter(sample_per_customer(K, seed))  # at most K lines per customer
    .select(
        dp.len(signed=True),
        value.dp.sum((low, high)).alias("revenue"),
        value.dp.median(candidates=MEDIAN_CANDIDATES).alias("median"),
    )
)
scalar_summary = scalars.summarize(alpha=0.05)
scalars_hat = scalars.release().collect()
signed=True keeps negative noisy counts, and summarize reports, before anything is released, each statistic’s noise and 95% error bar.
scalars len: Frame Length, Integer Gaussian, scale=1,453.38 95% accuracy=2,850.0
scalars revenue: Sum, Float Gaussian, scale=290,804.33 95% accuracy=569,966.0
scalars median: 0.5-Quantile, GumbelMin, scale=1,453.38 95% accuracy=none
With probability 0.95, the released count of lines is within 2,850 of the truth, and the revenue within £569,966. These bars depend only on the bounds and the budget, so you can read them before the release and decide whether the budget is enough.
The output also shows how OpenDP splits a query’s share among its statistics: each gets the same noise scale relative to its sensitivity. The count and the median both get 1,453.38, and the revenue, whose sensitivity is 200 times the count’s, about 200 times that. A mean, .dp.mean, is a sum and a count, so it takes two shares. Its error bar follows from theirs (The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms). To give one statistic more budget, put it in a query of its own with its own weight. The median is chosen by the exponential mechanism, sampled by GumbelMin, among candidates in steps of £0.50 across the value bounds. So its error bar is in ranks, and summarize gives none (Selection).
The error bars cover the noise only, not the bias of truncation and clipping, which together keep only 48.5% of the revenue. So the private revenue estimates a truncated total, not the shop’s takings. Say so, and choose a larger \(k\) if the full total matters more than the noise.
crumbs: 30  Release statistics with a library

title: 30  Release statistics with a library
section: 30.7 Group by a public key list
text:
30.7 Group by a public key list
Lines and revenue per country come next, and the key list must not come from the data. The distinct values of the Country column would publish which countries appear in the private data, which no noise covers. So the script fixes its keys in advance. They are the United Kingdom, the 27 EU member states, the 4 of the European Free Trade Association, the United States, Canada, Australia, Japan, China and “Other”. A rule renames three of the source’s spellings, such as EIRE to Ireland, and maps every other value to Other.
by_country = (
    context.query()
    .filter(sample_per_customer(K, seed))
    .group_by("Market")
    .agg(dp.len(signed=True), value.dp.sum((low, high)).alias("revenue"))
    .with_keys(pl.LazyFrame({"Market": MARKETS}))  # every key is released, zeros included
)
country_summary = by_country.summarize(alpha=0.05)
countries_hat = by_country.release().collect()
per country len: Frame Length, Integer Gaussian, scale=1,185.25 95% accuracy=2,324.0
per country revenue: Sum, Float Gaussian, scale=237,698.48 95% accuracy=465,880.5
Every key is released, including the 11 with no purchase lines, whose counts are pure noise, so the release says nothing about which markets have customers. Each market’s count has a 95% error bar of 2,324, and its revenue one of about £466,000. Germany’s true count of 5,379 is still useful, but its revenue of £131,902 is smaller than its error bar. So publish the error bar with every cell, or merge small markets into Other before the release.
crumbs: 30  Release statistics with a library

title: 30  Release statistics with a library
section: 30.8 Group by unknown keys with partition selection
text:
30.8 Group by unknown keys with partition selection
The list of products is not public, and a product bought by one customer would reveal that purchase simply by appearing in the table. So the release decides privately which products to show, by partition selection. It releases only the products whose noisy count clears a threshold, so a product with few customers almost never appears. The threshold is what costs \(\delta\) (Beyond global sensitivity).
To count customers rather than lines, the query first keeps one line per customer and product, so \(L_\infty = 1\). It then keeps at most \(m\) products per customer, so \(L_0 = m\), and the script measures the trade-off that \(m\) sets on this public set.
m=1: pairs kept 1.6%  customers truncated 97.9%  scale=5.93  threshold=29  products above it: 1
m=5: pairs kept 7.9%  customers truncated 92.4%  scale=13.27  threshold=66  products above it: 9
m=10: pairs kept 15.1%  customers truncated 83.6%  scale=18.77  threshold=96  products above it: 19
m=20: pairs kept 27.5%  customers truncated 68.3%  scale=26.54  threshold=138  products above it: 30
m=50: pairs kept 52.7%  customers truncated 38.6%  scale=41.96  threshold=225  products above it: 50
The threshold grows with \(m\), from 29 to 225, because each customer can push more groups over it, but the counts grow faster. So the number of products whose true count clears the threshold rises from 1 to 50, and the script takes \(m = 50\) (M in the code), again chosen on public data.
by_product = (
    context.query()
    .filter(sample_per_customer(1, seed, "StockCode"))  # one line per customer and product
    .filter(sample_per_customer(M, seed))  # at most M products per customer
    .group_by("StockCode")
    .agg(dp.len(signed=True).alias("customers"))
)
product_summary = by_product.summarize(alpha=0.05)
products_hat = by_product.release().collect()
per product customers: Frame Length, Integer Gaussian, scale=41.96 95% accuracy=83.0 threshold=225
A product is released only if its noisy count reaches 225, and a released count has a 95% error bar of 83. Never publish how many products were dropped, or which, since both come from the private data. Products just below the threshold get in when their noise is positive, so treat a count near 225 as a sign of popularity, not as a measurement.
OpenDP’s truncate_num_groups should bound the groups per customer, but in version 0.16.0 it does not work. With the default keep="sample", summarize accepts the query, but release fails after spending the query’s share, so run each query end to end on public data first. With keep="first" it keeps one group fewer than asked, the first in sort order, which biases the counts. The filters above avoid both problems only because \(L_\infty = 1\) turns groups into lines. For \(L_\infty > 1\) this book knows of no unbiased group bound in this version.
crumbs: 30  Release statistics with a library

title: 30  Release statistics with a library
text:
30.9 Check the release before publishing
To check that the code does what the plan says, the script compares the private values with the true ones, after the same truncation and clipping.
true lines after truncation: 219,291 (all purchase lines: 397,884)
true revenue after truncation and clipping: 4,318,947 (all lines, unclipped: 8,911,408)
true median line value after truncation: 15.00 (all lines: 11.80)
The release itself is random. One run printed the following.
released (one run):
  lines 218,972  revenue 4,397,410  median 14.50
  United Kingdom: lines 196,311  revenue 3,927,959
  Germany: lines 7,151  revenue 643,094
  Spain: lines -546  revenue -37,048
  country line counts within their 95% accuracy: 34 of 38
  products released: 63
Read it against the error bars: about 95% of the market counts should fall inside theirs. Negative values are noise on small markets, and rounding them up to zero is post-processing, which costs no budget. Expect more than the 50 products whose true count clears the threshold, since products just below it get in when their noise is positive. Compare the private median with the truncated £15.00, not the £11.80 of all lines.
The check fails when a value lies far outside its error bar, which points to a wrong sensitivity. It also fails when far more or far fewer than 95% of the cells fall inside, or when a released product’s true count lies far below the threshold. In production you cannot compare against the truth, because a decision to publish that depends on the true values is itself a release of them. So run this check on historical or public data while you develop, and release the real data once, with the code you checked.
crumbs: 30  Release statistics with a library

title: 30  Release statistics with a library
text:
30.10 Write the guarantee down
The script prints the claim from the variables that set the bounds and the budget, so it cannot drift from the code.
This release satisfies (epsilon = 1, delta = 1e-05)-differential privacy for adding or
removing one customer and all their invoice lines, with at most 100 lines per customer
(sampled at random), at most 50 random products per customer in the product counts, and
line values clipped to [0, 200] pounds, under the central model, using OpenDP 0.16.0 with
Gaussian noise (accounted as 0.0284-zCDP plus 5e-06 for thresholds, converted to epsilon
and delta). The market list was fixed in advance; the product list is not public.
The statement names everything a reviewer needs to recompute the claim (Writing the guarantee down). Next to it, say what it does not cover. Another release about the same customers adds its own budget. If that one is pure \(\varepsilon\)-DP, you can add the \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) pairs. Or convert it to \(\rho = \varepsilon^2/2\), add that to this release’s \(\rho\) and then convert, whichever total is smaller (Concentrated differential privacy). And the figures describe truncated data, which the dashboard should say. Release and governance maps such a claim to data-protection law.

title: Privacy accounting
text:
A model trained with stochastic gradient descent (SGD) under differential privacy (DP), the method called DP-SGD, takes thousands of noisy steps. Yet you report one guarantee for the run, a privacy level \(\varepsilon\) with a small slack \(\delta\). The composition theorems of Part 3 are far too loose for that. An accountant does better, because it tracks a summary of each step’s cost that composes tightly, and converts the total to \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) once, at the end.
The running example is a DP-SGD run of 10,000 steps. Each step samples every record with probability 0.01 and adds noise with multiplier 1. At \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), advanced composition certifies \(\varepsilon = 24{,}379.55\), while the privacy loss distribution accountant of Google’s dp_accounting certifies 6.19. So an \(\varepsilon\) means nothing until you name the accountant behind it, and the sampler and neighbouring relation it assumed.
The part starts with two jobs. Report and review an ε claim says what a privacy statement must contain and how to check one. Calibrate and account a DP-SGD run turns a target \(\varepsilon\) into a noise multiplier for the Adult run of Part 5.
Two full chapters explain what those jobs rely on. Amplification by subsampling shows how much a random batch helps, provided the data loader samples the way the accountant assumes. Rényi differential privacy defines the curve most libraries track.
Short reference pages follow. Three finish the DP-SGD story: the conversion from Rényi DP, numerical accounting, and Gaussian DP, which reads a guarantee as a limit on attacks. Then come adaptive composition for budgets decided during training, concentrated DP for analytics ledgers, and shuffling and iteration.
Every number comes from code you can run with Opacus or dp_accounting. By the end, you will be able to calibrate a DP-SGD run, account for it with two libraries, and report \(\varepsilon\) so that others can reproduce it.

title: 31  Choosing an accountant
text:
31.1 Why this matters
A model trained with differential privacy (DP) is reported with a privacy level \(\varepsilon\) and a small slack \(\delta\). The procedure that computes \(\varepsilon\) is an accountant, and the same run can get 6.24 or 24,379.55 depending on which one you use. Table 31.1 shows three, advanced composition, Rényi differential privacy (RDP) and the privacy loss distribution (PLD), on one run of private stochastic gradient descent (SGD), called DP-SGD. Each record joins each batch with probability \(q = 0.01\), the sampling rate, and the noise multiplier \(\sigma\), the noise as a multiple of the clipping norm, is 1.
Only the PLD’s lower column is a lower bound, so the true \(\varepsilon\) lies between the two PLD columns. Advanced composition, which adds up each step’s guarantee, is useless here, and RDP still overstates \(\varepsilon\), by 14.6% on the shorter run and 7.6% on the longer one. Hence the chapter’s rule. Report the tightest upper bound whose assumptions hold for the code you ran, and give enough detail that someone else can recompute it.

31.2 Which accountant
An accountant is tight only when the summary it keeps of each step fits the mechanism, so the mechanism decides (Table 31.2).

Mechanism

title: 31  Choosing an accountant
section: 31.3 The inverse problem: noise for a target ε
text:
31.3 The inverse problem: noise for a target ε
Usually you fix the target \(\varepsilon\), batch size and epochs, and ask for the smallest \(\sigma\) that meets them. A looser accountant overstates \(\varepsilon\), so it asks for more noise. For a target of 3 on the 10,000-step run, RDP needs 1.662 and the PLD only 1.584. So calibrate with the accountant you will report, passing accountant="prv" to Opacus’s get_noise_multiplier, whose default is "rdp" (Calibrate and account a DP-SGD run).

title: 31  Choosing an accountant
text:
31.4 Choosing δ
Treat \(\delta\) roughly as the chance that the guarantee fails for someone, possibly badly. On a dataset of \(n\) people, publishing one random record in full meets a \(\delta\) of about \(1/n\) with \(\varepsilon\) zero, yet exposes someone completely. So \(\delta\) must sit well below \(1/n\). This book follows Ponomareva et al. (2023) and chooses \[\delta \le \frac{1}{n^{1.1}}, \quad \text{rounded down to a power of ten.} \tag{31.1}\] Count \(n\) in the unit the claim protects, which at the user level means users, not records.
For example, run the 10,000 steps of Table 31.1 on 50,000 records, which at \(q = 0.01\) is 100 epochs. Then \(1/n^{1.1}\) is \(6.8\times10^{-6}\), which rounds down to \(10^{-6}\). The table’s \(10^{-5}\) is half of \(1/n\), so it fails the rule. The US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) recommends the stricter \(1/n^2\), so report \(\varepsilon\) there too.

31.6 Matching the accountant to the code
An accountant’s number holds only if the code does what its theorem assumes. Many papers have reported the Poisson-sampling number while training with shuffled fixed-size batches, a different algorithm (Ponomareva et al. 2023). So check Table 31.4 against the code before you report.

The sampler costs the most. At \(10^{-5}\), the 6.19 that dp_accounting’s PLD gives under Poisson sampling becomes 43.37 with fixed-size batches, and 91.82, for zero-out neighbours only, with shuffle and partition (Subsampling).

title: 31  Choosing an accountant
text:
31.7 Reviewing someone else’s claim
A reviewer works in this order.

Ask for the inputs of Table 31.3, and reject a claim that cannot be recomputed.
Check \(\delta\) against Equation 31.1, with \(n\) counted in the claim’s unit.
Recompute \(\varepsilon\) with a different library, and expect agreement within a few percent. A PLD accountant’s get_delta at the claimed \(\varepsilon\) gives the \(\delta\) at which it holds. A claim well above your value is valid but loose.
Read the training code against Table 31.4, starting with the sampler.
Ask what the claim leaves out, such as tuning runs, pretraining data and preprocessing fitted on the private rows.

For example, a team claims \((2, 10^{-5})\)-DP for a model trained on one million users with noise multiplier 0.65. Batches of 1,000 users make the sampling rate \(q\) 0.001, and 10 epochs 10,000 steps, but the loader shuffles and takes fixed batches. This snippet does steps 2 and 3, then accounts for the loader as it ran.
from math import floor, log10

from dp_accounting import GaussianDpEvent, PoissonSampledDpEvent, SelfComposedDpEvent
from dp_accounting.pld import PLDAccountant

n, q, sigma, steps, epochs = 1_000_000, 0.001, 0.65, 10_000, 10  # the claim's parameters
delta = 10.0 ** floor(log10(n**-1.1))  # the book's rule for one million users
print(f"{delta:.0e}")  # 1e-07
poisson = SelfComposedDpEvent(PoissonSampledDpEvent(q, GaussianDpEvent(sigma)), steps)
pld = PLDAccountant(value_discretization_interval=1e-4).compose(poisson)
print(f"{pld.get_epsilon(1e-5):.2f}")  # 1.72
print(f"{pld.get_delta(2.0):.1e}")  # 3.0e-06
print(f"{pld.get_epsilon(delta):.2f}")  # 2.84
# What the loader ran: shuffle and partition, zero-out neighbours, no amplification
shuffled = SelfComposedDpEvent(GaussianDpEvent(sigma), epochs)
print(f"{PLDAccountant(value_discretization_interval=1e-4).compose(shuffled).get_epsilon(delta):.2f}")  # 36.45
The arithmetic holds up, since the claim’s parameters give 1.72 at its \(\delta\). But that \(\delta\) is a hundred times the rule’s \(10^{-7}\), at which the run gives 2.84. And the loader voids both numbers, which assume Poisson sampling. What the code ran is certified only at 36.45, for zero-out neighbours, so the review asks for a Poisson loader and a \(\delta\) of \(10^{-7}\).

title: 31  Choosing an accountant
text:
31.8 Checking an accountant
An accountant is code, so test it on known answers. With sampling rate \(q = 1\), each step is a plain Gaussian mechanism, whose composition is exact (f-DP and Gaussian DP). Ten such steps at noise multiplier 1 are exactly \((17.8566, 10^{-5})\)-DP, so an upper bound must lie above 17.8566 and a PLD bracket must contain it. Also, \(\varepsilon\) must never fall as steps grow or rise as noise grows.
Then compare two maintained libraries, with pinned versions. This snippet recomputes Table 31.1 with Google’s dp_accounting.
import dp_accounting
from dp_accounting.pld import PLDAccountant
from dp_accounting.rdp import RdpAccountant

step = dp_accounting.PoissonSampledDpEvent(0.01, dp_accounting.GaussianDpEvent(1.0))
run = dp_accounting.SelfComposedDpEvent(step, 10_000)  # q = 0.01, sigma = 1, 10,000 steps
pld = PLDAccountant(value_discretization_interval=1e-4).compose(run)
rdp = RdpAccountant(orders=list(range(2, 65))).compose(run)  # integer orders only
print(f"{pld.get_epsilon(1e-5):.4f} {rdp.get_epsilon(1e-5):.4f}")  # 6.1877 6.7194
print(f"{pld.get_epsilon(1e-6):.4f} {rdp.get_epsilon(1e-6):.4f}")  # 6.9074 7.4869
Each PLD value lies inside the table’s bracket, and each RDP value sits just above the table’s, which also tries fractional orders. When libraries disagree, look for three causes. RDP values that differ by an amount depending only on the order, 0.3612 at order 10, come from different conversions (RDP conversions). PLD brackets that do not overlap mean a bug. And a factor of two often means different neighbouring relations.

title: 32  Calibrate and account a DP-SGD run
text:
32.1 Why this matters
An accountant turns a training run’s settings into its privacy level \(\varepsilon\) under differential privacy (DP). Before the run it finds the noise that meets your target, and after it the \(\varepsilon\) the run spent. Both can go wrong silently. The noise may be calibrated with one accountant and reported with another, the loader may not sample as the accountant assumes, or a restart may reset the step count. None changes the loss curve, but each makes the claim false.
This chapter does the accounting, and trains nothing, for a run of stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with DP, called DP-SGD, on the Adult census data from the UCI Machine Learning Repository. It trains on 30,000 people in batches of 1,000 for ten epochs, aiming at \(\varepsilon = 4\), and Train a model with DP-SGD trains it.
The script practitioner_calibrate.py runs the seven steps below in one to two minutes, with Opacus 1.6.0 and dp-accounting 0.6.0. Its defaults are Part 5’s run. Options such as --n, --batch, --epochs and --epsilon set your own, as the second command does for MNIST, and only the planning table stays fixed.

title: 32  Calibrate and account a DP-SGD run
section: 32.2 Fix the privacy unit, n and δ
text:
32.2 Fix the privacy unit, n and δ
The guarantee protects exactly one record, so first decide what a record is. In Adult each row is one person. If one person could own many rows, the number of records \(n\) would have to count people, and training would need the methods of User-level differential privacy.
The slack \(\delta\) is roughly the chance that the guarantee fails. The book’s rule sets it to at most \(1/n^{1.1}\), rounded down to a power of ten, well below \(1/n\) (Choosing δ).
def delta_for(n: int) -> float:
    """The book's default delta: at most 1/n^1.1, rounded down to a power of ten."""
    return 10.0 ** math.floor(math.log10(n**-1.1))
Adult rows: 48,842; Part 5's training split: n=30,000
delta_for(30,000) = 1e-05
delta_for(60,000) = 1e-06
delta_for(569) = 1e-04
Here \(n\) counts the people of the training split, not all of Adult’s rows, so \(\delta\) is \(10^{-5}\). Set the validation rows aside first, because rows that are not trained on are neither in \(n\) nor protected. The lines for MNIST and scikit-learn’s breast cancer data show that \(\delta\) must be recomputed for each dataset.
crumbs: 32  Calibrate and account a DP-SGD run

title: 32  Calibrate and account a DP-SGD run
text:
32.3 Choose the sampler
The accountants here assume Poisson sampling, in which each record joins each batch independently with probability \(q\), the sampling rate, so batches vary in size. Other samplers cost far more privacy (Section 32.6). With an expected batch size \(B\), the rate is \(q = B/n\). A run of \(E\) epochs then takes \(E/q\) steps, rounded down, which the output calls \(T\).
Poisson: B=1000, E=10: q=0.033333, T=300
Opacus DPDataLoader.from_data_loader: q=1/30=0.033333, 30 steps an epoch, 300 in 10 epochs
chosen run uses the loader's q and steps; get_noise_multiplier at that q counts int(E/q)=300: equal True
The second line is what training will run, because Opacus replaces your loader with a Poisson DPDataLoader. Its rate is one over the original loader’s number of batches, \(\lceil n/B \rceil\), with that many steps per epoch. Here \(B\) divides \(n\), so the two lines agree. When it does not, training runs the loader’s numbers. So the script takes \(q\) and \(T\) from the loader, and the third line checks that Opacus’s calibration counts the same steps. This step has gone wrong if the training code builds its own loader with shuffle=True and a fixed batch_size. The sign is that all batches in the logs have the same size (Amplification by subsampling).
crumbs: 32  Calibrate and account a DP-SGD run

title: 32  Calibrate and account a DP-SGD run
crumbs: 32  Calibrate and account a DP-SGD run

title: 32  Calibrate and account a DP-SGD run
section: 32.5 Check ε with a second accountant
text:
32.5 Check ε with a second accountant
Train with the calibrated \(\sigma\) unrounded, as Part 5 does with Opacus’s 0.9729. If you round it, round up to the three decimals the statement prints, because less noise means a larger \(\varepsilon\). Before training, compute the planned run’s \(\varepsilon\) with every accountant at hand, three from Opacus and two from dp_accounting.
def crosscheck_epsilon(sigma: float, q: float, steps: int, delta: float) -> dict[str, float]:
    """Epsilon of one planned run by five accountants (GDP is the trap: it is not an upper bound)."""
    epsilons: dict[str, float] = {}
    for name, opacus_accountant in [("Opacus RDP", RDPAccountant()), ("Opacus PRV", PRVAccountant())]:
        opacus_accountant.history = [(sigma, q, steps)]  # what `steps` calls of .step() would record
        epsilons[name] = opacus_accountant.get_epsilon(delta)
    run = SelfComposedDpEvent(PoissonSampledDpEvent(q, GaussianDpEvent(sigma)), steps)
    epsilons["dp_accounting RDP"] = RdpAccountant().compose(run).get_epsilon(delta)
    epsilons["dp_accounting PLD"] = PLDAccountant().compose(run).get_epsilon(delta)
    gdp = GaussianAccountant()
    gdp.history = [(sigma, q, steps)]
    epsilons["Opacus GDP"] = gdp.get_epsilon(delta)
    return epsilons
chosen cell: Adult, B=1000, E=10, eps=4: sigma=0.972900 (Opacus PRV, as Part 5)
Opacus RDP         eps=4.50
Opacus PRV         eps=3.99
dp_accounting RDP  eps=4.50
dp_accounting PLD  eps=3.98
Opacus GDP         eps=3.34
PLD <= target: True; RDP >= PLD: True; |PRV - PLD|/PLD < 3%: True
crosscheck: pass
PLD bracket (grid 1e-4): lower 3.9656 (optimistic), upper 3.9806 (pessimistic); width 0.0150
The two tight accountants, PRV and the PLD, agree at 3.99 and 3.98, and both meet the target. The two RDP implementations agree at 4.50, above the target, as a looser bound should, and Opacus’s warnings about RDP orders concern only that value. The trap is the Gaussian differential privacy (GDP) value of 3.34. It comes from a central limit theorem (CLT), which approximates the run rather than bounding it, and it lands below the certified values, so never report it.
The pass line runs three checks. The PLD value must be at most the target, which fails if \(\sigma\) was rounded down or the steps differ from the plan. RDP must lie at or above the PLD, up to its grid error, and PRV must agree with the PLD within 3%. If either of these fails, the accountants were given different runs.
The last line is the PLD’s error bar. Rounding each step’s privacy loss up to the grid gives the reported 3.9806, and rounding it down gives an optimistic 3.9656, so the true \(\varepsilon\) lies between them. Claim the upper value and report the lower one as its error bar (Which accountant). The bracket widens with the steps, so a long run needs a finer grid.
