title: 32  Calibrate and account a DP-SGD run
section: 32.6 If the loader is not Poisson
text:
32.6 If the loader is not Poisson
Not every training loop samples by the Poisson scheme, so price the alternatives before you train. The script accounts the chosen run, with its loader’s steps, under the four samplers of Amplification by subsampling.
Poisson (PLD)                              eps=3.98
fixed size, add/remove, sigma/2 (PLD)      eps=23.03
fixed size, replace-one (RDP)              eps=52.60
shuffle, zero-out, no amplification (PLD)  eps=18.51
PLDAccountant supports sampling without replacement: add/remove False, replace-one False
Fixed-size random batches cost more, because a record added to a full batch pushes another out, so the clipped sum can move by twice the clipping norm \(C\). Under add/remove neighbours, the Poisson accountant at half the noise multiplier covers them, which turns 3.98 into 23.03. Under replace-one neighbours only RDP accounts them, at \(\sigma/2\) too, since the PLD accountant cannot (last line). Its 52.60 protects a record’s value rather than its presence, so it does not compare with the add/remove values.
Shuffling once per epoch and cutting the data into batches gets no amplification, so all that is certain is one Gaussian step per epoch, 18.51 here. That holds for zero-out neighbours, which differ by one record’s gradient being replaced by zero, and the statement must name that relation. A step’s sum then moves by at most \(C\), as under add/remove, so the value compares with the add/remove ones. It beats fixed-size batches here, but on the 100-epoch run of Report and review an ε claim the order reverses. So the fix for a non-Poisson loader is the loader: keep the Poisson loader that Opacus’s make_private installs.
crumbs: 32  Calibrate and account a DP-SGD run

title: 32  Calibrate and account a DP-SGD run
text:
32.7 Train, stop early and resume
During training, Opacus’s optimizer calls accountant.step once per noisy update, which is once per logical batch, even when BatchMemoryManager splits it into smaller physical ones. The script simulates the run’s 300 calls and asks for \(\varepsilon\) after each epoch.
def train_epochs(
    accountant: PRVAccountant, sigma: float, q: float, steps_per_epoch: int, epochs: int, delta: float
) -> list[float]:
    """Step the accountant once per logical batch for `epochs` epochs; epsilon at the end of each epoch."""
    epsilons: list[float] = []
    for _ in range(epochs):
        for _ in range(steps_per_epoch):
            accountant.step(noise_multiplier=sigma, sample_rate=q)  # what the optimizer's step does
        epsilons.append(float(accountant.get_epsilon(delta)))
    return epsilons
Suppose the validation loss stalls and the run stops after six of its ten planned epochs. Stopping early is safe, because the stopped run releases a prefix of the planned run, which the planned guarantee covers. But you still report the planned maximum. The \(\varepsilon\) at the stopping point is not a valid claim, because the decision to stop depended on what the run released. Only a privacy filter running from the first step could certify it (Adaptive composition). Log \(\varepsilon\) every epoch anyway, because it must never decrease, so a drop means the accountant was reset.
Training past the maximum is not safe. If you add epochs after seeing the model, the number of steps depends on what the run released, so the longer run’s \(\varepsilon\) is not a valid claim either. An extension needs a new plan, accounted from the first step. So plan the longest run you might want, and treat stopping sooner as an early stop.
A job that stops and restarts must carry the accountant with it. Save its state_dict with the model and load it before the first new step, as Opacus’s PrivacyEngine.save_checkpoint and load_checkpoint do.
state = accountant.state_dict()  # saved with the model; PrivacyEngine.save_checkpoint stores it too
# ... the job stops, and later restarts ...
restarted = PRVAccountant()
restarted.load_state_dict(state)  # without this, epsilon would restart from zero
resumed = train_epochs(restarted, sigma, q, steps_per_epoch, epochs - stop, delta)
steps_recorded = sum(steps for _, _, steps in restarted.history)
steps per epoch: 30; planned: 10 epochs = 300 steps
epoch  1: eps=1.70
epoch  2: eps=2.09
epoch  4: eps=2.69
epoch  6: eps=3.18
epsilon never decreases over 10 epochs: True
stopped early at epoch 6: eps=3.18; report the planned maximum: eps=3.99
after resuming at epoch 6: eps at epoch 10=3.99; uninterrupted run: eps=3.99; equal: True
steps recorded: 300; planned (the loader's 10 x 30): 300; equal: True
The resumed run ends at 3.99, like a run that never stopped, with all 300 steps in its history. A fresh accountant would have counted only the last four epochs and reported 2.69.

title: 32  Calibrate and account a DP-SGD run
text:
32.8 Write the statement
The last step writes the claim with every input a reviewer needs to recompute it. The script fills the template from the run’s parameters, and rounds up the PLD’s \(\varepsilon\) at the rule’s \(\delta\) and at \(1/n^2\), where \(n\) is the training set’s size.
def privacy_statement(
    unit: str, dataset: str, n: int, batch: int, epochs: int, sigma: float, clip: float, delta: float, calibration: str
) -> str:
    """The filled template of the reporting page: every input a reviewer needs to recompute epsilon."""
    q, _, steps = opacus_loader_plan(n, batch, epochs)  # the steps the Poisson loader runs
    run = SelfComposedDpEvent(PoissonSampledDpEvent(q, GaussianDpEvent(sigma)), steps)
    epsilon = round_up(PLDAccountant().compose(run).get_epsilon(delta))
    epsilon_tiny_delta = round_up(PLDAccountant().compose(run).get_epsilon(1 / n**2))
    return f"""\
Unit: one {unit} (a row of {dataset}); neighbouring datasets differ by adding or removing one {unit}
Data: n = {n:,}; Poisson sampling with q = {q:.6f} (B = {batch}); T = {steps:,} steps ({epochs} epochs)
Mechanism: DP-SGD, clipping norm C = {clip}, noise multiplier sigma = {sigma:.3f}
Accountant: PLD, dp-accounting {version("dp-accounting")}; {calibration}
Guarantee: (epsilon = {epsilon:.2f}, delta = {delta:.0e}); epsilon = {epsilon_tiny_delta:.2f} at delta = 1/n^2 = {1 / n**2:.1e}
Not covered: hyperparameter tuning runs (see Part 5), and any model released before this one"""
Unit: one person (a row of Adult); neighbouring datasets differ by adding or removing one person
Data: n = 30,000; Poisson sampling with q = 0.033333 (B = 1000); T = 300 steps (10 epochs)
Mechanism: DP-SGD, clipping norm C = 1.0, noise multiplier sigma = 0.973
Accountant: PLD, dp-accounting 0.6.0; calibrated with Opacus 1.6.0 (PRV)
Guarantee: (epsilon = 3.99, delta = 1e-05); epsilon = 6.30 at delta = 1/n^2 = 1.1e-09
Not covered: hyperparameter tuning runs (see Part 5), and any model released before this one
The guarantee reads 3.99 because the PLD value printed as 3.98 above is rounded up here, not to the nearest value. The unit, dataset and clipping norm come from options, because the accountant never sees them. The last line matters most to a reviewer, because it names privacy spent outside this \(\varepsilon\). Tuning on the private data adds its own cost (Hyperparameter tuning), and so does every earlier model trained on the same people.
A published statement also gives what the script cannot know (The statement). That is the setting, the PLD’s grid and bracket, and the data outside the run, such as pretrained weights and the unprotected validation rows.

title: 33  Amplification by subsampling
text:
33.1 Why this matters
Most private models are trained with stochastic gradient descent (SGD) made to satisfy differential privacy (DP), a method called DP-SGD. Each step clips every record’s gradient to a maximum length, the clipping norm, sums the clipped gradients and adds Gaussian noise. The noise’s standard deviation is the clipping norm times the noise multiplier \(\sigma\). If every record paid a full Gaussian step’s cost each time, ten thousand steps at \(\sigma = 1\) would have a privacy level \(\varepsilon\) of 5425.5 at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) (Rényi DP), no guarantee at all.
DP-SGD escapes this cost because each step looks only at a small random batch. Write \(q\) for the sampling rate, the probability that a given record lands in the batch. An attacker must then first guess whether the record was used at all, and that uncertainty is worth a lot. This amplification by subsampling depends on exactly how the batch was drawn. So the accountant, the code that adds up a run’s privacy cost, must assume the sampler the training code runs. Getting that wrong is the largest single error in DP-SGD accounting, far larger than the choice of accountant (Section 33.4).

title: 33  Amplification by subsampling
text:
33.2 One step under Poisson sampling
The simplest sampler is Poisson sampling, in which each record enters the batch by its own coin flip, with probability \(q\), independently of every other record. It goes with add/remove neighbours, two datasets of which one has an extra record. For this sampler and these neighbours, Balle, Barthe and Gaboardi (2018) give the best possible one-step result. Suppose a step is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP when it sees every record, where \(\delta\) is the small additive slack of Part 3. Then the same step run on a Poisson sample is \((\varepsilon', \delta')\)-DP with \[\varepsilon' = \ln\big(1 + q(e^\varepsilon - 1)\big), \qquad \delta' = q\delta. \tag{33.1}\]
Small and large \(\varepsilon\) behave very differently. For small \(\varepsilon\) the amplified cost is about \(q\varepsilon\), so a 1% sample makes a step about a hundred times cheaper, and a 1-DP step costs 0.0170. For large \(\varepsilon\) the amplified cost is about \[\varepsilon' \approx \varepsilon - \ln(1/q), \tag{33.2}\] so sampling only subtracts a fixed amount, and a 10-DP step on the same sample still costs 5.3993. The switch happens where \(\varepsilon\) is near \(\ln(1/q)\). So amplification helps most when each step is already fairly private, which is why DP-SGD takes many cheap steps.
The result has two conditions. Each record’s coin must be independent of the others, so that every record is drawn with probability exactly \(q\) whatever else is in the batch. And the batch must stay secret, because an attacker who reads the list of drawn records, say in a log, knows whether the target was used.

title: 33  Amplification by subsampling
section: 33.3 Match the sampler to the accountant
text:
33.3 Match the sampler to the accountant
Most training code does not draw Poisson batches. Some draws a fresh random batch of a fixed size \(B\) from the \(n\) records at each step. Much more shuffles the data once per epoch and cuts it into consecutive batches, which is called shuffle and partition.
Each sampler needs its own accounting under each neighbouring relation. Under replace-one, the datasets have the same size and differ in one record’s value, and under zero-out, the target’s gradient is set to zero. Table 33.1 gives DP-SGD’s accounting as events of Google’s dp_accounting library, which a Rényi differential privacy (RDP) or privacy loss distribution (PLD) accountant then composes.

The factor of two for fixed-size batches comes from the gradient sum. Under Poisson sampling, adding or removing a record moves the clipped sum by at most the clipping norm. A fixed-size batch has no room for an extra record, so a drawn record takes another’s place, and the sum can move twice as far (Lebeda et al. 2025). Twice the shift with the same noise is the same as the original shift with half the noise multiplier. Replace-one swaps a record by definition, so its shift doubles too, and there only the RDP accountant of dp_accounting covers fixed-size batches.
Shuffle and partition is worse, because the source of amplification is missing. Within an epoch the record is in exactly one batch and is never absent, so the attacker only has to find which batch held it. Chua et al. (2024) build a dataset in which the target’s gradient points against all the others, so that its batch’s sum stands out. On it, at \(q = 0.01\) and \(\sigma = 1\), one shuffled epoch provably has an \(\varepsilon\) of at least 4.06, while a Poisson accountant reports at most 1.21. So a Poisson number for shuffled training can be provably false. The honest bound is the table’s last row, one full Gaussian release per epoch, since each epoch uses the record exactly once.
So read the data loader before you trust a reported \(\varepsilon\). A PyTorch DataLoader with shuffle=True and a batch_size is shuffle and partition. Opacus replaces the loader with a Poisson one by default, since PrivacyEngine.make_private takes poisson_sampling=True unless you turn it off. Its batch_sampler is then a UniformWithReplacementSampler, which despite its name flips one coin per record, so batch sizes vary from step to step, a quick check in the training log. When the largest batches do not fit in memory, Opacus’s BatchMemoryManager splits each into pieces that fit, and the optimizer and the accountant still count one step per sampled batch (Train a model with DP-SGD). If you cannot use Poisson sampling, report under the matching row of Table 33.1, and name the sampler next to \(\varepsilon\).

title: 33  Amplification by subsampling
text:
33.4 Accounting each sampler
DP-SGD is never accounted step by step with Equation 33.1. That route splits \(\delta\) into a tiny share per step, and a tiny \(\delta\) forces a large per-step \(\varepsilon\), which sampling barely reduces, as for the 10-DP step above. On 10,000 steps it gives 24379.55 with advanced composition, worse even than 5425.5 without sampling. An RDP accountant instead adds the steps’ Rényi curves order by order and converts the total to \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) once, which gives 6.71 (Rényi DP). A PLD accountant is tighter still (Numerical accounting).
The snippet below accounts that run under four rows of Table 33.1, with 50,000 records in batches of 500, so \(q = 0.01\). It uses \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) to compare with the rest of the part, not the \(10^{-6}\) a report would use (Report and review an ε claim).
from dp_accounting import GaussianDpEvent, NeighboringRelation, PoissonSampledDpEvent
from dp_accounting import SampledWithoutReplacementDpEvent, SelfComposedDpEvent
from dp_accounting.pld import PLDAccountant
from dp_accounting.rdp import RdpAccountant

n, batch, sigma, steps, delta = 50_000, 500, 1.0, 10_000, 1e-5  # q = 0.01, 100 epochs
poisson = SelfComposedDpEvent(PoissonSampledDpEvent(batch / n, GaussianDpEvent(sigma)), steps)
fixed_size = SelfComposedDpEvent(PoissonSampledDpEvent(batch / n, GaussianDpEvent(sigma / 2)), steps)  # add/remove
shuffled = SelfComposedDpEvent(GaussianDpEvent(sigma), 100)  # one Gaussian release per epoch, no amplification
pld = [PLDAccountant(value_discretization_interval=1e-3).compose(e) for e in (poisson, fixed_size, shuffled)]  # 1e-3: the PLD's grid spacing
print(" ".join(f"{accountant.get_epsilon(delta):.2f}" for accountant in pld))  # 6.19 43.37 91.82
replace_one = RdpAccountant(neighboring_relation=NeighboringRelation.REPLACE_ONE)
swap = SampledWithoutReplacementDpEvent(n, batch, GaussianDpEvent(sigma / 2))  # replace-one: the sum moves by up to 2C
replace_one.compose(SelfComposedDpEvent(swap, steps))
print(f"{replace_one.get_epsilon(delta):.2f}")  # 118.73
Poisson sampling costs 6.19. With the same noise, fixed-size batches cost 43.37 under add/remove neighbours, about seven times more, and shuffling costs 91.82 under zero-out. The replace-one value, 118.73, protects a record’s value rather than its presence, so compare it only with other replace-one numbers. So the sampler moves \(\varepsilon\) sevenfold or more, while the accountant moves it by under 10%, from 6.71 by RDP to 6.19 by PLD.
Before you compose an unusual event, call PLDAccountant().supports(event), which returns False, for example, for a SampledWithoutReplacementDpEvent under either relation.

title: 33  Amplification by subsampling
text:
33.5 Batch size, epochs and noise
Amplification also shapes how you plan a run. Write \(E\) for the number of epochs, so that a run takes \(E/q\) steps at sampling rate \(q\). For small \(q\) and a large noise multiplier, the run’s Rényi curve, its cost at each order \(\alpha\), is then roughly \[\varepsilon(\alpha) \approx \frac{E\,q\,\alpha}{2\sigma^2}. \tag{33.3}\] So at a fixed number of epochs a smaller sampling rate costs less privacy, because each step costs about \(q^2\) while the number of steps grows only as \(1/q\). Use this only for planning, never as the reported number, because at high orders the true curve rises far above it (from about order 9 at \(\sigma = 1\) and \(q = 0.01\)).
Privacy is not the only cost, because the noise lands on the averaged gradient. With \(C\) for the clipping norm, the noise on the sum of \(B\) records has standard deviation \(\sigma C\), so the noise on their average has \(\sigma C/B\). So compare plans by \(\sigma/B\), not by \(\sigma\). The planning table of Calibrate and account a DP-SGD run shows why. At a fixed \(\varepsilon\), a ten times larger batch needs a larger \(\sigma\), yet its \(\sigma/B\) is six times smaller.
Plan in this order, then. First fix the batch size \(B\) and the epochs \(E\) that your accuracy needs. They set \(q = B/n\) and the number of steps, where \(n\) is the size of the dataset you actually train on, after any filtering. Then let the accountant solve for \(\sigma\), naming the numerical accountant in Opacus’s get_noise_multiplier, whose default is RDP (Calibrate and account a DP-SGD run).

Account for the sampler you run, check that its batches vary in size, and state the neighbouring relation next to \(\varepsilon\). ## References

title: 34  Rényi differential privacy
text:
34.1 Why this matters
Training a model runs thousands of private steps, and you report one differential privacy (DP) guarantee for all of them: a privacy level \(\varepsilon\) with a small slack \(\delta\). Adding up the steps’ pairs with the advanced composition of Part 3 (Composition) is far too pessimistic. Take 1000 steps of full-batch noisy gradient descent, each adding Gaussian noise with a standard deviation 20 times the most one record can move the gradient. At \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), advanced composition gives \(\varepsilon = 68.01\), nine times the exact 7.51, so a run calibrated to it adds more noise than it needs.
Rényi differential privacy (RDP) fixes this by keeping a whole curve of privacy costs for each step instead of one point. The curves of the steps add, with no \(\delta\) spent along the way, and you convert the total into \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) once, at the end. Even with Mironov’s original conversion (Section 34.6), the same run then costs 8.84, only 18% above the exact value. Opacus and Google’s dp_accounting both ship an RDP accountant.

title: 34  Rényi differential privacy
text:
34.2 The RDP curve
A DP guarantee compares the outputs of a mechanism on two neighbouring datasets, which differ in one person’s record. RDP measures how far apart those two output distributions are with the Rényi divergence of Divergences. That divergence has a dial, the order \(\alpha\), any number above 1. A small order looks at the typical output, and a large order weighs more heavily the rare outputs that are much likelier on one dataset than on the other.
A mechanism is \((\alpha, \varepsilon)\)-RDP if, at order \(\alpha\), the divergence is at most \(\varepsilon\) for every pair of neighbours. The smallest such \(\varepsilon\) at each order traces out the mechanism’s RDP curve \(\varepsilon(\alpha)\), and a higher curve means less privacy. The curve never decreases with the order. At order infinity it is the largest privacy loss of any output, which is what pure DP, the case \(\delta = 0\), bounds. You never compute the divergence yourself, because accountants know the curves of the standard mechanisms on a grid of orders.

title: 34  Rényi differential privacy
section: 34.3 RDP curves of the basic mechanisms
text:
34.3 RDP curves of the basic mechanisms
To account for a mechanism you need its curve, and the basic mechanisms have one in closed form (Mironov 2017). For the Gaussian mechanism, write \(\sigma\) for its noise multiplier, the noise standard deviation in units of the \(\ell_2\) sensitivity, which is the most one record can move the answer. Its curve is the straight line \[\varepsilon(\alpha) = \frac{\alpha}{2\sigma^2}. \tag{34.1}\] Table 34.1 gives the curves of the Gaussian, Laplace and randomized-response mechanisms at a few orders, each at sensitivity 1.

The Laplace and randomized-response curves level off at their pure DP level. The Gaussian curve grows without limit, so the Gaussian mechanism is not \(\varepsilon\)-DP for any \(\varepsilon\), but an accountant only converts at finite orders, where the curve is finite. These curves are for steps on the whole dataset. The private form of stochastic gradient descent (SGD), called DP-SGD, runs each step on a random batch, whose much smaller curves libraries compute for you (Amplification by subsampling).

title: 34  Rényi differential privacy
text:
34.4 Composition adds curves
Training runs thousands of mechanisms in sequence, each of which may depend on what the earlier ones released, as a gradient step depends on the current model. RDP composes them by adding their curves, order by order. Write \(\varepsilon_i\) for the curve of the \(i\)-th step. Then a whole run of \(k\) steps has a curve \(\varepsilon_M\) with \[\varepsilon_M(\alpha) \le \sum_{i=1}^k \varepsilon_i(\alpha) \qquad\text{for every order } \alpha. \tag{34.2}\] Different mechanisms mix freely, because you only add numbers at the same order.
Two conditions come with the sum. First, every curve must describe the same neighbouring relation, such as add/remove or replace-one, and the same unit of privacy, such as one record or one user. Second, each step’s curve must be fixed before the run. Steps may adapt to earlier outputs, but if the noise level or the number of steps is chosen from the data, the curves depend on the data too. Stopping when a validation metric looks good is such a choice, and needs Adaptive composition instead.
The sum is simplest for Gaussian steps, because their curve is the straight line \(\alpha/(2\sigma^2)\). Adding \(k\) such lines multiplies the slope by \(k\), which gives the line of one step with noise multiplier \(\sigma/\sqrt k\). So \(k\) Gaussian steps cost as much privacy as one step with \(\sqrt k\) times less noise, which is bad news for training. If 10,000 steps with noise multiplier 1 each used the whole dataset, they would cost as much as one step with noise multiplier \(1/\sqrt{10{,}000} = 0.01\), whose \(\varepsilon\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) is 5425.5, no guarantee at all. DP-SGD escapes this by running each step on a small random sample. This part’s running example is such a run: 10,000 steps with noise multiplier 1, each on a random 1% of the data.

title: 34  Rényi differential privacy
text:
34.5 Post-processing and group privacy
Post-processing is free in RDP. Any computation on the output that does not look at the data again leaves the curve no larger. So releasing the trained model or its predictions costs nothing beyond the training run.
Groups are harder: when one user contributes several records, you need a guarantee for all of them at once. RDP’s generic group rule is loose, so for Gaussian noise use the group’s sensitivity instead. A group of \(m\) records moves the answer by at most \(m\) times as much as one record, so the curve becomes \[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{group}}(\alpha) = \frac{m^2\alpha}{2\sigma^2}, \tag{34.3}\] which is \(m^2\) times the single-record curve. Ten records per user cost a hundred times as much. The fix is to clip each user’s whole contribution to one clipping norm and account per user (User-level privacy).

title: 34  Rényi differential privacy
text:
34.6 Compose, then convert once
After composing, you hold a curve, but you report an \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) pair. Both libraries turn the curve into a pair with the improved conversion (Balle et al. 2020, and independently Canonne, Kamath and Steinke 2020). From the curve’s value \(\varepsilon(\alpha)\) at one order and a target \(\delta\), it gives the privacy level \[\varepsilon' = \varepsilon(\alpha) + \ln\frac{\alpha - 1}{\alpha} - \frac{\ln\delta + \ln\alpha}{\alpha - 1}. \tag{34.4}\] You report the smallest \(\varepsilon'\) over the grid of orders, or 0 if that is negative, and libraries call the order that gave it the best order.
Older papers and code use Mironov’s original conversion, which gives larger numbers from the same curve, 7.43 instead of 6.71 on the DP-SGD running example. The moments accountant of the original DP-SGD paper (Abadi et al. 2016) is the RDP curve in a rescaled form, converted with Mironov’s formula. So its \(\varepsilon\) is loose but not wrong. The exact value is lower still (From Rényi DP to (ε, δ) and to tests).

title: 34  Rényi differential privacy
text:
34.7 Check the order grid
A conversion can only use the orders on the accountant’s grid, so the grid must contain the best order, which moves with the run. Long runs with little noise want orders close to 1, short runs with much noise want large ones. For the noisy gradient descent at the start of the chapter, it falls from 128 after one step to 4 after 1000.
The default grid of Opacus, RDPAccountant.DEFAULT_ALPHAS, stops at order 63, while that of dp_accounting, DEFAULT_RDP_ORDERS, goes on to 1024. A best order at either end of the grid means the true optimum lies outside it, so pass a longer list, with alphas=[...] in Opacus or orders=[...] in dp_accounting. Opacus warns when this happens, but with dp_accounting you compare the returned order with the ends of the list yourself.

title: 34  Rényi differential privacy
text:
34.8 Accounting with a library
In practice you describe each step to a library and let it compose and convert. In dp_accounting a DP-SGD step is a GaussianDpEvent inside a PoissonSampledDpEvent, which samples each record independently, with probability 0.01 in the running example. This snippet composes the 10,000 steps and prints \(\varepsilon\) with the best order.
import dp_accounting

step = dp_accounting.PoissonSampledDpEvent(0.01, dp_accounting.GaussianDpEvent(1.0))
accountant = dp_accounting.rdp.RdpAccountant()
accountant.compose(step, count=10_000)
eps, order = accountant.get_epsilon_and_optimal_order(1e-5)
print(f"{eps:.4f} {order:g}")  # 6.7128 4.1
In Opacus the accountant is attached to the optimizer, which calls step after every noisy update. Making those calls by hand gives the same \(\varepsilon\) to the fourth decimal, at the same order, 4.1, which is well inside both grids.
from opacus.accountants import RDPAccountant

accountant = RDPAccountant()
for _ in range(10_000):  # what the optimizer does at each step of training
    accountant.step(noise_multiplier=1.0, sample_rate=0.01)
eps, order = accountant.get_privacy_spent(delta=1e-5)
print(f"{eps:.4f} {order:g}")  # 6.7127 4.1
Opacus’s defaults mix two accountants, so name the one you want. In Opacus 1.6.0, PrivacyEngine defaults to "prv", a numerical accountant, and accountant="rdp" selects this class. But get_noise_multiplier, which solves for \(\sigma\), defaults to RDP. Both give valid upper bounds, but different ones: the numerical accountant gives 6.19 for the running example.
Two more checks catch most mistakes. The event must match the sampler your data loader runs, because shuffled fixed-size batches get none of a Poisson event’s amplification (Amplification by subsampling). And a manual call to step on top of the optimizer’s own charges each update twice.

title: 35  From Rényi DP to (ε, δ) and to tests
text:
35.1 What it is
An accountant that tracks Rényi differential privacy (RDP) ends a run holding a curve, a privacy level \(\varepsilon(\alpha)\) at each order \(\alpha\) above 1 (Rényi differential privacy). A report needs a differential privacy (DP) guarantee instead, a privacy level \(\varepsilon'\) with a small slack \(\delta\). A conversion turns each point of the curve into such a pair, and you keep the smallest \(\varepsilon'\).
There are two conversions in use. The original one, Mironov’s conversion (Mironov 2017), gives at each order \[\varepsilon' = \varepsilon(\alpha) + \frac{\ln(1/\delta)}{\alpha - 1}. \tag{35.1}\] The improved conversion, found independently by three groups in 2020, gives \[\varepsilon' = \varepsilon(\alpha) + \ln\frac{\alpha - 1}{\alpha} - \frac{\ln\delta + \ln\alpha}{\alpha - 1}. \tag{35.2}\] Both are valid, but at the same order the improved one is always lower, by an amount that depends only on the order: 0.3612 at order 10, and more at smaller orders. If the improved value comes out negative, report 0.
For example, one Gaussian release with noise multiplier 1 has the curve \(\alpha/2\). At \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) its exact value is 4.377, while Mironov’s conversion gives 5.299 and the improved one 4.729.
crumbs: 35  From Rényi DP to (ε, δ) and to tests

title: 35  From Rényi DP to (ε, δ) and to tests
text:
35.2 When you meet it
You meet the conversion whenever you compare an RDP number with someone else’s. Opacus 1.6.0 and dp_accounting 0.6.0 use the improved conversion. Older papers and code use Mironov’s, including the moments accountant of the original paper on the private form of stochastic gradient descent (SGD), called DP-SGD. On this part’s running example, 10,000 DP-SGD steps on a random 1% of the data with noise multiplier 1, Mironov’s conversion gives 7.43 and the improved one 6.71.
Because the saving depends only on the order, two RDP accountants that report values about 0.36 apart for one run, with a best order near 10, differ in their conversion. Recompute both with one library before comparing them.
crumbs: 35  From Rényi DP to (ε, δ) and to tests

title: 35  From Rényi DP to (ε, δ) and to tests
text:
35.3 How to use it
In dp_accounting, get_epsilon_and_optimal_order converts at the best order of the grid and returns both, so you never type the formula in. One curve answers every \(\delta\), so get_epsilon can report several pairs at no extra privacy cost. This snippet converts the single Gaussian release above.
from dp_accounting import GaussianDpEvent
from dp_accounting.rdp import RdpAccountant

accountant = RdpAccountant()
accountant.compose(GaussianDpEvent(1.0))  # one release, noise multiplier 1
eps, order = accountant.get_epsilon_and_optimal_order(1e-5)
print(f"{eps:.4f} {order:g}")  # 4.7285 5.4
print(f"{accountant.get_epsilon(1e-8):.4f}")  # 6.0864
A \(\delta\) a thousand times smaller raises \(\varepsilon\) only from 4.7285 to 6.0864, because \(\delta\) enters the conversion through a logarithm. The accountant picks the best order from its fixed grid, and short runs with much noise can want orders above 63, where the Opacus default grid stops. So whenever the returned order sits at an end of the grid, extend the grid and convert again (Rényi differential privacy).
crumbs: 35  From Rényi DP to (ε, δ) and to tests

title: 35  From Rényi DP to (ε, δ) and to tests
text:
35.4 What goes wrong
No conversion closes the whole gap to the exact value. The curve is only a summary, and other mechanisms with the same curve have a larger exact \(\varepsilon\). The improved conversion sits 5 to 10% above the exact value for the plain Gaussian, and can sit further above for the subsampled steps of DP-SGD. A privacy loss distribution (PLD) accountant keeps the whole distribution instead, and reaches the exact 4.377 for the single release (Numerical accounting).
The conversion also works in one direction only, because a guarantee with \(\delta\) above 0 gives no RDP curve. A mechanism that publishes your record with probability \(\delta\) is \((0, \delta)\)-DP, yet its Rényi divergence is infinite. So never feed an \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) pair into an RDP accountant, and take the curve from the mechanism behind it instead.
Converting also throws away what the curve says about attacks. Take a membership attack on the single release above, run at a false-positive rate of \(10^{-3}\). The curve caps its true-positive rate at \(2.4910 \times 10^{-2}\). The pair at \(\varepsilon = 4.729\) only caps it at 0.1131 (f-DP and Gaussian differential privacy).

title: 36  Numerical accounting with privacy loss distributions
text:
36.1 What it is
A privacy loss distribution (PLD) accountant computes the privacy level \(\varepsilon\) of a whole differential privacy (DP) run numerically. Take a dataset and a neighbour that differs in one record, and run the mechanism on the first. The privacy loss \(L\) of that run is the logarithm of how much likelier the output is on the first dataset than on the second. Because the output is random, \(L\) is too, and its distribution is the PLD. Only outputs whose loss exceeds \(\varepsilon\) add to the slack \(\delta\), and with \((\cdot)_+\) turning a negative value into 0, the smallest slack is \[\delta(\varepsilon) = \mathbb E\big[(1 - e^{\varepsilon - L})_+\big]. \tag{36.1}\]
When steps draw their noise independently, their losses add up, so the PLD of a run is the convolution of the steps’ PLDs. All the error comes from storing each PLD on a grid of losses, with a spacing \(h\) between grid points. Rounding every loss up can only raise \(\delta\), so the \(\varepsilon\) it gives is an upper bound, the pessimistic side. Rounding down gives a lower bound, the optimistic side. Each rounding moves a step’s loss by at most \(h\). So after a number \(T\) of steps the two values are at most \(Th\) apart, a width known in advance.
crumbs: 36  Numerical accounting with privacy loss distributions

title: 36  Numerical accounting with privacy loss distributions
text:
36.2 When you meet it
You meet a PLD accountant every time you train with Opacus, whose default "prv" is the privacy loss random variable (PRV) accountant of Gopi, Lee and Wutschitz (2021). It rounds each loss to the nearest grid point, so the errors partly cancel, then adds a proven error bound and reports the upper value. Google’s dp_accounting has PLDAccountant, which by default rounds up with connect the dots, the tightest pessimistic rounding a grid allows.

title: 36  Numerical accounting with privacy loss distributions
text:
36.3 How to use it
In dp_accounting you describe the run as an event, compose it, and read off \(\varepsilon\) at your \(\delta\). The method get_delta runs the other way, from a claimed \(\varepsilon\) to a bound on its \(\delta\).
from dp_accounting import GaussianDpEvent, PoissonSampledDpEvent, SelfComposedDpEvent
from dp_accounting.pld import PLDAccountant
from opacus.accountants import PRVAccountant

run = SelfComposedDpEvent(PoissonSampledDpEvent(0.01, GaussianDpEvent(1.0)), 10_000)
pld = PLDAccountant(value_discretization_interval=1e-4).compose(run)  # h, 10x the table's
print(f"{pld.get_epsilon(1e-5):.4f}")  # 6.1877
print(f"{pld.get_delta(6.24):.1e}")  # 8.5e-06

prv = PRVAccountant()
prv.history = [(1.0, 0.01, 10_000)]  # (noise multiplier, sample rate, steps)
print(f"{prv.get_epsilon(delta=1e-5):.4f}")  # 6.1980
Both answers are upper bounds inside the bracket of Table 36.1, so you can report either. Connect the dots reaches 6.1877 on a grid ten times coarser than the table’s. And get_delta lets a reviewer confirm the claim \((6.24, 10^{-5})\), since it bounds the run’s slack at that \(\varepsilon\) by \(8.5\times10^{-6}\).
Each library has one accuracy setting. In dp_accounting it is the grid spacing value_discretization_interval, and a tenfold finer grid narrows the bracket tenfold for about ten times the memory. In Opacus it is eps_error, the error allowed in \(\varepsilon\). The error grows with the steps, so set either for your longest run.
crumbs: 36  Numerical accounting with privacy loss distributions

title: 36  Numerical accounting with privacy loss distributions
text:
36.4 What goes wrong
The commonest mistake is reporting the wrong side of the bracket. Only the pessimistic value, or the PRV accountant’s upper value, is a guarantee. The optimistic value and the bracket’s midpoint are estimates.
Under add-or-remove neighbours, a subsampled step has a different PLD for adding a record than for removing one, and neither is larger in general. So an accountant must compose both and report the larger, as dp_accounting does by default. Opacus’s PRV accountant models only removal, the larger direction in the running example. Both assume Poisson sampling, which shuffled or fixed-size batches break (Amplification by subsampling).
A run whose steps or noise are chosen from the outputs needs a filter, which enforces a budget fixed in advance (Adaptive composition).

title: 37  f-DP and Gaussian differential privacy
text:
37.1 What it is
Every differential privacy (DP) guarantee limits how well an attacker can tell whether the data held a target’s record. The attacker runs a hypothesis test, so the fullest guarantee is a trade-off curve, the lowest false negative rate any test can reach at each false positive rate. A mechanism is \(f\)-DP when its curve never falls below a given curve \(f\) (Dong, Roth and Su 2022). A privacy level \(\varepsilon\) with its slack \(\delta\) only summarizes that curve.
For Gaussian noise the curve has one parameter. Write \(\sigma\) for the noise multiplier, the noise’s standard deviation in units of the query’s \(\ell_2\) sensitivity. In those units the attacker must tell a standard normal draw from one shifted by a distance \(\mu\) equal to \(1/\sigma\). So the mechanism satisfies Gaussian differential privacy (GDP) with parameter \(\mu\), written \(\mu\)-GDP. Write \(\Phi\) for the standard normal distribution function and \(\Phi^{-1}\) for its inverse. No membership attack at a false positive rate \(\alpha\) then reaches a true positive rate above \[1 - \Phi\big(\Phi^{-1}(1 - \alpha) - \mu\big). \tag{37.1}\]
crumbs: 37  f-DP and Gaussian differential privacy

37.2 When you meet it
You meet GDP when deciding whether a guarantee is enough, and as a trap in Opacus (Section 37.4). Table 37.1 reads \(\mu\) as the best true positive rate (TPR) of an attack at a given false positive rate (FPR), whatever else the attacker knows.

That is the ceiling for any membership inference attack, and what a privacy audit tests. Dong et al. suggest that \(\mu \le 0.5\) is a reasonable guarantee and that \(\mu \ge 6\) promises almost nothing, so report \(\mu\) next to a Gaussian pipeline’s \((\varepsilon, \delta)\).

title: 37  f-DP and Gaussian differential privacy
text:
37.3 How to use it
Gaussian releases compose exactly within GDP, even when each one depends on the earlier ones. Write \(\mu_i\) for the parameter of the \(i\)-th release. The run is then \(\mu\)-GDP with \[\mu = \sqrt{\mu_1^2 + \mu_2^2 + \dots + \mu_k^2}, \tag{37.2}\] so the quantity that adds up is \(\mu^2\). No accountant does better for releases on the whole dataset, such as analytics queries and full-batch noisy gradient descent. So keep a ledger of \(\mu^2\) and convert once, at the end. For example, four 1-GDP releases compose to 2-GDP, which is \((9.9973, 10^{-5})\)-DP. Converting each release first, with a quarter of the slack, and adding the four values of \(\varepsilon\) gives 18.7607, almost twice as much.
The snippet computes the attack reading and converts both ways. The dp_accounting functions take a noise multiplier, so for \(\mu\)-GDP you pass \(1/\mu\).
from statistics import NormalDist

import dp_accounting

N = NormalDist()


def attack_power(mu: float, fpr: float) -> float:
    """Best true positive rate of any membership attack on mu-GDP at a false positive rate."""
    return 1 - N.cdf(N.inv_cdf(1 - fpr) - mu)


print(" ".join(f"{attack_power(mu, 0.001):.4f}" for mu in (0.5, 1.0, 2.0)))  # 0.0048 0.0183 0.1378
print(f"{dp_accounting.get_epsilon_gaussian(1.0, 1e-5):.4f}")  # 4.3772
print(f"{dp_accounting.get_sigma_gaussian(1.0, 1e-5):.4f}")  # 3.7306
The second print converts 1-GDP to \((4.3772, 10^{-5})\)-DP. The third finds the noise multiplier of a single \((1, 10^{-5})\)-DP release. Both use the exact curve, which asks for less noise than the classical formula of the Gaussian mechanism.
crumbs: 37  f-DP and Gaussian differential privacy

title: 37  f-DP and Gaussian differential privacy
text:
37.4 What goes wrong
Opacus offers accountant="gdp" for the private form of stochastic gradient descent (SGD), DP-SGD. It estimates \(\mu\) with a central limit theorem (CLT), by which many steps that each leak little compose to nearly a Gaussian curve. For a number \(T\) of steps, each sampling a record with probability \(q\), Bu et al. (2020) estimate \[\mu \approx q\sqrt{T\big(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1\big)}. \tag{37.3}\] It is an approximation, not a bound, and it errs on the unsafe side, because a small \(\delta\) is decided by rare, large losses, whose tails a CLT fits poorly. On the part’s running example of 10,000 steps, the CLT gives 6.0071, but a numerical accountant proves that the true \(\varepsilon\) is at least 6.1377. So report with Opacus’s default numerical accountant, "prv".
A mix of Laplace and Gaussian releases needs a numerical accountant, because a curve that is not Gaussian takes the composition out of GDP. Gaussian pipelines without subsampling, though, are best accounted in GDP, since even the best conversion from a Rényi DP curve loses ground. For 1-GDP at \(\varepsilon = 1\), it certifies a \(\delta\) of 0.2149 against the exact 0.1269.

title: 38  Adaptive composition: filters, odometers and individual accounting
text:
38.1 What it is
The composition theorems of differential privacy (DP) assume that each step’s privacy parameter, and the number of steps, are fixed before the run (Composition). Real runs often choose them from the outputs, as when training stops on the validation loss. Plugging the realized values into the theorems afterwards is then invalid (Rogers et al. 2016). This plug-in mistake can make the bound fail about three times as often as its \(\delta\) claims.
A privacy filter fixes a total budget in advance and refuses any step that would exceed it, so the run keeps the budget’s guarantee whatever the stopping rule. A privacy odometer, for open-ended analyses, reports the spend so far instead, valid at every step but at a higher \(\varepsilon\).
crumbs: 38  Adaptive composition: filters, odometers and individual accounting

title: 38  Adaptive composition: filters, odometers and individual accounting
text:
38.2 When you meet it
Early stopping with a planned maximum needs neither. You fix the noise, sampling rate and maximum number of steps in advance, then stop when the validation loss stalls. Report the \(\varepsilon\) of the planned maximum, not of the steps you ran. Those steps are a prefix of the planned run, so the planned guarantee covers them. If 100 planned full-batch Gaussian steps with noise multiplier 10 are \((5.299, 10^{-5})\)-DP, a run that stops at step 60 reports that.
The rule needs three conditions. The stopping signal must come from the released models or from held-out data, so that stopping is post-processing. Training past the maximum needs a new plan, accounted from the first step. And a resumed run must restore its accountant (the calibration workflow).
You meet filters when the noise is changed during training in response to the outputs, and in analytics services, such as OpenDP’s make_privacy_filter or Tumult Analytics’ Session.
crumbs: 38  Adaptive composition: filters, odometers and individual accounting

title: 38  Adaptive composition: filters, odometers and individual accounting
text:
38.3 How to use it
The Rényi filter of Feldman and Zrnic (2021) works in Rényi differential privacy (RDP) at one order, written \(\alpha\) and fixed in advance. It charges each step its spend at that order (Rényi DP), which may depend on earlier outputs but must be known before the step runs. It refuses a step that would take the total past a budget \(B\). To aim at a target privacy level \(\varepsilon_g\) with slack \(\delta\), run the conversion from RDP backwards, which sets \[B = \varepsilon_g - \frac{\ln(1/\delta)}{\alpha - 1}. \tag{38.1}\]
A Gaussian step with a noise multiplier, written \(\sigma\), spends \(\alpha/(2\sigma^2)\) at order \(\alpha\). At order 5.8, the best fit for the early-stopping target, the budget is \(B = 2.900\). That lasts 100 full-batch steps at \(\sigma = 10\). Suppose training plateaus at step 60 and you halve the noise. Each later step then costs four times as much, so the budget left for 40 steps buys 10 more, and the run still meets the target.
OpenDP’s filter works in zero-concentrated DP (zCDP). Write \(\rho\) for its single budget number, which bounds the RDP spend at every order at once (Concentrated DP).
import opendp.prelude as dp

dp.enable_features("contrib")
domain, metric = dp.atom_domain(T=float, nan=False), dp.absolute_distance(T=float)
odometer = dp.c.make_fully_adaptive_composition(domain, metric, dp.zero_concentrated_divergence())
queryable = dp.c.make_privacy_filter(odometer, d_in=1.0, d_out=0.5)(0.0)  # rho = 0.5, i.e. 2.9 at order 5.8

answered = 0
try:
    for _ in range(1000):  # sigma = 10: rho = 1 / (2 sigma^2) = 0.005 each
        queryable(dp.m.make_gaussian(domain, metric, scale=10.0))
        answered += 1
except dp.OpenDPException:  # the release that would exceed the budget
    pass
print(answered)  # 99
OpenDP lets through 99 releases, not 100, because it rounds each charge up for floating-point safety. For pure-DP queries, the Whitehouse filter (Whitehouse et al. 2023) fits many more small queries than a plain sum of their \(\varepsilon\).
crumbs: 38  Adaptive composition: filters, odometers and individual accounting

title: 38  Adaptive composition: filters, odometers and individual accounting
text:
38.4 What goes wrong
An odometer costs more than a filter. The Ville odometer converts the RDP spend at the best of a grid of orders fixed in advance, It pays for that late choice by dividing \(\delta\) by the grid’s size. On the 100-step run above, that raises \(\varepsilon\) from 5.299 to 6.253.
Individual accounting charges each training record by its own clipped gradient norm, since a small gradient moves the model less, and drops a record once its spend would pass the budget. In the full edition’s simulation, the median record ends at an individual \(\varepsilon\) of 3.17, against 5.299 for the worst case. But that number comes from realized norms, so it is an estimate, not a guarantee, and it is sensitive, since a small one says the model fits that record well. And the records dropped first, with large gradients, are often those the model serves worst (Disparate impact).
Choosing hyperparameters from several runs is a separate cost (Hyperparameter tuning).

title: 39  Concentrated differential privacy
text:
39.1 What it is
Zero-concentrated differential privacy (zCDP) keeps a differential privacy (DP) budget as one number that adds up. It builds on the curve of Rényi differential privacy (RDP), which bounds how far apart a mechanism’s outputs on neighbouring datasets can be at each order \(\alpha\). A mechanism is \(\rho\)-zCDP when that curve lies under the straight line \(\rho\alpha\), so \(\rho\) is a slope. Composition adds the slopes, even when each step is chosen after seeing the earlier outputs.
The Gaussian mechanism’s curve is exactly such a line. Write \(\sigma\) for the standard deviation of its noise. The query \(f\) has an \(\ell_2\) sensitivity \(\Delta_2 f\), the most one record can move it in Euclidean distance. One release then costs \[\rho = \frac{(\Delta_2 f)^2}{2\sigma^2}. \tag{39.1}\] So a release with noise multiplier 1, where \(\sigma = \Delta_2 f\), costs \(\rho = 0.5\), and doubling the noise cuts \(\rho\) to a quarter.

title: 39  Concentrated differential privacy
text:
39.2 When you meet it
You meet zCDP in releases that add Gaussian noise to the whole dataset, such as noisy counts or the marginals behind a synthetic dataset. The 2020 United States Census used it with the discrete Gaussian mechanism (Discrete and floating-point-safe mechanisms), and Tumult Analytics and OpenDP keep budgets in \(\rho\).

title: 39  Concentrated differential privacy
text:
39.3 How to use it
Keep a ledger, a running list of releases, and charge each its \(\rho\) from Table 39.1.



Table 39.1: What each kind of step costs in a zCDP ledger.










Step

Notes

\((\Delta_2 f)^2/(2\sigma^2)\)

\(\varepsilon^2/2\), or \(\varepsilon^2/8\) for an exponential mechanism

Add the charges and convert the total once, at the end, to a privacy level \(\varepsilon\) and a small slack \(\delta\). Then you pay the conversion’s slack only once. An all-Gaussian total \(\rho\) costs the same as one Gaussian release with noise multiplier \(1/\sqrt{2\rho}\), so get_epsilon_gaussian converts it exactly. The snippet does this, then calibrates a \((1, 10^{-5})\)-DP release.
from math import sqrt

import dp_accounting

rho = 1 / (2 * 1.0**2)  # one Gaussian release, noise multiplier 1
print(f"{rho:.1f} {dp_accounting.get_epsilon_gaussian(1 / sqrt(2 * rho), 1e-5):.4f}")  # 0.5 4.3772
sigma = dp_accounting.get_sigma_gaussian(1.0, 1e-5)  # one release that must be (1, 1e-5)-DP
budget = 1 / (2 * sigma**2)
quarter = budget / 4  # four releases share it
print(f"{budget:.5f} {sigma:.3f} {1 / sqrt(2 * quarter):.3f}")  # 0.03593 3.731 7.461
So the budget for \((1, 10^{-5})\) is \(\rho = 0.03593\). A single query meets it with noise multiplier 3.731, so four queries sharing it each get a quarter and need twice the noise. Split the budget in \(\rho\), which adds exactly, never in \(\varepsilon\). A histogram in which each person sits in one cell is charged once, not once per cell (Parallel composition).
A ledger with steps that are not Gaussian has no exact conversion. The simple conversion of Bun and Steinke (2016) gives \[\varepsilon = \rho + 2\sqrt{\rho\ln(1/\delta)}. \tag{39.2}\] It is safe but loose, overshooting the exact Gaussian value by 21% at \(\rho = 0.5\). The improved conversion of Canonne, Kamath and Steinke (2020) overshoots by only 8%, and the RDP accountant in dp_accounting applies it. So use it, or the exact one for an all-Gaussian ledger, and name it in the report.

title: 39  Concentrated differential privacy
text:
39.4 What goes wrong
The commonest error is reading \(\rho\) as \(\varepsilon\). A Gaussian release at \(\rho = 0.5\) is \((4.3772, 10^{-5})\)-DP, so reading it as \(\varepsilon = 0.5\) badly overrates the protection. And \(\rho\) covers only what passed through the noise. The Census Bureau released some counts exactly, and such invariants sit outside the guarantee, so list them next to the budget.
Subsampled steps belong outside zCDP, which gives them no amplification. On this part’s running example, a run of the private form of stochastic gradient descent (SGD), DP-SGD, zCDP reports \(\varepsilon = 5475.8\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) where RDP gives 6.719. So keep a pipeline that includes DP-SGD in RDP or a numerical accountant, where a \(\rho\)-zCDP release joins without loss as a GaussianDpEvent with noise multiplier \(1/\sqrt{2\rho}\).
Several records of one user cost more, because a group of \(m\) records costs \(m^2\rho\). Four records in a 0.1-zCDP release cost \(\rho = 1.6\).
A budget never renews, because next year’s releases about the same people compose with this year’s, so fix the period and its total in advance (Release and governance). And keep a long ledger in \(\rho\), not in diffprivlib’s BudgetAccountant, which adds \(\varepsilon\) by plain composition (Keeping a budget).

title: 39  Concentrated differential privacy
text:
39.5 References

Bun & Steinke, “Concentrated Differential Privacy: Simplifications, Extensions, and Lower Bounds” (TCC 2016): the definition.
Canonne, Kamath & Steinke, “The Discrete Gaussian for Differential Privacy” (NeurIPS 2020): the improved conversion.

title: 40  Amplification by shuffling and by iteration
text:
40.1 What it is
In the shuffle model, each of \(n\) users randomizes their own data, so each report satisfies local differential privacy (DP) at a level \(\varepsilon_0\). A shuffler strips identities and mixes the order, so each report hides among the others. The bag of reports then satisfies central DP at a much smaller \(\varepsilon\), which falls like \(\sqrt{\ln(1/\delta)/n}\) for a slack \(\delta\) that must be above 0. All results here are for replace-one neighbours.
For binary randomized response, the analyst learns only the count of 1-reports, so the shuffled guarantee can be computed exactly. For any other local randomizer, use the clone bound of Feldman, McMillan and Talwar (2021). With probability \(e^{-\varepsilon_0}\), another user’s report looks exactly like one you could have sent, and such clones hide yours. The numeric clone bound computes this exactly, while the paper’s closed form is looser and needs enough users.
crumbs: 40  Amplification by shuffling and by iteration

title: 40  Amplification by shuffling and by iteration
text:
40.2 When you meet it
Shuffling appears in telemetry systems such as Prochlo (Bittau et al. 2017), where the decision is how large \(\varepsilon_0\) can be. No maintained library accounts for it, so use the full edition’s shuffling_iteration.py.
Two other things share the name but get none of this amplification. A data loader that shuffles the training set once per epoch is a sampler (Match the sampler to the accountant), Federated clients that join rounds when available pass through no shuffler either, so account them without amplification or with matrix mechanisms.
You also meet amplification by iteration, where later training noise protects earlier records, in papers that release only the final model (Section 40.4).
crumbs: 40  Amplification by shuffling and by iteration

Work backwards from the target: compute the numeric clone bound for a few values of \(\varepsilon_0\), and keep the largest that meets it.

The choice of bound can decide feasibility. For 100,000 users and a target of 0.2, the closed form allows \(\varepsilon_0\) up to 2 but the numeric bound allows 4, so deploy the numeric bound.
Before reporting a shuffled \(\varepsilon\), check the bound’s assumptions, because if one fails, such as a leaked order or a colluding shuffler, only \(\varepsilon_0\) remains.

The order is uniformly random and hidden, with no metadata such as arrival time or network address.
The shuffler does not collude with the analyst.
Only honest users count in \(n\), since colluders reveal their reports to the analyst.
The count of users is the number of reports shuffled, so with several batches it is the smallest batch.
Each user sends one report per batch, or the reports compose like any other releases.
crumbs: 40  Amplification by shuffling and by iteration

title: 40  Amplification by shuffling and by iteration
text:
40.4 What goes wrong
Shortcuts fail where users are few or \(\varepsilon_0\) is large. For 1,000 users at \(\varepsilon_0 = 4\), the closed form says nothing, and a normal approximation of the count of 1-reports gives 0.9667 against the exact 1.6910.
Amplification by iteration covers one pass of noisy stochastic gradient descent (SGD) that keeps the weights in a fixed convex set (Feldman et al. 2018). It needs two conditions. Only the final model may be released, and every step must be a contraction, never moving two sets of weights further apart. That takes a convex, smooth loss and a small enough step. Even then the gain depends on the record. Over 10,000 records with noise multiplier 1, the middle record gets \(\varepsilon = 0.0707\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), but the last gains nothing and gets 5.2985, as one Gaussian step does. So report the worst record’s value.
Deep learning breaks both conditions. Checkpoints, logged models and a best checkpoint picked from several all release more than the final model, and non-convex losses are not contractions. Annamalai (2024) builds one whose final model leaks as much as all the intermediate models together. So claim amplification by iteration only for convex models, such as logistic regression, that release just their final weights.

title: Differential privacy in machine learning
text:
This part is for anyone who trains, ships or reviews a model under differential privacy (DP). It builds on the Gaussian mechanism and composition from Part 3 and an accountant from Part 4. Its audits reuse the membership-inference attacks of Part 2.
Every private training method has two halves. The privacy half, the guarantee \(\varepsilon\), is computed by an accountant, while the utility half, accuracy, can only be measured. The main private algorithm is stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with clipped per-example gradients and Gaussian noise, called DP-SGD. Its accountant needs just three settings: the noise multiplier, the sampling rate and the number of steps. So every page asks whether the \(\varepsilon\) is correct and whether the accuracy at that \(\varepsilon\) is good enough.
Three pages are workflows, each a whole job done with real libraries on public data. Train a model with DP-SGD trains a classifier on the Adult census data with Opacus. Fine-tune a language model privately with LoRA adapts a small public language model to a private text and checks it for memorized secrets. Release and governance recomputes the guarantee, writes it down, maps it to the law and lists what to check before a model ships.
The other pages explain the decisions those jobs make, in the order a project meets them. A short page on private empirical risk minimization for convex models leads to DP-SGD. Then come hyperparameter tuning, the privacy unit in User-level differential privacy and the budget in Choosing ε. Public data and private fine-tuning explains why a public starting model helps so much. Disparate impact and Auditing private training are the checks before release. Three reference pages cover rarer methods: private prediction, correlated noise across steps and adaptive data analysis.
Every number on these pages comes from a script you can run. At the end, you can train a private model, defend its settings and its \(\varepsilon\), audit it, and write its release statement.

title: 41  Private empirical risk minimization
text:
41.1 What it is
Most of machine learning is empirical risk minimization (ERM), which picks the weights \(\theta\) with the least average loss over a training set. Write \(D\) for that set and \(n\) for its number of records. A ridge penalty usually keeps the weights small. Its strength is a number \(\lambda\), and training minimizes \[\mathcal L(\theta; D) = \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\ell(\theta; z_i) + \frac\lambda2\|\theta\|^2, \tag{41.1}\] where \(\ell(\theta; z)\) is the loss of the weights on one record \(z\). Differential privacy (DP) asks that replacing one record barely change the released weights. So noise must enter the trained weights, the objective or each gradient step.
Output perturbation trains as usual and adds Gaussian noise to the final weights, with a small slack \(\delta\). The noise is scaled to the most the trained weights \(\theta^*\) can move between two datasets \(D\) and \(D'\) that differ in one record. For a convex loss, the ridge limits that move to \[\|\theta^*(D) - \theta^*(D')\| \le \frac{2L}{\lambda n}. \tag{41.2}\] Here the constant \(L\) bounds the length of each record’s loss gradient. It is 1 for logistic regression with labels \(\pm1\) and features of length at most 1.
Objective perturbation adds a random linear term to the objective and minimizes the result exactly. Part of the privacy budget \(\varepsilon\) pays for the loss’s curvature, which is at most a constant \(c\), one quarter for the logistic loss. The noise is scaled to what is left, \[\varepsilon' = \varepsilon - 2\ln\Big(1 + \frac{c}{n\lambda}\Big). \tag{41.3}\] The subtracted term grows as \(n\lambda\) shrinks, so with little data the ridge must grow to keep \(\varepsilon'\) positive.
Gradient perturbation adds noise to every gradient step instead. With random batches and clipped per-record gradients, it becomes noisy stochastic gradient descent (SGD), DP-SGD. It is the only option for a model that is not convex.

title: 41  Private empirical risk minimization
text:
41.2 When you meet it
You meet these methods for linear models, such as a linear probe on features from a public pretrained network (Public data and private fine-tuning). Objective perturbation is usually the most accurate, because the objective’s full curvature damps its noise, while only the ridge damps output perturbation’s. So use output perturbation only when training is a black box.
Whether you have enough data depends on \(n\) and \(\varepsilon\). On the training objective they matter only through their product, so halving \(\varepsilon\) costs as much as halving the data. On new data, with \(d\) features, privacy adds less error than sampling does once \(n\) is well above \(d\ln(1/\delta)/\varepsilon^2\).

title: 41  Private empirical risk minimization
text:
41.3 How to use it
IBM’s diffprivlib offers objective perturbation as LogisticRegression(epsilon=..., data_norm=...), with data_norm bounding each row’s length. Its version 0.6.6 fails with scikit-learn 1.8, so the snippet calls the mechanism it wraps, mechanisms.Vector, with the curvature bound \(c\) as function_sensitivity. The breast-cancer data has no public data dictionary to take feature bounds from. So the snippet treats 500 rows as private and 69 as a public stand-in. It clips the private rows to the stand-in’s log-transformed ranges and maps them to \([-1, 1]\). A constant 1 replaces the intercept, and dividing by \(\sqrt{31}\) keeps each row’s length at most 1.
import numpy as np
from diffprivlib.mechanisms import Vector
from scipy.optimize import minimize
from sklearn.datasets import load_breast_cancer
data = load_breast_cancer()
public, private = np.log1p(data.data[:69]), np.log1p(data.data[69:])  # 69 stand-in rows fix the bounds
lo, hi = public.min(axis=0), public.max(axis=0)
X = np.hstack([2 * (np.clip(private, lo, hi) - lo) / (hi - lo) - 1, np.ones((500, 1))]) / np.sqrt(31)
y = 2 * data.target[69:] - 1
Xt, yt, n = X[::2], y[::2], 250  # even rows train, odd rows test
lam = 1 / n  # diffprivlib's default ridge, fixed in advance

def objective(w):  # J(w) and its gradient
    m = yt * (Xt @ w)
    return np.logaddexp(0, -m).mean() + lam / 2 * w @ w, lam * w - Xt.T @ (yt / (1 + np.exp(m))) / n

def accuracy(eps, seed):  # eps = inf adds no noise
    vector = Vector(epsilon=eps, function_sensitivity=0.25, dimension=31, alpha=n * lam, n=n, random_state=seed)
    w = minimize(vector.randomise(objective), np.zeros(31), jac=True, options={"gtol": 1e-9}).x
    return np.mean(np.sign(X[1::2] @ w) == y[1::2])

print(" ".join(f"{np.mean([accuracy(e, s) for s in range(20)]):.3f}" for e in [1, 4, np.inf]))  # 0.783 0.946 0.964
Averaged over 20 noise draws, test accuracy is 0.783 at \(\varepsilon = 1\) and 0.946 at \(\varepsilon = 4\), against 0.964 without noise. With only 250 training records, accuracy comes close only at \(\varepsilon = 4\). Nothing was tuned on the private rows, so the guarantee is pure DP for the 250 training rows, against replacing one record. The 69 stand-in rows, whose ranges the code prints, get none.

title: 41  Private empirical risk minimization
text:
41.4 What goes wrong
The most common failure is a bound taken from the data. Left unset, data_norm is computed from the training rows with a PrivacyLeakWarning, and the guarantee is gone. A range table computed from the same rows, like breast cancer’s, is no better, because each minimum and maximum is one record’s value. So take every bound from public knowledge or public rows, and clip the private rows to it.
The second failure is the solver, because output and objective perturbation assume the exact minimizer. A solver that stops where the gradient still has length \(g\) adds \(2g/\lambda\) to the sensitivity. That is small beside the exact sensitivity \(2L/(\lambda n)\) only when \(g\) is well below \(L/n\). So set the tolerance there, and check the final gradient rather than the number of steps.
The third failure is an unpenalized weight, because the sensitivity bound needs the ridge’s curvature in every direction. Scikit-learn’s loss, which diffprivlib reuses, leaves the intercept out of the ridge, hence the snippet’s constant feature. Fix \(\lambda\) by a rule or on public data, since tuning it on private data is a search that must be paid for (Hyperparameter tuning). Finally, these guarantees assume replaced records, unlike the add/remove accountants of later chapters. The two do not convert freely, so state the relation next to every \(\varepsilon\).
Derivations. Every result here is derived step by step in the full edition’s chapter.

title: 42  DP-SGD
text:
42.1 Why this matters
Nearly every deep-learning system that satisfies differential privacy (DP) runs one algorithm. It is stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with clipped per-record gradients and Gaussian noise at every step, called DP-SGD (Abadi et al. 2016). Clipping limits how far one record moves the model at each step, and the noise hides that move. An accountant adds up the cost of the steps into the guarantee’s \(\varepsilon\), with a small additive slack \(\delta\).
The accountant sees only the noise, the sampling rate (the chance that a record joins a batch) and the number of steps, never the model. So those three decide \(\varepsilon\), and the clipping norm and learning rate can be tuned for accuracy alone. Most failures come from code that breaks an assumption of the privacy proof, so the checks matter as much as the settings. Train a model with DP-SGD does the whole job in Opacus.

title: 42  DP-SGD
text:
42.2 The algorithm and its guarantee
A training set holds \(n\) records. The gradient of one record’s loss is its per-example gradient, written \(g_i\) for record \(i\). Each step of DP-SGD does five things.

Sample a batch. Each record enters independently with probability \(q\), the sampling rate, which is called Poisson sampling.
Compute the per-example gradient of each record in the batch.
Clip each gradient longer than the clipping norm \(C\) to length \(C\).
Sum the clipped gradients, and add Gaussian noise with standard deviation \(\sigma C\) to each coordinate, where the noise multiplier \(\sigma\) measures the noise in units of \(C\).
Divide the noisy sum by the expected batch size \(B = qn\), a fixed public number, and step against it, scaled by the learning rate \(\eta\).

Write \(\theta_t\) for the weights at step \(t\) and \(S_t\) for its batch. With Gaussian noise \(\xi_t\) drawn afresh on each coordinate, the update is \[\theta_{t+1} = \theta_t - \frac{\eta}{B}\Big(\sum_{i\in S_t}g_i\min\Big(1, \frac{C}{\|g_i\|}\Big) + \xi_t\Big), \qquad \xi_t \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2C^2I). \tag{42.1}\] Releasing every intermediate set of weights then satisfies \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP for add/remove neighbours, datasets that differ by one record (Amplification by subsampling).
This part’s running example (Section 42.7) trains a small network on 10,000 synthetic records. It runs 10,000 steps with \(\sigma = 1\), and each record joins a batch with probability \(q = 0.01\). For this run, the Rényi differential privacy (RDP) accountant, a standard and slightly loose upper bound, gives \(\varepsilon = 6.71\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). That \(\delta\) follows the book’s default of \(1/n^{1.1}\) rounded down to a power of ten (Choosing ε). To pick \(\sigma\) for a target \(\varepsilon\), let the accountant you will report solve for it (Train a model with DP-SGD).

title: 42  DP-SGD
text:
42.3 The implementation checklist
The guarantee rests on four properties of your code, and code that breaks one still trains and reports as before.
First, one record must move the clipped sum by at most \(C\). Batch normalization breaks this, because its statistics let one record change every other record’s gradient. So private models use group or layer normalization, which works on each record alone. With strict=False, Opacus’s validator lists the layers to replace instead of raising an error.
from opacus.validators import ModuleValidator
from torchvision.models import resnet18

model = resnet18(weights=None)
print(len(ModuleValidator.validate(model, strict=False)))  # 20
model = ModuleValidator.fix(model)
print(len(ModuleValidator.validate(model, strict=False)))  # 0
Also fix \(C\) in advance, from public data or a private estimate. A \(C\) read off the current batch makes the noise depend on the data.
Second, the accountant must assume the sampler the code actually runs (Amplification by subsampling). The Poisson accountant’s saving comes from each record’s chance of being left out of a batch. A loader that shuffles once per epoch and cuts fixed batches puts every record in exactly one batch per epoch. That chance is then gone, and the true \(\varepsilon\) can be far above the Poisson number.
Fixed-size batches drawn afresh at every step can still use a Poisson accountant, at the batch’s share of the data and half your noise multiplier. The halving is needed because a record that enters a fixed-size batch pushes another out, so the sum can move by \(2C\). It is expensive, raising the running example’s \(\varepsilon\) from 6.71 to 47.42, and it holds only for add/remove neighbours.
Third, divide the noisy sum by the public number \(B\), never by the actual batch size. The actual size is one larger when the protected record is drawn, so dividing by it reveals whether it was.
Fourth, the accountant must count every step that touched the data, including those of runs discarded in tuning.
Beyond the proof, state the neighbouring relation next to every \(\varepsilon\), and make data-dependent preprocessing private too. The guarantee covers one record, so a person with many records needs user-level privacy. For a model you release, turn on Opacus’s secure_mode=True, because floating-point sampling is not the exact Gaussian noise of the proof (Discrete and floating-point-safe mechanisms).

title: 42  DP-SGD
text:
42.4 Clipping and the learning rate
Clipping must happen per record. PyTorch’s torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_ clips a whole batch’s gradient, which bounds no single record and so gives no privacy at any threshold.
The clipping norm \(C\) does not change \(\varepsilon\), but it costs accuracy either way. A small \(C\) clips more gradients, so records with large gradients count for less, and they are often rare records (Disparate impact). A large \(C\) means more noise, since the noise is \(\sigma C\).
When every gradient is clipped, each has length exactly \(C\) and the noise is proportional to \(C\) too. So the step depends only on the product \(\eta C\) of the learning rate and the clipping norm. Clip hard, and tune that one number. On the running example, holding \(\eta C\) at 0.25 keeps test accuracy at 0.9599 or above for every \(C\) up to 0.3. Holding \(\eta\) at 0.5 instead, \(C = 10\) drops it to 0.8347.
Noise and clipping also move the best learning rate. Noise lowers it, as on the logistic problem of Optimization, while clipping raises it, because clipped gradients are shorter. The two do not cancel predictably, so search the step again whenever \(\sigma\) or \(C\) changes, and count the search’s runs in \(\varepsilon\).
Gradient norms also drift. The running example’s median per-example norm falls from 3.592 to 0.006 in a thousand steps. So a \(C\) that clips everything early clips only a minority later. Adaptive clipping follows the drift by moving \(C\) toward a quantile of the norms, measured by a small private count. Opacus offers it with clipping="adaptive" and five more parameters. Because the count spends part of the budget, the gradient gets more noise at the same \(\sigma\).

title: 42  DP-SGD
section: 42.5 Batch size at a fixed budget
text:
42.5 Batch size at a fixed budget
Averaging the noisy sum over \(B\) records divides the added noise by \(B\), so larger batches dilute it. At a fixed budget and number of epochs, a larger batch means fewer steps. The noise multiplier must then rise to keep \(\varepsilon\), but more slowly than \(B\) does. For a small sampling rate \(q\) and a \(\sigma\) well above 1, the accountant’s cost over a fixed number of epochs depends on \(q/\sigma^2\). So \(\sigma\) only has to grow like \(\sqrt q\). Since \(q = B/n\), with \(n\) the number of records, the noise on the averaged gradient falls with the batch size, \[\sigma \propto \sqrt{\frac Bn}, \qquad \frac{\sigma C}{B} \propto \frac{C}{\sqrt{Bn}}. \tag{42.2}\]
So choose the largest batch your hardware allows, with a larger learning rate for the fewer steps. When it does not fit in memory, Opacus’s BatchMemoryManager splits the batch the sampler draws into physical batches that fit. It still steps once per sampled batch, so the accounting stays the same.

title: 42  DP-SGD
text:
42.6 Making it fast
Computed one record at a time, DP-SGD can run tens or hundreds of times slower than ordinary training. Two fixes cost nothing. Vectorized per-example gradients, from torch.func.vmap or Opacus’s hooks, compute the same clipped sum in parallel. Ghost clipping also saves memory, because it gets each record’s gradient norm from each layer’s inputs and errors without the gradient itself. Opacus turns it on with grad_sample_mode="ghost".
The third fix, microbatching, costs accuracy. It clips the average gradient of each group of \(m\) records. One record can change its group’s clipped average by up to \(2C\), so the noise doubles. The update then averages over \(B/m\) groups rather than \(B\) records, so the noise on each coordinate of the averaged update becomes \[2m\cdot\frac{\sigma C}{B}. \tag{42.3}\] On the running example at \(\sigma = 1\), groups of 4 cut test accuracy from 0.9589 to 0.9336. So use microbatching only as a last resort.

title: 43  Train a model with DP-SGD
text:
43.1 Why this matters
You have a PyTorch training loop on sensitive data, and it must become private. The algorithm is stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with differential privacy (DP), called DP-SGD, which clips each record’s gradient and adds noise at every step (DP-SGD). The library is Opacus, and the hard part is not the call that wraps the model but the dozen decisions around it. Most are inputs to the guarantee. A mistake in any of them leaves code that trains as before but reports a false privacy level \(\varepsilon\).
This chapter does the whole job on Adult, a census survey of 48,842 people from the UCI Machine Learning Repository. The task is to predict whether a person earns more than $50,000 a year. The script practitioner_dp_sgd.py runs every step except tuning, which practitioner_tuning.py does. Each runs in one to two minutes without a GPU.
