title: 43  Train a model with DP-SGD
section: 43.2 Fix the privacy unit, n and δ
text:
43.2 Fix the privacy unit, n and δ
The first decision is what one record is, because the guarantee protects exactly that (User-level differential privacy). In Adult each row is one person, which rests on how the survey was collected, since Adult has no person identifier. When your data has one, count distinct identifiers, not rows, and give a person with many rows user-level training.
The script splits the rows with seed 0 into 30,000 private training rows and 16,842 test rows. The other 2,000, the stand-in rows from here on, play the part of public data. The script chooses the clipping norm (the length each record’s gradient is cut to) and the learning rate on them, and never trains on them. Since they come from the same survey, this is an assumption for the demonstration. In production the role belongs to genuinely public data, and without any, tuning costs privacy (Section 43.10).
Next comes \(\delta\), the small additive slack the guarantee allows on top of \(\varepsilon\). It depends only on the number of people \(n\) in the private training set. The book’s default is \(\delta \le 1/n^{1.1}\), rounded down to a power of ten, which keeps it safely below \(1/n\) (Choosing ε).
def delta_for(n: int) -> float:
    """The book's default: delta <= 1/n^1.1, rounded down to a power of ten."""
    return 10.0 ** math.floor(math.log10(n**-1.1))
For the 30,000 private training rows, not the 48,842 of the whole dataset, the script prints \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). The usual mistake is quoting a \(\delta\) above \(1/n\).
crumbs: 43  Train a model with DP-SGD

title: 43  Train a model with DP-SGD
text:
43.3 Preprocess from public facts
Every statistic computed from the private rows is itself a release. The accountant, which adds up the privacy cost of training, does not count it. A scaler fitted on the training set leaks each column’s mean and spread. An encoder fitted on it leaks which categories occur, even a country only one person comes from.
So the script takes its category lists from the dataset’s documentation. It scales each number by bounds the survey publishes, such as ages from 17 to 90. Capital gains and losses go on a log scale first, and a missing value becomes its own category.
def features(rows: pl.DataFrame) -> Array:
    """One-hot categories from the documented lists, numbers scaled by public bounds."""
    rows = rows.with_columns(pl.col("capital-gain", "capital-loss").log1p())
    numeric = [
        np.clip((rows[name].to_numpy() - low) / (high - low), 0.0, 1.0) for name, (low, high) in NUMERIC_BOUNDS.items()
    ]
    encoder = OneHotEncoder(categories=list(CATEGORIES.values()), sparse_output=False)
    text = rows.select(pl.col(list(CATEGORIES)).fill_null("?")).to_numpy()
    encoder.fit(text[:1])  # the categories are given, so fitting learns nothing from the rows
    return np.hstack([np.column_stack(numeric), encoder.transform(text)])
This gives 91 features, and the model is a small network with one hidden layer of 64 units and 6,018 weights in all. To check this step in someone else’s code, search for every fit call and ask what data it sees.
crumbs: 43  Train a model with DP-SGD

title: 43  Train a model with DP-SGD
text:
43.4 Train the baselines
A private accuracy means little on its own, so train three baselines with the same model, batch size, epochs and optimizer. The non-private model shows the best you can hope for. A model with clipping and no noise separates the cost of clipping from the cost of noise. Always predicting the majority class shows the floor, where a private model whose training collapsed lands.
non-private: test accuracy 0.847
clip only (C=1, no noise): test accuracy 0.845
always '<=50K': test accuracy 0.759
Clipping alone costs little here. Had clip-only accuracy been far below non-private, no privacy budget would fix it, because the problem would be the clipping norm or the learning rate.
crumbs: 43  Train a model with DP-SGD

title: 43  Train a model with DP-SGD
text:
43.5 Check the model
Opacus computes one gradient per record, and some layers break that. Batch normalization is the common case, because its statistics mix the records of a batch, so one record changes every other record’s gradient. The validator lists such layers before you train.
errors = ModuleValidator.validate(model, strict=False)
print(f"validator errors: {len(errors)}")
Here it finds none. For a model with such layers, ModuleValidator.fix replaces batch normalization with group normalization (DP-SGD shows it on a ResNet).
crumbs: 43  Train a model with DP-SGD

title: 43  Train a model with DP-SGD
section: 43.6 Choose the clipping norm, batch and epochs
text:
43.6 Choose the clipping norm, batch and epochs
These settings are fixed before the private data is touched, because choosing them on it costs privacy. The usual guide for the clipping norm \(C\) is the typical per-example gradient norm on public data. So the script measures it on the stand-in rows.
wrapped = GradSampleModule(model)  # adds hooks that keep one gradient per row
wrapped.train()
logits: torch.Tensor = wrapped(split.x)
nn.CrossEntropyLoss()(logits, split.y).backward()  # fills p.grad_sample for every weight p
norms = stacked_norms(wrapped)
at initialisation: median norm 1.444  90th percentile 1.538
fraction clipped at C=1: 1.000
The median rule would give a \(C\) of about 1.4. The script keeps the usual default \(C = 1\), just below the median, so every gradient is clipped at the start. That costs nothing, because when every gradient is clipped, only the learning rate times \(C\) matters (DP-SGD).
The batch should be as large as you can afford. The noise on the averaged gradient is \(\sigma C/B\). Here \(B\) is the expected batch size, and the noise multiplier \(\sigma\) is the noise’s standard deviation in units of \(C\). The size is only expected because every batch is drawn at random (Section 43.8).
With \(B = 1{,}000\), Opacus sets the sampling rate \(q\), the chance that a row joins a batch, to one over the number of batches per epoch. That is \(B/n = 0.0333\) for the \(n = 30{,}000\) training rows, but not when \(B\) does not divide \(n\), so plan with Opacus’s value. Ten epochs of \(1/q\) steps each make 300 steps, and the epochs must be fixed now, since the noise is calibrated to them.
The optimizer is SGD with momentum 0.9. The script picks its learning rate on the stand-in rows too. It trains a non-private model on 1,500 of them at six rates and scores each on the other 500.
  lr=0.05: 0.814  lr=0.1: 0.816  lr=0.2: 0.826  lr=0.5: 0.792  lr=1: 0.812  lr=2: 0.768
non-private learning rate 0.2; DP-SGD learning rate 2 (x10)
DP-SGD then uses ten times the winning rate. That factor is a rule of thumb, not a measurement. Private runs usually need a step several times the non-private one, because clipped gradients are shorter (DP-SGD). No private row has been touched, so this choice costs no privacy.
crumbs: 43  Train a model with DP-SGD

title: 43  Train a model with DP-SGD
text:
43.7 Calibrate the noise
Fix the target \(\varepsilon\), the slack \(\delta\), the sampling rate \(q\) and the number of epochs. Then let the accountant solve for the smallest noise multiplier that meets them. Use the accountant you will report, here the privacy loss random variable (PRV) accountant, which computes \(\varepsilon\) almost exactly. Calibrating with a looser accountant pays for its overestimate of \(\varepsilon\) with extra noise (Calibrate and account a DP-SGD run).
sigma = get_noise_multiplier(
    target_epsilon=epsilon,
    target_delta=delta,
    sample_rate=sample_rate,
    epochs=epochs,
    accountant="prv",
)
For \(\varepsilon = 4\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) it prints sigma=0.973. The result holds only for the epochs and sampling rate you gave it. If you later train longer or change the batch size, recompute \(\sigma\) before training. Otherwise report the larger \(\varepsilon\) of what actually ran.
crumbs: 43  Train a model with DP-SGD

title: 43  Train a model with DP-SGD
text:
43.8 Train
The privacy engine wraps the model, the optimizer and the data loader. Its optimizer clips each record’s gradient and adds the noise. Its loader draws Poisson batches, in which each row joins each batch independently with probability \(q\), which is the sampling the accountant assumes. The script’s own loader shuffles and cuts fixed batches, so make_private must replace it for that assumption to hold.
engine = PrivacyEngine(accountant="prv")
optimizer = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=lr, momentum=0.9)
model, optimizer, data_loader = engine.make_private(
    module=model,
    optimizer=optimizer,
    data_loader=data_loader,
    noise_multiplier=sigma,
    max_grad_norm=CLIP,
)  # Poisson sampling is the default: each row joins each batch with probability q
The training loop is an ordinary one inside BatchMemoryManager. It splits each logical batch of about 1,000 rows into physical batches of at most 500 that fit in memory. The optimizer still steps once per logical batch, so the accounting does not change.
with BatchMemoryManager(
    data_loader=data_loader, max_physical_batch_size=PHYSICAL_BATCH, optimizer=optimizer
) as batches:
    for x, y in batches:  # Opacus splits each logical batch; it steps once per logical batch
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        loss = criterion(model(x), y)
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()
steps=300  q=0.0333
epsilon (Opacus PRV) = 3.99
test accuracy at epsilon=4: 0.846
The script leaves secure_mode off, so that its noise is seeded and its numbers repeat, and its record says so. For a model you release, pass secure_mode=True to PrivacyEngine. It draws the noise from a cryptographically secure generator and guards against the floating-point flaws of ordinary Gaussian samples (Discrete and floating-point-safe mechanisms).
crumbs: 43  Train a model with DP-SGD

title: 43  Train a model with DP-SGD
text:
43.9 Cross-check ε
An \(\varepsilon\) from one library is a claim about that library’s arithmetic. So recompute it with Google’s dp_accounting from the noise multiplier, sampling rate and step count of your plan. Opacus counts the steps it actually took. Its privacy loss distribution (PLD) accountant is almost exact, like PRV, but uses a different numerical method, so the two should agree to within rounding. Its Rényi differential privacy (RDP) accountant, an older and slightly loose bound, runs alongside.
step = dp_accounting.PoissonSampledDpEvent(sample_rate, dp_accounting.GaussianDpEvent(sigma))
training = dp_accounting.SelfComposedDpEvent(step, steps)
epsilon_pld = dp_accounting.pld.PLDAccountant().compose(training).get_epsilon(delta)
epsilon_rdp = dp_accounting.rdp.RdpAccountant().compose(training).get_epsilon(delta)
epsilon PRV (Opacus) = 3.99
epsilon PLD (dp_accounting) = 3.98
epsilon RDP (dp_accounting) = 4.50
The PRV and PLD values agree. RDP gives 4.50 for the same run, a valid but looser bound, so a statement must name its accountant. If the two tight accountants disagree by more than rounding, the run did not do what the plan says.
crumbs: 43  Train a model with DP-SGD

title: 43  Train a model with DP-SGD
text:
43.10 Tune honestly
The default is the one this run used: choose every hyperparameter on public data, or on a public stand-in, and tuning costs nothing. When no public data exists, tuning runs on the private rows. Then every private run that influences the release costs privacy, including the runs you discard (Hyperparameter tuning).
The tuning script measures that cost for six learning rates at a total \(\varepsilon\) of 4, against a single untuned run. A grid runs all six rates and pays for each by composition. A random search runs a Poisson number of models with mean 4, each at a rate drawn from the six, and releases only the best. Only RDP handles a random number of runs, so the script uses it throughout. That is why its single-run \(\sigma\) is larger than the PRV value above.
def random_search(sigma: float) -> dp_accounting.DpEvent:
    """A Poisson number of runs with mean 4 (shape=inf selects the Poisson case); only the best is released."""
    return dp_accounting.dp_event.RepeatAndSelectDpEvent(one_run(sigma), mean=MEAN_RUNS, shape=math.inf)


def sigma_for(strategy: Callable[[float], dp_accounting.DpEvent], epsilon: float, delta: float) -> float:
    """The smallest noise multiplier per run that keeps the whole strategy within (epsilon, delta).

    The search starts at 0.1 and tries 1 first.
    """
    return dp_accounting.calibrate_dp_mechanism(
        dp_accounting.rdp.RdpAccountant, strategy, epsilon, delta, dp_accounting.LowerEndpointAndGuess(0.1, 1.0)
    )
one run, no tuning: sigma=1.029
grid of 6, all runs counted: sigma=1.816
random search, Poisson mean 4 runs: sigma=1.256
naive grid of 6 at sigma=1.029: reports epsilon=4.00
naive grid, true epsilon of all 6 runs = 9.84
The naive grid is the common mistake. It trains six models at the single-run noise, reports the \(\varepsilon\) of one, and actually spends 9.84. The random search pays for its honesty with a modest rise in \(\sigma\), from 1.029 to 1.256.
With seed 0, the search drew only two runs, both at the learning rate 0.05. Its model reaches 0.828 on the test set, below the 0.846 of the run tuned on public data. A search with few runs can miss. Do not redraw until you like the answer, because the guarantee depends on the randomness of the draw. So spend private runs on tuning only when no public data can stand in.

title: 44  Hyperparameter tuning and private selection
text:
44.1 Why this matters
Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with clipped gradients and Gaussian noise satisfies differential privacy (DP) at the level its accountant reports for one run. It is called DP-SGD. But nobody trains once. You try several learning rates, score each model and ship the best, and every run and every score touched private data. So the privacy level \(\varepsilon\) you report must pay for the search too.
Releasing only the best of a fixed number of runs can cost as much as releasing all of them. On the Adult census data, a grid of six runs that each meet \(\varepsilon = 4\) really costs 9.84. If instead you draw the number of runs at random, from a distribution fixed in advance, the whole search costs little more than one run.
crumbs: 44  Hyperparameter tuning and private selection

title: 44  Hyperparameter tuning and private selection
text:
44.2 The procedure and the report
The cheapest tuning is the tuning you don’t do on private data. Runs on public or proxy data cost nothing, and neither do published settings for similar tasks. Fix a large batch, the number of epochs and a small clipping norm in advance. With the clipping norm below the typical gradient norm, only its product with the learning rate matters, so often only that product needs a search (DP-SGD).
If you must tune on private data, fix the search before you touch the data. Write down the candidate set, the distribution of the number of runs (Section 44.4), the score and the validation set. Trying “a few more” later, or restarting a disappointing search, makes the search depend on the data, which no accountant covers. The score must be private as well (Section 44.5).
Then account for the whole search. For two or three candidates, charge for every run (Section 44.3), and for more, use random search with a random number of runs (Section 44.4). Either way, count every run that touched the private data, including crashed and debugging runs and evaluations for early stopping.
Finally, log the candidate set, the drawn number of runs and each run’s settings and score. Then report two numbers. The \(\varepsilon\) of the released run says what the model alone would leak if its hyperparameters had been public. The \(\varepsilon\) of the whole procedure is what the release guarantees. An audit cannot check it, because an audit tests only the released model. With the book’s default slack for 30,000 records, \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) (Choosing ε), the Adult search of Section 44.6 reports as follows.

DP-SGD ran for 300 steps with Poisson sampling at rate 1/30. It clipped gradients to norm 1 and added noise with multiplier 1.256, so one run satisfies \((2.73, 10^{-5})\)-DP. The learning rate was chosen by random search over \(\{0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.5, 1, 2\}\). The number of runs was drawn from a Poisson distribution with mean 4, and each run was scored on 2,000 validation records treated as public. The whole procedure satisfies \((4.00, 10^{-5})\)-DP for add/remove neighbours, datasets that differ by one record. It was computed with dp_accounting from the Rényi bound of Papernot & Steinke (2022).
crumbs: 44  Hyperparameter tuning and private selection

title: 44  Hyperparameter tuning and private selection
text:
44.3 Paying for every run
A common argument says that choosing among eight learning rates reveals at most three bits. It is wrong, because the release is a whole private run, picked because of how it came out. If each run says only “good” or “bad”, the best is bad only when every run was bad. So a bad best reveals all of them, which in the worst case is as much as releasing every run. Even tuning without privacy and then training once privately leaks. The winning regularization weight can change when a few outliers are added, and so reveal whether they were in the data (Membership inference).
The safe answer is to charge for every run, because the best run is computed from all the runs’ outputs (Composition). For DP-SGD, a grid of \(k\) runs, each of \(T\) steps, costs exactly as much as one run of \(kT\) steps. One run of the synthetic running example of DP-SGD costs \(\varepsilon = 6.71\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). Ten such runs cost 27.23, about four times one run rather than ten, because the conversion to \(\varepsilon\) pays its \(\delta\) cost only once.
crumbs: 44  Hyperparameter tuning and private selection

title: 44  Hyperparameter tuning and private selection
text:
44.4 A random number of runs
The way out is to draw the number of runs \(K\) at random, independently of the data. A search whose runs all came out bad then most likely drew few runs, which says little about the data. So the whole search costs about one run, plus a term that grows with the logarithm of the expected number of runs. For DP-SGD, use the version of Papernot & Steinke (2022), which works with the Rényi differential privacy (RDP) that DP-SGD’s accountants already compute (Rényi DP).
To use it, fix the candidate set and the distribution of \(K\), either Poisson or a truncated negative binomial with a shape parameter \(\nu\). That family includes the geometric distribution, \(\nu = 1\), which is the random stopping of Liu & Talwar, and the logarithmic one, \(\nu = 0\). Then draw \(K\), run that many candidates drawn at random from the set, and release the best one by a private score. To get the cost from Google’s dp_accounting, wrap the event of one run in a RepeatAndSelectDpEvent. Give it \(\nu\) as its shape (infinite for Poisson), and compose it in an RdpAccountant.
NumPy draws \(K\) with rng.poisson(mean), rng.geometric(1 / mean) or rng.logseries(p). The last takes \(p\) rather than a mean, so solve its mean \(-p/((1 - p)\ln(1 - p))\) for \(p\).

Table 44.1 shows how the choice plays out. The geometric and logarithmic searches barely grow from 10 to 1,000 runs, while composition grows almost linearly. A smaller \(\nu\) gives a cheaper bound, but the search also stops after one run more often. The Poisson bound needs runs that are already very private, which a run at \(\varepsilon = 6.71\) is not, so here it grows almost like composition. A random number of runs may also miss the best candidate. With eight candidates and a geometric number of runs with mean eight, it never tries the best one with probability 0.4667.
The theorems have three conditions, and each is easy to break. First, each run must draw its candidate independently from a fixed distribution, as random search does. Bayesian optimization picks each candidate from earlier scores, so it is not covered and needs adaptive composition. Second, the number of runs must be drawn independently of the data. Third, the score that ranks the runs must be private and counted in each run’s cost.

title: 44  Hyperparameter tuning and private selection
section: 44.5 Selecting by a noisy validation score
text:
44.5 Selecting by a noisy validation score
Sometimes the candidates are fixed in advance, such as public pretrained checkpoints, and only the choice among them uses private data. That is a selection problem, which Selection solves with the exponential mechanism, a random choice weighted toward high scores. Score each candidate by its number of correct predictions, which one record changes by at most 1. An accuracy divides by a private set size. The mechanism’s shortfall from the best count then grows only with the logarithm of the number of candidates.
For the random-number bounds, add Gaussian noise to each run’s count of correct predictions, since an exact validation accuracy leaves the validation records unprotected. With noise of standard deviation 20, one noisy count costs \(\varepsilon = 0.182\). If the validation set is disjoint from the training set, each record pays only one of the two costs. So the event for one run is the costlier of its training and its count, not their sum. Otherwise compose both into one event. On the running example the counts are the cheaper, so they add nothing to the total.

def one_run(sigma: float) -> dp_accounting.DpEvent:

title: 45  User-level differential privacy
text:
45.1 Why this matters
Every differential privacy (DP) guarantee in this part so far protects one record. Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with clipping and noise, this part’s DP-SGD, gives each record of its running example a privacy loss \(\varepsilon\) of 6.71. But a messaging user contributes hundreds of messages, and together a person’s records can reveal far more than any one of them.
A DP guarantee protects whatever differs between two neighbouring datasets, so the neighbouring relation sets the privacy unit. So this chapter gives the running example’s 10,000 synthetic records to 1,000 users, very unevenly. The median user holds 4 records and the largest 348.

title: 45  User-level differential privacy
text:
45.2 The privacy unit and δ
Take a mechanism \(M\), and call two datasets neighbours, \(D\) and \(D'\), when they differ by adding or removing all the records of one user. The mechanism is user-level \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP, with a small slack \(\delta\), if every such pair and every set \(S\) of outputs satisfy \[\Pr[M(D) \in S] \le e^\varepsilon\Pr[M(D') \in S] + \delta. \tag{45.1}\] Example-level DP is the same inequality for datasets that differ in one record. So every property and accountant of Part 4 holds for user-level DP unchanged. What changes is the sensitivity, because one user can move the computation with all of their records at once.
The right unit, such as a record, a user, a household or a device, answers the question “whose participation do I want to hide?”. Report it with every \(\varepsilon\) (Report and review an ε claim). The unit also sets the slack, because the book’s default \(\delta\) (Choosing ε) now counts users. For 1,000 users it gives \(10^{-4}\) (Section 45.8), so this chapter’s \(10^{-5}\) is stricter than it needs to be.
The textbook answer for a person with \(k\) records is group privacy (Post-processing, group privacy and composition). An example-level \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP mechanism is also user-level DP for users with at most \(k\) records, at level \(k\varepsilon\) and with slack \[\delta_k = \delta\,\frac{e^{k\varepsilon} - 1}{e^\varepsilon - 1}. \tag{45.2}\] The fraction grows like \(e^{(k-1)\varepsilon}\), so a record-level \(\delta\) must never be read as a user’s. Holding a user’s slack at \(10^{-5}\) needs a much smaller per-record \(\delta\), and so a larger per-record \(\varepsilon\). On the running example a user with two records therefore gets \(\varepsilon = 18.61\), not twice 6.71. For ten records no per-record \(\delta\) is small enough.

title: 45  User-level differential privacy
section: 45.3 What an example-level model gives a user
text:
45.3 What an example-level model gives a user
Group privacy treats DP-SGD as a black box, but you know how a user’s records enter each step.
Each step includes every record independently with the sampling rate \(q\). So it sees some record of a user with \(k\) records with probability about \(kq\). While \(kq\) is small, two of their records rarely share a batch. So a user with \(k\) records looks like one record sampled at rate \(kq\). So you can screen a user’s exposure by rerunning the record-level accountant at rate \(kq\) (Section 45.8). An exact accountant for a user with \(k\) records also exists (Charles et al. 2024).

The rate-\(kq\) screen stays within 8% of the exact value up to ten records, but always a little low. It ignores steps that draw several of the user’s records together. So report the exact value when you have an implementation. The libraries this book uses offer only the screen. Then report its value, say it can be a few percent low, and keep \(kq\) small.
Treat the screen as the guarantee, not as a pessimistic bound, because a person’s similar records do push the gradient partly the same way.

title: 45  User-level differential privacy
text:
45.4 User-level DP-SGD
The better route makes the user the unit that DP-SGD samples, clips and accounts for (McMahan et al. 2018). Federated learning does this with a device as the user. Starting from weights chosen without looking at the data, each step does five things.

Sample users. Put each user in the batch independently with probability \(q\), now the user sampling rate.
Compute one vector per user. From that user’s records alone, compute their average gradient, or the change in weights after a few training steps on their records.
Clip per user. Rescale that vector to length at most the clipping norm \(C\).
Add noise. Sum the clipped vectors and add Gaussian noise of standard deviation \(\sigma C\), for a noise multiplier \(\sigma\).
Step. Divide by the expected number of sampled users and take a gradient step.

One user moves the sum by at most \(C\), however many records they have. So the guarantee is user-level DP with exactly the accountant of example-level DP-SGD, run at the user sampling rate.
That has two consequences. First, you pay for having fewer units. On a shorter schedule of the running example, 1,000 steps with about 100 units per batch, sampling records needs \(\sigma = 0.778\) for \(\varepsilon = 4\). Sampling the ten times fewer users needs a ten times higher rate for the same batch, and so \(\sigma = 3.78\). Second, records inside a user are free, since they can be averaged, used for several training steps or subsampled without changing \(\varepsilon\).
Carry a user identifier through the pipeline to sample by. Split training and test data by user, so that no user’s records sit on both sides. Opacus clips each row of a batch, so for user-level training you write a data loader that yields users and clip each user’s vector yourself. Three things break the guarantee:

A user’s vector depends on other users’ data, for example through normalization statistics computed over all users.
One person is spread over several accounts, so the unit is the account and the person is again a group.
Users are iterated in a fixed shuffled order instead of Poisson-sampled, which is a different mechanism that this accountant does not cover (Matrix factorization).

title: 45  User-level differential privacy
text:
45.5 Contribution bounding
A pipeline built around records can still protect users. Contribution bounding keeps at most \(k\) records of each user, the cap, and runs example-level DP-SGD on what remains. The result is user-level DP with the \(\varepsilon\) the user accountant gives for \(k\) records. The condition is that each user’s kept records are chosen without looking at other users’ data, for example at random. Otherwise adding one user could change which records other users keep, and neighbours would differ by more than one user’s records. To calibrate the noise for a cap, solve for \(\sigma\) with dp_accounting.calibrate_dp_mechanism at rate \(kq\) (Train a model with DP-SGD).
import polars as pl

rows = pl.DataFrame({"user": ["a", "a", "a", "a", "b", "c", "c"], "x": [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7]})
k = 2  # the cap, fixed from public knowledge of the population
capped = rows.sample(fraction=1.0, shuffle=True, seed=0).group_by("user").head(k)
print(capped.height)  # 5
print(capped.group_by("user").len()["len"].max())  # 2
Choosing the cap trades noise against bias (Amin et al. 2019). A larger cap keeps more data but needs more noise, while a smaller cap discards records and reweights the data toward light users. On the running example at a user-level \(\varepsilon = 4\), a cap of fifty records instead of one multiplies the noise by 5.8. Accuracy falls from 0.8917 to 0.6401.
So take the cap from public knowledge of the population. Or choose it privately and count the cost, for example with a private quantile of records per user (Beyond global sensitivity). Trying caps on test accuracy spends privacy the accountant does not see.

title: 45  User-level differential privacy
text:
45.6 Heterogeneous users
User-level training also changes the objective. Averaging per user weights users equally, while example-level training weights them by their number of records (Disparate impact). If heavy users should count for more, sum a user’s gradients before clipping instead of averaging them. Their influence then rises with their records until clipping caps the sum at \(C\), and \(\varepsilon\) does not change.

title: 45  User-level differential privacy
text:
45.8 Code
The rate-\(kq\) screen needs only a record-level accountant, such as Google’s dp_accounting. This snippet screens users with one and two records, and computes the default \(\delta\) for 1,000 users.
import math

import dp_accounting


def screen(k: int, q: float = 0.01, sigma: float = 1.0, steps: int = 10_000) -> float:
    """The epsilon of a user with k records, screened as one record sampled at rate k * q."""
    step = dp_accounting.PoissonSampledDpEvent(k * q, dp_accounting.GaussianDpEvent(sigma))
    accountant = dp_accounting.rdp.RdpAccountant()
    accountant.compose(dp_accounting.SelfComposedDpEvent(step, steps))
    return accountant.get_epsilon(1e-5)


print(f"{screen(1):.2f}")  # 6.71
print(f"{screen(2):.2f}")  # 15.35
print(10 ** math.floor(math.log10(1_000**-1.1)))  # 0.0001
Its 15.35 is a little above the table’s 15.32, because the two accountants use different Rényi orders. So quote the value you ran and name its accountant. With \(k = 1\) and \(q\) the user sampling rate, the same code accounts for user-level DP-SGD.

title: 46  Choosing ε
text:
46.1 Why this matters
Every model trained with differential privacy (DP) ships with a privacy budget \(\varepsilon\). The chapter on private stochastic gradient descent (SGD), DP-SGD, showed what each budget costs in accuracy. This chapter adds what it means for the people in the data, without which \(\varepsilon\) gets chosen by habit (“everyone uses 8”).
An attacker who wants to know whether a record was used for training runs a membership test. The test catches real members, its true positives, and wrongly flags non-members, its false positives. The budget \(\varepsilon\) and its small slack \(\delta\) cap the first rate in terms of the second (The definition of differential privacy). But each training run also has its own curve of the best rates an attacker can reach, which usually lies far below the cap. To choose \(\varepsilon\) well, compute that curve, read it at the false positive rate of your threat, and set it beside the accuracy each budget buys.

title: 46  Choosing ε
text:
46.2 Justifying a choice
A defensible choice says what the budget protects before it picks the number, in six steps.

Unit and period. Say whether one unit is a record, a user or a device, and whether neighbouring datasets differ by adding or removing one unit or by replacing one. Say which runs the budget covers, since every tuning run spends budget too (Hyperparameter tuning).
Threat. Say whether the concern is membership, reconstruction or attribute inference, and what the attacker knows and sees. This sets the false positive rate at which you read the curve, a low one for an attacker who must rarely accuse a non-member.
Whole guarantee. Choose \(\delta\) by the book’s default (Section 46.5), then compute the trade-off curve (Section 46.3) and read it there.
Evidence. The curve is a theorem about an algorithm, not about your code, so run an audit that could refute it (Auditing private training).
Utility. Put accuracy against \(\varepsilon\) next to the risk, and pick the smallest budget past the bend, where accuracy stops improving. Draw it on public or proxy data, because private runs that choose \(\varepsilon\) are a search whose cost the reported \(\varepsilon\) leaves out.
Comparison. Only now compare with deployments (Section 46.6) and with the tiers in the rules of thumb.

Adult, a public census survey, shows step 5 on a real run. Train a model with DP-SGD trains a small network on 30,000 of its people at five budgets, each with \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). title: 46  Choosing ε
section: 46.3 The pair and the whole curve
text:
46.3 The pair and the whole curve
A membership test says “member” or “non-member” about one target record. Its TPR is the chance that it says “member” when the target was in the training set, and its FPR the chance when it was not. Every test against an \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP mechanism satisfies \[\mathrm{TPR} \le \min\big\{1,\ e^\varepsilon\,\mathrm{FPR} + \delta,\ 1 - e^{-\varepsilon}(1 - \delta - \mathrm{FPR})\big\}. \tag{46.1}\] The middle term is the one that binds at low FPR, and the last applies the same cap to the members a test misses. Attacks are judged at a low FPR, because an attack that rarely flags a non-member identifies people with confidence (Membership inference). Yet at \(\varepsilon = 8\) and an FPR of \(10^{-3}\), the pair caps the TPR at 0.9997, which constrains almost nothing.
A real training run satisfies DP for a whole range of pairs, one \(\delta(\varepsilon)\) for each \(\varepsilon\), because its accountant can trade \(\varepsilon\) for \(\delta\). Each pair gives a line, the middle term of Equation 46.1, and every test must stay under all of these lines at once. The best test reaches the lowest line exactly, which is called the trade-off curve: \[\mathrm{TPR}^*(\mathrm{FPR}) = \min_{\varepsilon}\big(e^\varepsilon\,\mathrm{FPR} + \delta(\varepsilon)\big). \tag{46.2}\] For DP-SGD, a privacy loss distribution (PLD) accountant computes this curve. It can round the privacy loss up or down, and the two curves it gets bracket the true one (Numerical accounting).
Table 46.2 compares the pair with the curve for this part’s running example from DP-SGD, a synthetic run sampled at rate 0.01 for 10,000 steps.

So a budget of 8 means little as a bare pair, while its curve caps the TPR at 0.0589 at an FPR of \(10^{-3}\).
With Google’s dp_accounting, build the run’s PLD, ask it for \(\delta\) on a grid of \(\varepsilon\), and take the lowest line. The snippet’s first print, for the running example at \(\varepsilon = 4\), falls inside the bracket of Table 46.2. Its second uses Adult’s sampling rate of 1/30 and 300 steps, and gives the last column of Table 46.1.
import numpy as np
from dp_accounting.pld import privacy_loss_distribution as pld

EPS_GRID = np.linspace(0.0, 20.0, 2001)


def tpr_at(sigma: float, q: float, steps: int, fpr: float) -> float:
    run = pld.from_gaussian_mechanism(sigma, sampling_prob=q).self_compose(steps)
    deltas = np.array(run.get_delta_for_epsilon(EPS_GRID))
    return float(np.min(np.exp(EPS_GRID) * fpr + deltas))


print(f"{tpr_at(1.36, 0.01, 10_000, 1e-3):.4f}")  # 0.0126
adult = [tpr_at(sigma, 1 / 30, 300, 1e-3) for sigma in (8.125, 2.383, 1.431, 0.973, 0.722)]
print(" ".join(f"{tpr:.4f}" for tpr in adult))  # 0.0013 0.0023 0.0046 0.0123 0.0445
The library’s default PLD rounds the loss up, so its curve is a valid upper bound. A Rényi differential privacy (RDP) accountant gives a valid but looser curve. The Gaussian differential privacy (GDP) approximation is quick but not a bound, so use it to explain and the PLD to certify.
The curve is also a worst case, for an attacker who sees every intermediate model. A typical record attacked through the final model alone is much safer. It bounds reconstruction too, since a guess among \(m\) equally likely records is a membership test at an FPR of \(1/m\) (Reconstruction attacks).

title: 46  Choosing ε
text:
46.4 What an attacker can believe
Most people ask how sure an attacker can become that a given person was in the data. Write \(p\) for the attacker’s prior, its probability of “member” before it sees the model. A privacy loss of at most \(\varepsilon\) means that no output is more than \(e^\varepsilon\) times as likely with the person’s record as without it. So the attacker’s belief afterwards is at most \[\Pr[\text{member} \mid \text{output}] \le \frac{p\,e^\varepsilon}{p\,e^\varepsilon + 1 - p}. \tag{46.3}\] So DP bounds the change of belief, not the belief itself.
An attacker who starts at 1% can end at 35.55% when \(\varepsilon = 4\). That is the worst output, though, and in DP-SGD the privacy loss of the model actually released is usually far below \(\varepsilon\).
Base rates matter as much as the loss. An attacker who accuses every person its test flags as a member is right with probability \[\Pr[\text{member} \mid \text{flag}] = \frac{p\,\mathrm{TPR}}{p\,\mathrm{TPR} + (1 - p)\,\mathrm{FPR}}. \tag{46.4}\] Take the running example’s \(\varepsilon = 8\) run and an attacker with a 1% prior who flags at an FPR of \(10^{-2}\). The curve caps its TPR there at 0.2092 (Table 46.2), so at most 0.1744 of its flags are right, and five out of six are false. An insider with a prior of 0.5 would be right far more often, so a statement about beliefs must name the attacker.

title: 46  Choosing ε
text:
46.5 How small δ must be
A deliberately bad mechanism shows what \(\delta\) permits. It publishes each of \(n\) records in full, independently with probability \(\delta\). It is \((0, \delta)\)-DP, because adding or removing one record changes the output only when that record’s own coin comes up. Yet it publishes at least one record with probability \[1 - (1 - \delta)^n \approx 1 - e^{-n\delta}. \tag{46.5}\] For 10,000 records at \(\delta = 1/n\), that is 0.6321, so \(n\delta\) must be below 1. Here \(n\) counts privacy units, which means people when one person has many records (User-level differential privacy).
This book’s default is \(\delta \le 1/n^{1.1}\), rounded down to a power of ten, which keeps \(n\delta\) below 1 for every \(n\). It gives \(10^{-5}\) for both of this page’s runs, and the delta_for function of Train a model with DP-SGD computes it. When \(n\) is just above a power of ten, as with Adult’s 30,000 people, the default is not far below \(1/n\). NIST SP 800-226, the US guidelines for evaluating DP claims, calls a \(\delta\) above \(10^{-5}\) suspicious unless justified.
For DP-SGD a smaller \(\delta\) is cheap. The RDP accountant that set the running example’s \(\varepsilon = 4\) run puts it at only 5.209 when \(\delta\) falls to \(10^{-8}\). So report \(\varepsilon\) at a second, smaller \(\delta\) too, and never quote a \(\delta\) as large as one over the number of units.

title: 46  Choosing ε
text:
46.6 Comparing with deployed values
“Industry uses \(\varepsilon\) between 1 and 10” hides what every \(\varepsilon\) needs, its privacy unit and the period over which it is spent. The Census Bureau’s 2020 redistricting data used zero-concentrated differential privacy (zCDP), which states the guarantee as one number, written \(\rho\), that converts to \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) pairs. Its unit was one person’s record under the replace-one relation, and persons got \(\rho = 2.56\), reported as \(\varepsilon = 17.14\) at \(\delta = 10^{-10}\).
So before comparing, convert both budgets to the same unit, neighbouring relation and \(\delta\). A zCDP parameter \(\rho\) converts to a pair by \[\varepsilon = \rho + 2\sqrt{\rho\ln(1/\delta)}. \tag{46.6}\] For the Census figures this formula gives 17.92, and the Bureau’s 17.14 comes from a tighter conversion. Since a replacement is a removal followed by an addition, an add/remove guarantee \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) implies only the replace-one guarantee \((2\varepsilon, (1 + e^\varepsilon)\delta)\) (The definition of differential privacy). And a budget stated per day adds up over time by composition, to 365 a year at \(\varepsilon = 1\) per day.
So it would be wrong to call the running example’s \(\varepsilon = 8\) run “less than half the Census budget”. At the Census’s \(\delta = 10^{-10}\) it is at 11.627, and under the Census’s replace-one relation that can double.

title: 47  Public data and private fine-tuning
text:
47.1 Why this matters
The differential privacy (DP) version of stochastic gradient descent (SGD), DP-SGD, loses much accuracy when it trains a model from random weights. The loss is large at a privacy loss \(\varepsilon\) of 1 or below. The most accurate private models avoid it by starting from a model pretrained without privacy on a large public dataset. They only fine-tune it privately on the sensitive data (Tramèr & Boneh 2021).
Fine-tuning only a small part of the model often helps further. DP-SGD adds noise to every weight it trains, while the useful signal does not grow with their number. So fewer weights mean less noise for the same signal. The workflow Fine-tune a language model privately with LoRA does the job end to end.
crumbs: 47  Public data and private fine-tuning

title: 47  Public data and private fine-tuning
text:
47.2 How many weights to train
Which weights you train leaves \(\varepsilon\) unchanged, because DP-SGD’s guarantee needs only that one record moves the clipped sum by at most the clipping norm \(C\). The choice changes only how much noise lands on the model. Anything else computed only from public data, such as the starting weights, is also free, if no choice in it looked at the private data. So a tokenizer or normalization statistics fitted on public data are free, while fitted on the private data they leak.
The noise grows with the number \(d\) of trainable weights. Write \(\sigma\) for the noise multiplier and \(B\) for the expected batch size, expected because DP-SGD’s Poisson sampling draws batches of random size. Then the noise on the averaged gradient has length about \[\text{noise length} \approx \frac{\sigma C\sqrt d}{B}. \tag{47.1}\] The signal, the average clipped gradient, is at most \(C\) long whatever \(d\) is. It can even get longer when fewer weights train, because clipping then cuts each record’s gradient less.
Take the running example of DP-SGD, a small network with 3,329 weights. It is pretrained on a similar public task and then fine-tuned on the 10,000 private records. At \(\varepsilon = 1\), the noise is 92.0 times longer than the signal at the pretrained weights when all weights train. It is only 6.7 times longer when the 65 weights of the last layer train. That gap is wider than the formula predicts, because the signal is longer when only the last layer trains (0.0250 against 0.0130).
Counting weights overstates the cost of training them all, though. Noise does harm only along the directions in which the loss is curved, because a step along a flat direction barely changes the loss. Near a pretrained model few directions are curved (Li, Liu et al. 2022). So on the running example, full fine-tuning trains 51 times as many weights as the last layer, but its noise should raise the loss only 7.5 times as much. A larger learning rate lets the noise into more of the nearly flat directions, so private fine-tuning wants smaller steps than training from scratch.
Training fewer weights has its own cost, a bias, because no private data can move the model along a frozen direction that the task needs.
crumbs: 47  Public data and private fine-tuning

title: 47  Public data and private fine-tuning
text:
47.3 Linear probing first
The simplest option freezes everything but the last layer and trains a linear classifier on the frozen features, which is linear probing. Because the features are fixed, the probe’s loss is convex. So linear probing turns private deep learning back into Private empirical risk minimization, which makes it the safe first baseline.
A private probe’s error has two parts. One is the error that privacy adds to convex empirical risk minimization (ERM), which grows with the number \(d\) of features, and the other is the feature gap. That gap is how far the best linear model on the features falls short of the best model of any kind. No number of records or size of \(\varepsilon\) closes it. For example, the running example’s probe without privacy, its ceiling, has a test accuracy of 0.9536, while a non-private network trained from scratch reaches 0.9606. The private probe stays within 0.006 of that ceiling, but never passes it.
So measure the probe’s ceiling first, by fitting it without privacy on labelled public data that resemble the task. If it already meets your target, stop there. To train the probe privately, feed the frozen features to diffprivlib’s LogisticRegression (Private empirical risk minimization), or run DP-SGD on the one layer.
crumbs: 47  Public data and private fine-tuning

title: 47  Public data and private fine-tuning
text:
47.4 Low-rank adapters and full fine-tuning
When the probe’s ceiling is below your target, only changing the earlier layers can lift it. Low-rank adaptation (LoRA, Hu et al. 2022) freezes each pretrained matrix and learns a small correction to it. The correction is the product of two thin matrices that each have \(r\) columns, where \(r\) is the rank. A matrix with \(d_{\text{in}}\) inputs and \(d_{\text{out}}\) outputs has \(d_{\text{in}}d_{\text{out}}\) weights, while its adapter has only \[d = r(d_{\text{in}} + d_{\text{out}}). \tag{47.2}\]
The adapter comes from Hugging Face’s peft library. This snippet puts a rank-4 adapter on the first layer of a network shaped like the running example, and trains its last layer in full.
import torch
from peft import LoraConfig, get_peft_model

model = torch.nn.Sequential(torch.nn.Linear(50, 64), torch.nn.Tanh(), torch.nn.Linear(64, 1))
print(sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters()))  # 3329
config = LoraConfig(r=4, lora_alpha=8, target_modules=["0"], modules_to_save=["2"], lora_dropout=0.0)
adapted = get_peft_model(model, config)  # freezes every pretrained weight
print(sum(p.numel() for p in adapted.parameters() if p.requires_grad))  # 521
In the snippet, target_modules and modules_to_save name layers by their index in the Sequential, and lora_alpha scales the correction. It trains 521 weights, the adapter’s \(4 \times (50 + 64) = 456\) and the last layer’s 65. The run in Section 47.5 treats the first layer’s biases as a 51st input, which gives 525. Opacus’s PrivacyEngine then computes per-example gradients only for the parameters that require them, so the frozen weights cost nothing. Call model.train() before make_private, since Opacus rejects a model left in evaluation mode, as a pretrained model often is after you measure it.
The adapter’s second factor starts at zero, so training begins exactly at the pretrained model. The first factor starts random, and that draw must not depend on the private data.
Yu et al. (2022) showed that private fine-tuning of language models with LoRA matches or beats private full fine-tuning, at a fraction of the compute and memory. And since each adapter factor is an ordinary linear layer, the ghost clipping of DP-SGD applies to it. Still, full fine-tuning is not ruled out. Li, Tramèr et al. (2022) matched the adapters with it, using large batches and a learning rate tuned for private training.

Here pretraining is worth about a factor of eight in \(\varepsilon\), since the adapter at \(\varepsilon = 1\) matches training from scratch at \(\varepsilon = 8\).
At \(\varepsilon = 0.5\) the last layer is best, because its noise is 7.2 times shorter than full fine-tuning’s, and its ceiling does not yet bind. So rerun the comparison on a public stand-in for your task before you commit.

title: 47  Public data and private fine-tuning
section: 47.6 What public data does not buy
text:
47.6 What public data does not buy
Whatever the public data are, training on the private data is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP, where \(\delta\) is the small additive slack the guarantee allows. The public data get no guarantee of any kind. Non-private pretraining can memorize individual records (Memorization and training-data extraction), and the fine-tuned model inherits whatever the pretrained weights encode (Tramèr, Kamath & Carlini 2024).
So a person in both datasets is protected only in the private copy. A membership attack against the pretrained model (Membership inference) has no bound at all. Web-scale “public” datasets contain posts, profiles and leaked documents, so private notes or emails may well overlap with them. For text, also mind the privacy unit. One person’s documents span many training sequences, so a guarantee per sequence protects far less than a person (User-level differential privacy).
Check three things before you train and when you report.

Check that the public data resemble the private task, and deduplicate the private set against them. Deduplication protects copies, not people, since exact matching misses paraphrases.
Choose the public model and the hyperparameters on public data. Otherwise every private run costs privacy (Hyperparameter tuning).
Name the public data and the overlap check, and state that the guarantee covers the private data given the pretrained model.

title: 48  Fine-tune a language model privately with LoRA
text:
48.1 Why this matters
You have a pretrained language model and private text, such as support tickets or clinical notes. You want the model to learn from that text without being able to repeat it. Yet a model fine-tuned without privacy can write out a phone number or a password that was often in its training text (Memorization and training-data extraction). The fix is to fine-tune with the differential privacy (DP) version of stochastic gradient descent (SGD), called DP-SGD. It costs least when it trains only a small adapter on the frozen model, which is often as accurate as training every weight (Public data and private fine-tuning). Here the adapter is low-rank adaptation (LoRA), from Hugging Face’s peft library, and Opacus does the private training.
The model is Pythia-14m, a public language model of 14 million parameters from EleutherAI. The private text is Tiny Shakespeare, a million characters of Shakespeare’s plays. The script fine-tunes the model twice, once without privacy and once at a privacy loss \(\varepsilon\) of 8 for each sequence of training text. It first plants made-up secrets, called canaries, in the text, so that you can see what each model memorized. The script practitioner_lora.py runs in a few minutes without a GPU.

title: 48  Fine-tune a language model privately with LoRA
section: 48.2 Fix the privacy unit, n and δ
text:
48.2 Fix the privacy unit, n and δ
The guarantee protects one unit, so decide first what the unit is. A language model trains on fixed-length sequences of tokens, the word pieces its tokenizer cuts text into. The script cuts the text into sequences of 32 tokens, about one or two lines of verse, and makes each sequence the unit. To keep the run short, it uses only the first 1,024 sequences for training and the last 128 as a held-out set.
sequences of 32 tokens: 10,632  training n=1,024  held out 128
delta=1e-04 (privacy unit: one training sequence)
The slack \(\delta\) is the small additive term the guarantee allows beside \(\varepsilon\). The book’s default for \(n\) units is \(\delta \le 1/n^{1.1}\), rounded down to a power of ten (Choosing ε). For 1,024 sequences that is \(10^{-4}\).
A sequence is the right unit for this demonstration, but rarely in production. One person’s document spans many sequences, and one user writes many documents, so a guarantee per sequence protects a person much less than it seems. In production, make the unit a document or a user, and bound how many sequences each contributes. Then set \(\delta\) from the number of users (User-level differential privacy).
crumbs: 48  Fine-tune a language model privately with LoRA

title: 48  Fine-tune a language model privately with LoRA
text:
48.3 Plant canaries
To check memorization later, you need secrets whose presence you control. The script writes canaries into the training text. Each is a sentence such as “the pin of Alice is 8 6 5 2 3”, whose last five digits are the secret. There are four groups of three canaries, inserted 1, 4, 16 and 64 times each. Three more, the controls, are drawn the same way but never inserted, so they show what an unseen secret scores in the audit of Section 48.9.
def insert_canaries(
    train: torch.Tensor, canaries: list[Canary], tokenizer: PreTrainedTokenizerBase, rng: np.random.Generator
) -> torch.Tensor:
    """Write each copy of each canary over the start of a different training sequence."""
    train = train.clone()
    total = sum(c.copies for c in canaries)
    rows = iter(rng.choice(len(train), size=total, replace=False).tolist())
    for canary in canaries:
        tokens = torch.tensor(tokenizer(canary.text)["input_ids"])
        for _ in range(canary.copies):
            train[next(rows), : len(tokens)] = tokens
    return train
Each copy overwrites the start of a different training sequence, so the 255 copies take up a quarter of the training set. That is far denser than secrets in real data, and deliberately so, because it lets a model this small memorize within a short run. The audit then has a positive control, a model known to leak.
canary sequences: 255 (3 canaries each at (1, 4, 16, 64) copies)
tokens per secret: [5]
candidates: 2,000  exposure cap 10.97 bits  (full space 16.61)
The digits are separated by spaces so that every possible secret is exactly five tokens long, which the second line confirms over 1,000 random secrets.

title: 48  Fine-tune a language model privately with LoRA
section: 48.4 Load a public model and tokenizer
text:
48.4 Load a public model and tokenizer
Everything not trained privately must come from outside the private data. That includes the tokenizer, whose vocabulary would leak rare words if it were built from the private text. So the weights and the tokenizer both come from the same public checkpoint, Pythia-14m, pinned to one revision. The script loads the model in float32, because transformers loads some checkpoints in float16, which is far slower on a CPU.
The guarantee then covers the private text given the pretrained model, and says nothing about the model’s own training data. Here that caveat is real, because Pythia was pretrained on the Pile, which includes Project Gutenberg’s books and so very likely Shakespeare’s plays. That is harmless here, but with real data, check for overlap with the public model’s training data (Public data and private fine-tuning).
crumbs: 48  Fine-tune a language model privately with LoRA

title: 48  Fine-tune a language model privately with LoRA
text:
48.5 Choose what to train
DP-SGD adds noise to every weight it trains. So the noise on the averaged gradient grows with the square root of the number of trained weights, but the clipped signal does not (Public data and private fine-tuning). That makes the choice of trainable weights one of the two main levers on accuracy, with the learning rate. LoRA freezes each pretrained matrix and learns a correction to it, the product of two thin factors whose width is the rank.
attention_and_mlp = ["query_key_value", "dense", "dense_h_to_4h", "dense_4h_to_h"]  # every linear layer
config = LoraConfig(r=rank, lora_alpha=2 * rank, target_modules=attention_and_mlp, lora_dropout=0.0)
lora_model = get_peft_model(model, config)  # freezes the pretrained weights
trainable_count = sum(p.numel() for p in lora_model.parameters() if p.requires_grad)
total_count = sum(p.numel() for p in lora_model.parameters())
print(f"trainable parameters: LoRA {trainable_count:,}  full fine-tuning {total_count - trainable_count:,}")
full model parameters: 14,067,712
trainable parameters: LoRA 98,304  full fine-tuning 14,067,712
By default the adapters have rank 8 and sit on every linear layer, in attention and in the feed-forward blocks. They train 98,304 weights, against about 14 million that full fine-tuning would train. lora_alpha scales the adapters’ correction, set to the usual twice the rank. For a real task, choose the rank and the layers on public data, because a choice made from private runs costs privacy (Hyperparameter tuning).
crumbs: 48  Fine-tune a language model privately with LoRA

title: 48  Fine-tune a language model privately with LoRA
text:
48.6 Make the model Opacus-compatible
Opacus needs one gradient per sequence, and layers that mix the records of a batch, such as batch normalization, make that impossible. Opacus’s ModuleValidator.validate lists such layers before you train.
validator errors: 0
Pythia has none, and only the adapters train in any case. They are ordinary linear layers, which Opacus’s default hooks handle, so the script passes grad_sample_mode="hooks". Opacus computes per-sequence gradients only for the weights that require gradients, so the 14 million frozen weights add no cost. Call model.train() before wrapping a model you have just evaluated, since Opacus rejects one in evaluation mode. After training, the hooks stay attached and slow down everything the model does next. So the script calls remove_hooks() before it evaluates the private model.
crumbs: 48  Fine-tune a language model privately with LoRA

title: 48  Fine-tune a language model privately with LoRA
text:
48.7 Calibrate and train
Fix the target \(\varepsilon\), \(\delta\), the sampling rate and the number of epochs, and let the accountant find the noise. The script asks for \(\varepsilon = 8\) over 3 epochs with an expected batch of 32 sequences. The sampling rate \(q\), the share of the data in an average batch, is then \(32/1{,}024\), so the 3 epochs take 96 steps. The accountant is the privacy loss random variable (PRV) accountant, which computes \(\varepsilon\) almost exactly (Report and review an ε claim).
privacy_engine = PrivacyEngine(accountant="prv")
private_model, optimizer, loader = privacy_engine.make_private_with_epsilon(
    module=model,
    optimizer=optimizer,
    data_loader=loader,  # replaced by Poisson sampling with rate BATCH / n
    target_epsilon=epsilon,
    target_delta=delta,
    epochs=EPOCHS,
    max_grad_norm=MAX_GRAD_NORM,
    grad_sample_mode="hooks",
)
print(f"noise multiplier: {optimizer.noise_multiplier:.3f}")
The training loop is an ordinary one. Opacus’s loader draws Poisson batches, in which each sequence joins each batch independently with probability \(q\).
for (batch,) in loader:  # each batch holds a random number of sequences
    optimizer.zero_grad()
    loss = private_model(input_ids=batch, labels=batch).loss
    loss.backward()  # Opacus's hooks keep one gradient per sequence
    optimizer.step()  # clips each one to MAX_GRAD_NORM, sums, adds noise
    steps += 1
noise multiplier: 0.553
sample rate q=0.03125  steps=96  noise multiplier=0.553
epsilon (Opacus PRV)=7.99  epsilon (dp_accounting PLD)=7.98  at delta=1e-04
The noise multiplier is the noise’s standard deviation in units of the clipping norm, MAX_GRAD_NORM, which the script sets to 1. The last line cross-checks the claimed \(\varepsilon\) of 8 with the privacy loss distribution (PLD) accountant of Google’s dp_accounting. The two values agree to within rounding.
Both runs use AdamW at a learning rate of \(10^{-3}\), and the private run differs only by clipping, noise and Poisson sampling. That learning rate, the rank and the epochs were chosen in a few non-private trial runs on the same text. A real run must choose them on similar public text, such as other public-domain plays, or pay for the trials in \(\varepsilon\) (Hyperparameter tuning).
Two more settings change for a real run. With more data, use batches in the thousands, not 32. Opacus’s BatchMemoryManager splits them into physical batches that fit in memory (Train a model with DP-SGD). And a model you release needs secure_mode=True in PrivacyEngine, whose cryptographically secure noise cannot be seeded, which is why the script leaves it off.

title: 48  Fine-tune a language model privately with LoRA
text:
48.8 Evaluate
A language model is judged by how well it predicts held-out text. The script measures the mean cross-entropy per token on the 128 held-out sequences, and its exponential, the perplexity. A perplexity of 159.3 means the model is as unsure as if it chose among about 159 equally likely tokens. So lower is better.
held-out loss pretrained: 5.306 nats/token  perplexity 201.6
held-out loss LoRA non-private: 5.071 nats/token  perplexity 159.3
held-out loss LoRA DP eps=8: 5.044 nats/token  perplexity 155.1
Both fine-tuned models improve on the pretrained one, and the private model is no worse than the non-private one. On one seed, its slightly lower perplexity means only that DP costs nothing measurable here. Both gains are modest, because a quarter of the training sequences begin with canaries rather than Shakespeare.
Do not expect privacy to be this cheap on every task. This run is short, trains few weights, and uses text that is very likely in the pretraining data already. With a harder task or a smaller \(\varepsilon\), compare the private model with both baselines at several budgets, as Train a model with DP-SGD does.
crumbs: 48  Fine-tune a language model privately with LoRA

title: 48  Fine-tune a language model privately with LoRA
text:
48.9 Check memorization
The canaries show what perplexity cannot, whether the model will repeat a secret. The script measures each canary in two ways, first by extraction. It gives the model the prefix “the pin of Alice is” and lets it write the likeliest next token five times. Then it checks whether the result is the secret.
@torch.no_grad()
def greedy_completion(model: PeftModel, tokenizer: PreTrainedTokenizerBase, prefix: str) -> str:
    """The five tokens the model writes after the prefix when it always picks the likeliest one."""
    ids = tokenizer(prefix, return_tensors="pt")["input_ids"]
    for _ in range(5):
        next_token = model(input_ids=ids).logits[:, -1].argmax(dim=-1, keepdim=True)
        ids = torch.cat([ids, next_token], dim=1)
    return tokenizer.batch_decode(ids[:, -5:])[0].strip()
The second is the exposure of Memorization and training-data extraction. It ranks the canary’s secret among random secrets of the same format by how likely the model finds each, and turns the rank into bits. The script’s likelihood is the summed log-probability of the five digits. Each bit halves the number of guesses an attacker needs.
@torch.no_grad()
def secret_scores(model: PeftModel, tokenizer: PreTrainedTokenizerBase, prefix: str, secrets: list[str]) -> Scores:
    """Summed log-probability of each secret's five digit tokens after the prefix."""
    prefix_ids = tokenizer(prefix)["input_ids"]
    rows = [prefix_ids + tokenizer(" " + s)["input_ids"] for s in secrets]
    ids = torch.tensor(rows)  # every secret is five tokens, so the rows have equal length
    logits = model(input_ids=ids[:, :-1], logits_to_keep=5).logits  # the predictions of the five digits
    logprobs = logits.log_softmax(dim=-1).gather(-1, ids[:, -5:, None])
    return logprobs.sum(dim=(1, 2)).double().numpy()


def canary_exposure(
    model: PeftModel, tokenizer: PreTrainedTokenizerBase, canary: Canary, candidates: list[str]
) -> tuple[float, float]:
    """The exposure of the canary's secret among the candidates, measured and extrapolated past the cap."""
    candidate_scores = scores_batched(model, tokenizer, canary.prefix, candidates)
    score = float(scores_batched(model, tokenizer, canary.prefix, [canary.secret])[0])
    return exposure(score, candidate_scores), extrapolated_exposure(score, candidate_scores, SECRET_SPACE)
No library installed with this book computes exposure, so exposure and extrapolated_exposure come from the book’s helper module practitioner_privacy_tests.py, after TensorFlow Privacy’s versions. With 2,000 random candidates, a canary that beats them all reaches a cap of 10.97 bits. A secret the model has never seen has a random rank and averages about 1.44 bits (\(\log_2 e\)). Each line below gives a group’s mean exposure, the same past the cap, and how many of its three secrets greedy decoding wrote out.
non-private 1 copies: mean exposure 2.0 bits  extrapolated 2.0  extracted 0/3
non-private 4 copies: mean exposure 5.9 bits  extrapolated 5.7  extracted 0/3
non-private 16 copies: mean exposure 10.0 bits  extrapolated 13.0  extracted 0/3
non-private 64 copies: mean exposure 11.0 bits  extrapolated 16.3  extracted 3/3
non-private controls: mean exposure 1.4 bits  extrapolated 1.5  extracted 0/3
DP 1 copies: mean exposure 0.9 bits  extrapolated 0.9  extracted 0/3
DP 4 copies: mean exposure 0.6 bits  extrapolated 0.6  extracted 0/3
DP 16 copies: mean exposure 4.2 bits  extrapolated 4.3  extracted 0/3
DP 64 copies: mean exposure 4.0 bits  extrapolated 3.9  extracted 0/3
DP controls: mean exposure 2.2 bits  extrapolated 2.2  extracted 0/3
The non-private model, the positive control, leaks. Exposure rises with the number of copies, from 2.0 bits for one copy to the cap for 64. The model writes out all three 64-copy secrets. The extrapolated column sees past the cap by fitting a skew-normal distribution, a normal with one heavier tail, to the candidates’ scores. It puts the 64-copy secrets near the 16.61 bits of the whole space.
The 4-copy canaries are the instructive case. Two of the three reach 6.9 and 8.2 bits, yet none is extracted, so exposure detects memorization that extraction alone would miss.
Nothing can be extracted from the private model. Its canaries with 1 or 4 copies score no higher than its controls. Their 2.2 bits are within the scatter of a mean over three secrets. Still, DP limits the effect without erasing it, since the canaries with 16 and 64 copies still average about 4 bits.
The guarantee allows that, because \(\varepsilon = 8\) protects one sequence, while a canary with many copies is many sequences. Group privacy bounds a group of units at about their number times \(\varepsilon\). So 16 copies get \(16 \times 8\), far too much to promise anything (User-level differential privacy). A secret that a user repeats across many documents is the same case, one more reason to make the unit the user.
Two cautions apply. Because the canaries are so dense, a real non-private model may leak less than this one, and a real audit should plant fewer copies. And three canaries per group is a small sample. For a fuller assessment before release, run the attacks of Pre-release privacy risk assessment. For a statistical lower bound on \(\varepsilon\), run the one-run audit of Auditing private training.

48.10 Variants
Three variants matter for real models: ghost clipping, LoRA on GPT-2, and packages that wrap the whole loop. The block below shows them with pinned versions, and it was not run.
# opacus==1.6.0: ghost clipping, when per-sequence gradients do not fit in memory
model, optimizer, criterion, loader = privacy_engine.make_private_with_epsilon(
    module=model, optimizer=optimizer, data_loader=loader, criterion=torch.nn.CrossEntropyLoss(),
    target_epsilon=8.0, target_delta=1e-4, epochs=3, max_grad_norm=1.0, grad_sample_mode="ghost",
)
logits = model(input_ids=batch).logits[:, :-1]                 # predict each next token
loss = criterion(logits.flatten(0, 1), batch[:, 1:].flatten(), shape=logits.shape)
loss.backward()                                                # norms first, then the clipped sum

# peft==0.21.2: GPT-2 stores its attention as Conv1D, with the weight transposed
LoraConfig(r=8, lora_alpha=16, target_modules=["c_attn"], fan_in_fan_out=True)

# dp-transformers==1.0.0 (Microsoft): Opacus inside the Hugging Face Trainer
# private-transformers (Li et al.): install from its GitHub repository, pinned to a commit
Ghost clipping gets each sequence’s gradient norm without storing the gradient, so memory no longer holds one gradient per sequence (DP-SGD).

48.11 Report
The release statement names the unit, here one sequence of 32 tokens, with the number of units \(n\) and the slack \(\delta\). It names the accountant and its three inputs, which are the noise multiplier, the sampling rate and the number of steps. It says that the guarantee covers the private text given the pretrained model, named with its revision. It says how the hyperparameters were chosen, here by non-private trials on the private text, which a real release could not claim for free. Attach the canary audit as evidence, with its caveats. Release and governance assembles all of this into a record and a statement.
What ships is the adapter. With --save-adapter FOLDER, the script saves it after remove_hooks() and loads it back onto the same pinned checkpoint.
private.save_pretrained(path)  # only the adapter weights and config, after Opacus's hooks are removed
base_model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(folder, dtype=torch.float32)  # the same pinned checkpoint
reloaded = PeftModel.from_pretrained(base_model, path)
The folder holds only the adapter, so the statement names the base checkpoint and revision it fits. The guarantee covers the adapter and anything computed from it.

title: 49  Private prediction: PATE and in-context learning
text:
49.1 What it is
Private prediction applies differential privacy (DP) to each answer instead of to the model. You split the private records into disjoint shards and train an ordinary model, a teacher, on each one. The teachers stay secret. Each query gets the winner of their vote after noise is added to the counts, private at a level \(\varepsilon\) with a small slack \(\delta\). A record lives in one shard, so it can move one teacher’s vote to another label. That changes the counts by at most \(\sqrt2\) in Euclidean length.
GNMax adds Gaussian noise with a standard deviation \(\sigma\) to each count and releases only the label with the largest noisy count. In Rényi differential privacy (RDP), each answer costs a straight line of slope \(1/\sigma^2\) in the order \(\alpha\), and the slopes add (Rényi DP). So write \(\rho(\varepsilon, \delta)\) for the largest slope that still converts to your target. A fixed number \(Q\) of answers, even adaptively chosen, then needs the noise \[\sigma = \sqrt{\frac{Q}{\rho(\varepsilon, \delta)}}. \tag{49.1}\] For example, at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) a budget of \(\varepsilon = 1\) allows a slope of 0.0306, so 1,000 answers need \(\sigma = 181\).
crumbs: 49  Private prediction: PATE and in-context learning

title: 49  Private prediction: PATE and in-context learning
text:
49.2 When you meet it
You meet private prediction when you cannot train a private model. The common case is a large language model (LLM) behind an interface. Its prompt holds private records, and its answers leak them. The fix splits the records into disjoint groups, prompts the model once per group, and releases the GNMax label (Duan et al. 2023). At \(\varepsilon = 1\), Wu et al. (2024) answered 10,000 sentiment queries this way as accurately as one non-private prompt.
Otherwise the choice is between private answers and a private model, whose accuracy is fixed. The vote’s noise grows with \(\sqrt Q\), so answers win up to a break-even number of queries, and the model wins beyond it. On the full edition’s 10,000-record synthetic task, the vote beats noisy stochastic gradient descent (SGD), DP-SGD, only on the first 18 queries at \(\varepsilon = 1\). So compare the two at your budget and expected number of queries, with the DP-SGD baseline of Train a model with DP-SGD.
PATE (private aggregation of teacher ensembles) spends the budget once. It labels public, unlabelled inputs by GNMax and trains a new model, the student, on them. Only the student is released, at exactly the cost of its labels, so PATE needs public inputs from the private data’s distribution. Papernot et al.’s MNIST student comes within a percentage point of non-private accuracy, but at a data-dependent \(\varepsilon\) (Section 49.4). On the synthetic task, DP-SGD beats the best student at every budget.

title: 49  Private prediction: PATE and in-context learning
text:
49.3 How to use it
dp_accounting accounts for the vote. One GNMax answer is a GaussianDpEvent whose noise multiplier, the noise over the sensitivity, is \(\sigma/\sqrt2\).
import numpy as np
from dp_accounting import GaussianDpEvent, SelfComposedDpEvent
from dp_accounting.pld import PLDAccountant
from dp_accounting.rdp import RdpAccountant

sigma, queries = 181.0, 1000  # noise per count, answers to release
event = SelfComposedDpEvent(GaussianDpEvent(sigma / np.sqrt(2)), queries)  # sensitivity sqrt(2)
rdp = RdpAccountant().compose(event).get_epsilon(1e-5)
pld = PLDAccountant().compose(event).get_epsilon(1e-5)
print(f"{rdp:.3f} {pld:.3f}")  # 0.999 0.914
The RDP accountant confirms \(\varepsilon = 0.999\). The privacy loss distribution (PLD) accountant, exact for Gaussian noise, gives 0.914, so solving for \(\sigma\) with it gives less noise. To solve, pass a function from \(\sigma\) to this event to dp_accounting.calibrate_dp_mechanism. For many answers the PLD is much slower, and RDP is the fallback. When each query draws a fresh Poisson sample of records, as in Wu et al., wrap each event in a PoissonSampledDpEvent.
crumbs: 49  Private prediction: PATE and in-context learning

title: 49  Private prediction: PATE and in-context learning
text:
49.4 What goes wrong
The guarantee needs each record in exactly one shard. So assign shards by a hash of the record’s or the user’s identifier. Never assign them by position in a file, where one inserted record shifts every later shard. Release the label only, and fix \(Q\) in advance.
Noise this large wipes out close votes. With two labels and a gap \(g\) between the counts, the vote returns the plurality with probability \(\Phi(g/(\sqrt2\sigma))\), where \(\Phi\) is the standard normal distribution function.
For example, the noise for 1,000 answers at \(\varepsilon = 4\) is \(\sigma = 51.8\). Then a lopsided vote of 98 to 2 is right with probability 0.9051, but a close vote of 52 to 48 only about half the time. So measure the noiseless vote first, since no budget beats it. Adding teachers widens the gaps, since \(\sigma\) does not depend on their number, until the shards get too small to train on.
Finally, beware of a data-dependent \(\varepsilon\). When teachers agree, a sharper analysis charges less, but that smaller \(\varepsilon\) is computed from the votes and leaks them. Until it is released with noise, it is a measurement, not a guarantee.
Confident-GNMax answers only queries on which a noisy check finds agreement, the cheap and accurate ones.
