title: 50  DP-FTRL and matrix factorization
text:
50.1 What it is
Gradient descent without momentum adds up its steps. So its weights after each step depend on the sum of all clipped gradients so far, a prefix sum. Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with differential privacy (DP), DP-SGD, adds fresh noise at every step. So the noise in the prefix sums grows like a random walk. Matrix mechanisms correlate the noise across steps, so that each step’s noise partly cancels earlier noise in the sums.
Stack the gradient sums of the steps as the rows of a matrix \(x\). The prefix sums are then \(Ax\), where \(A\) has ones on and below the diagonal. The matrix factorization mechanism writes \(A\) as a decoder \(L\) times an encoder \(R\). It adds a matrix of Gaussian noise, written \(z\), to the encoded gradients and decodes the result, \[\hat S = L(Rx + z) = Ax + Lz. \tag{50.1}\] A record enters only through the column of \(R\) for its step, so privacy depends on the longest column of the encoder, its sensitivity. Accuracy depends on the decoder, whose row \(t\) carries the noise into the \(t\)-th prefix sum.
The first such method ran the follow the regularized leader (FTRL) optimizer on sums from a binary tree. It is called DP-FTRL (Kairouz et al. 2021). Today’s usual factorization is the square-root factorization, which uses the lower-triangular square root of \(A\) for both factors. At equal privacy over one epoch of 100 steps, it leaves about a quarter of independent noise’s standard deviation in the final sum.

title: 50  DP-FTRL and matrix factorization
text:
50.2 When you meet it
You meet matrix mechanisms when your pipeline cannot honestly claim Poisson sampling, the random batches that DP-SGD’s accountant assumes. Fixed batches cut from a shuffled order fail it. So do data read in arrival order, and phones in federated learning that check in when they can. Accounting them as Poisson understates \(\varepsilon\) (Amplification by subsampling), while a matrix mechanism needs no sampling.
Without sampling, independent noise loses much accuracy, and correlated noise wins most of it back. On the full edition’s synthetic task, trained in a fixed order for ten epochs at \(\varepsilon = 2\), independent noise reaches a test accuracy of 0.8641. The banded square root of Section 50.4 reaches 0.9491, against 0.9493 for DP-SGD with Poisson sampling. So if you can implement Poisson sampling, use DP-SGD with Opacus. If you cannot, use a banded matrix mechanism, as Google did for its Gboard keyboard models (Xu et al. 2023).

title: 50  DP-FTRL and matrix factorization
text:
50.3 How to use it
Google’s JAX Privacy implements banded matrix factorization. The block below was not run, since JAX is not in this book’s environment. It cycles through 100 fixed groups of records, one per step, so each record takes part once every 100 steps.
# jax-privacy==2.0.0 (not run)
from jax_privacy.experimental.execution_plan import BandMFExecutionPlanConfig

config = BandMFExecutionPlanConfig.default(
    num_bands=100,       # at most the 100 steps between a record's turns
    iterations=1000,     # ten epochs of 100 steps
    epsilon=2.0,
    delta=1e-5,
    sampling_prob=1.0,   # all of the step's group joins: no amplification claimed
    l2_clip_norm=1.0,
)
plan = config.plan       # calibrates the noise multiplier with dp_accounting
The training loop draws each batch from plan.batch_selection_strategy and sums its clipped gradients with plan.clipped_grad. Then plan.noise_addition_transform adds the noise before the optimizer sees the sum. A dp_accounting accountant turns plan.dp_event into the \(\varepsilon\) you report. The module is marked experimental, so pin the version.

title: 50  DP-FTRL and matrix factorization
text:
50.4 What goes wrong
The pitfalls come from records that take part more than once. Over \(E\) epochs a record enters through \(E\) columns of the encoder. The square root’s columns for nearby steps are nonzero in the same rows, so they add up and the sensitivity grows faster than \(\sqrt E\). Banding keeps a number \(b\) of the encoder’s diagonals, the main one and those just below it. It needs every two participations of a record to be at least \(b\) steps apart, a condition called \(b\)-min-separation. The record’s columns then share no rows, so the sensitivity is at most \(\sqrt E\) times the longest column, as for independent noise.
So the data order is part of the mechanism. Fix it before training, independently of the data, and keep the same permutation every epoch. A new shuffle each epoch can put a record at the end of one epoch and the start of the next, which breaks the banded bound.
The neighbouring relation changes the numbers too. The analysis here leaves a neighbour’s slot empty, so a step moves by at most the clipping norm. If a neighbour replaces the record with another instead, every sensitivity doubles, so state the relation next to every \(\varepsilon\).
dp_accounting 0.6.0 enforces this. Its tree-aggregation event works only in a Rényi differential privacy (RDP) accountant built with NeighboringRelation.REPLACE_SPECIAL, where a neighbour replaces the record with an empty one. Under add/remove, DP-SGD’s default, it raises UnsupportedEventError, and the privacy loss distribution accountant rejects it too. So DP-FTRL and DP-SGD runs cannot share one add/remove ledger.

title: 51  Disparate impact
text:
51.1 Why this matters
A private model’s test accuracy is an average over everyone, so it cannot show which people lose the accuracy that privacy costs. Bagdasaryan, Poursaeed & Shmatikov (2019) trained networks with differential privacy (DP), using the private form of stochastic gradient descent (SGD) called DP-SGD. They found that the lost accuracy fell mostly on under-represented groups, and called this the disparate impact of DP.
So a model that is a point worse on average can be ten points worse for one group, often a small group that privacy should protect. Before you ship a private model, measure its cost for each group against a non-private baseline, with a confidence interval on every number.

title: 51  Disparate impact
section: 51.2 Evaluating a private model per group
text:
51.2 Evaluating a private model per group
Decide which groups matter before you look at any results, so that the results cannot steer the choice. Then train a non-private baseline with the same data and recipe. A gap between groups may exist without privacy. DP is responsible only for how far each group’s own accuracy drops when training becomes private.
Write \(\mathrm{acc}_g\) for a model’s accuracy on the test records of group \(g\). Private training is random, so its accuracy is averaged over several training runs, written \(\mathbb E\). The privacy cost \(\pi_g\) is the accuracy the group loses when the same data and hyperparameters are trained privately, \[\pi_g = \mathrm{acc}_g(\text{non-private}) - \mathbb E\big[\mathrm{acc}_g(\text{private})\big]. \tag{51.1}\] DP has disparate impact when groups have different privacy costs.
Every accuracy needs an interval. Each test record is classified correctly or not, so a group’s accuracy is a binomial proportion. Its exact Clopper–Pearson interval contains the true accuracy in at least 95% of test samples (Hypothesis testing).
The gap between two groups needs its own interval. Write \(\hat p_g\) for group \(g\)’s measured accuracy and \(m_g\) for its number of test records. For two groups \(a\) and \(b\) measured on disjoint test records, the variances of the two estimates add. So for large counts an approximate 95% interval for the gap is \[(\hat p_a - \hat p_b) \pm 1.96\sqrt{\frac{\hat p_a(1 - \hat p_a)}{m_a} + \frac{\hat p_b(1 - \hat p_b)}{m_b}}. \tag{51.2}\]
These intervals are wider than most people expect. Suppose a test split holds only 100 records of a minority, and 88 of them are classified correctly. The majority gets 1,812 of its 1,900 records right, an accuracy of 0.954, so the measured gap is 0.074. SciPy gives the minority’s interval, and Equation 51.2 gives the gap’s.
from math import sqrt

from scipy.stats import binomtest

minority = binomtest(88, 100).proportion_ci(confidence_level=0.95, method="exact")
print(f"{minority.low:.3f} {minority.high:.3f}")  # 0.800 0.936

gap, se = 0.954 - 0.880, sqrt(0.954 * 0.046 / 1_900 + 0.880 * 0.120 / 100)
print(f"{gap - 1.96 * se:.3f} {gap + 1.96 * se:.3f}")  # 0.010 0.138
So the gap is real, since its interval excludes zero, but it could be anywhere from one point to fourteen. An interval separates a 5-point gap from zero only with a few hundred test records from the group, and a 1-point gap only with thousands.
The privacy cost needs a different interval. Both models are scored on the same test records, so their accuracies are not independent and Equation 51.2 does not apply. Pair them instead. Among group \(g\)’s \(m_g\) test records, write \(u\) for the number only the non-private model gets right, and \(v\) for those only the private one gets right. One run’s cost is then \((u - v)/m_g\), and for large counts an approximate 95% interval is \[\frac{u - v}{m_g} \pm \frac{1.96}{m_g}\sqrt{u + v - \frac{(u - v)^2}{m_g}}. \tag{51.3}\]
Training adds a second source of variation, which no test set removes. A small group’s accuracy varies far more between training runs than a large group’s, so a one-run comparison of two recipes can reverse. Train each recipe with several seeds, and report the mean cost and its spread.
The evaluation can also leak, because per-group accuracies on private test data are statistics of that data. To publish them, add noise to each group’s count of correct predictions and charge it to a budget of its own (Release statistics with a library).

title: 51  Disparate impact
text:
51.3 Disparate impact, measured
The script practitioner_dp_sgd.py of Train a model with DP-SGD trains a small network on the Adult census data to predict whether a person’s income exceeds $50K. It trains once without privacy and once with DP-SGD at a privacy level \(\varepsilon\) of 4 and a slack \(\delta\) of \(10^{-5}\). It scores both on the test rows of each sex. For each group, it counts the correct predictions, marked in the boolean array right, and gets the exact interval from SciPy.
in_group = sex == group
correct, total = int(right[in_group].sum()), int(in_group.sum())
interval = binomtest(correct, total).proportion_ci(confidence_level=0.95, method="exact")

title: 51  Disparate impact
section: 51.4 Why small groups pay: clipping and noise
text:
51.4 Why small groups pay: clipping and noise
DP-SGD loses accuracy through two steps, clipping and noise, and both treat every record alike. The clipping row of Table 51.2 clips without adding noise, so it gives no privacy at all, yet the minority already loses 4.04 points there. So clipping by itself treats the groups unequally.
Clipping caps every record’s pull on the update at the clipping norm \(C\), so it cuts back the groups with long gradients hardest. A group’s gradients are long where the model fits it badly, as it does a rare pattern the rest of the data does not teach. So training gives such a group less weight than its share of the records.
The noise is the same for every group, while a group’s signal grows with its size. So a small group’s signal is the weakest against the noise, and its privacy cost grows roughly like one over its share of the training records. The two causes compound, because the noise acts on the weight that clipping has already shrunk. A group whose gradients clipping halves pays like a group half its size.
To see which cause hurts your model, measure per-example gradient norms by group. Opacus’s GradSampleModule, the wrapper DP-SGD training already uses, keeps one gradient per row in each parameter’s grad_sample. So one backward pass gives the norms.
wrapped = GradSampleModule(model)  # adds hooks that keep one gradient per row
wrapped.train()
logits: torch.Tensor = wrapped(split.x)
nn.CrossEntropyLoss()(logits, split.y).backward()  # fills p.grad_sample for every weight p
norms = stacked_norms(wrapped)
Group the norms by each row’s group label, kept beside the batch but not fed to the model. Log each group’s median norm and fraction clipped as training goes on, because the groups can separate late. At initialization on Adult, the median norm is 1.444, so \(C = 1\) clips every row, whatever its group.

text:
51.5 Mitigations and what they cost
At a fixed budget, a change to the training recipe only moves the cost between the groups or between clipping and noise (Table 51.3). Only the last row, which changes the data, the starting model or the budget, reduces it.

Oversampling costs the group’s privacy, because a record’s guarantee depends on its own chance of being sampled (Amplification by subsampling). So run the accountant at the oversampled rate. In the running example, sampling the minority four times as often at \(\varepsilon = 4\) raises the noise multiplier from 1.36 to 4.71. The gap between the groups’ accuracies then narrows from 9.93 points to 3.99, but by levelling down, since the majority loses 8.01 points.
Some of the cost cannot be avoided by any algorithm. Learning a small group’s own rule means estimating it privately from that group’s few records. Private estimation from few records has an error floor that no mechanism beats (Lower bounds).

title: 52  Auditing private training
text:
52.1 Why this matters
When you train with differential privacy (DP), the accountant turns your configuration into a privacy level \(\varepsilon\) at a slack \(\delta\). That number is a proof about an algorithm, but what ships is code. A bug in the noise, the clipping or the sampling makes the model less private but barely changes its accuracy. Accuracy is flat across a wide range of noise levels (the training workflow), so the usual tests never notice the bug.
An audit checks the code by attacking it. It plants records called canaries, trains with and without them, and counts how often a membership test guesses right. DP caps how often any test can be right. So a test that is right too often proves that the code is less private than claimed. A test that is rarely right proves nothing, since a weak attack also fails against a leaky model.

title: 52  Auditing private training
section: 52.2 Known bugs, and which audit catches them
text:
52.2 Known bugs, and which audit catches them
These bugs break the private form of stochastic gradient descent (SGD), DP-SGD.

The variance passed where the standard deviation is expected, or noise scaled for the mean but added to the sum, which adds the batch size times too little noise. A unit test in continuous integration (CI) catches both (Section 52.3).
Clipping applied after averaging, or noise from a weak seed. Nasr et al. (2023) found both in real code with per-step audits like the CI test.
The accountant told the wrong numbers, such as a record count that includes augmented copies, which makes \(\varepsilon\) look smaller than it is. Only an end-to-end audit can catch it, and only if the error is large.
Batches shuffled but accounted as Poisson sampling, which can make the true \(\varepsilon\) several times the reported one (Amplification by subsampling). No audit here exercises the sampling, so check the loader itself.

Audits catch errors only in the unsafe direction, so code that adds too much noise passes them all.

title: 52  Auditing private training
section: 52.3 A CI test for the noise and the clipping
text:
52.3 A CI test for the noise and the clipping
The cheapest strong audit tests one step of the optimizer, many times. A Dirac canary is a per-example gradient that is zero except on one coordinate, where every other record’s gradient is zero. Put it into every step of one run and leave it out of another. The reading \(x_t\) is step \(t\)’s noisy gradient sum on that coordinate, divided by the clipping norm \(C\). The canary is longer than \(C\), so a correct optimizer clips it to length \(C\) and it adds exactly 1 to the reading. The optimizer also adds noise of standard deviation \(\sigma C\), where \(\sigma\) is the noise multiplier, so each reading follows \[x_t \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2) \text{ without the canary}, \qquad x_t \sim \mathcal N(1, \sigma^2) \text{ with it}. \tag{52.1}\]
A threshold test says “canary in” whenever a reading exceeds a threshold. Its true positive rate (TPR) is how often it says so when the canary was there. Its false positive rate (FPR) is how often it says so when the canary was not.
For two normal distributions a distance \(\mu\) apart, every threshold gives \(\Phi^{-1}(\mathrm{TPR}) - \Phi^{-1}(\mathrm{FPR}) = \mu\), where \(\Phi\) is the standard normal distribution function. So measured rates bound the true separation \(\mu\), which a correct optimizer keeps at \(1/\sigma\): \[\mu \ge \Phi^{-1}(\mathrm{TPR}) - \Phi^{-1}(\mathrm{FPR}). \tag{52.2}\] The test plugs in the low end of the TPR’s Clopper–Pearson interval and the high end of the FPR’s. Each end is taken at level \(\beta/2\), so the bound holds with probability \(1 - \beta\) (Hypothesis testing). If this bound exceeds \(1/\sigma\), the code adds less noise than it claims.
The script practitioner_audit.py runs the test on Opacus’s own DPOptimizer. It writes per-example gradients into grad_sample by hand, as Opacus’s hooks would, and reads the noisy sum that optimizer.step() leaves in grad.
def canary_coordinate(sigma: float, planted_bug: str, with_canary: bool, steps: int) -> Array:
    """Run the optimizer for `steps` steps; return the canary coordinate of each noisy sum, in units of C."""
    layer = torch.nn.Linear(DIM_CI, 1, bias=False)
    optimizer = make_optimizer(layer, sigma, planted_bug)
    observations = np.empty(steps)
    for t in range(steps):
        setattr(layer.weight, "grad_sample", batch_grad_samples(with_canary))  # as Opacus's hooks would
        optimizer.step()  # clip each row to C, sum, add N(0, σ²C²)
        assert layer.weight.grad is not None
        observations[t] = layer.weight.grad[0, CANARY_COORD].item() / CLIP_CI
        optimizer.zero_grad()
    return observations
The canary’s gradient is ten times \(C\), so the test also exercises clipping. The threshold is chosen on the first half of the steps and the rates are counted on the second half. The test also checks that the canary-free readings have a standard deviation within 10% of \(\sigma\), since with no noise every reading is 0. The command uv run python code/part05-dp-ml/practitioner_audit.py tests three optimizers at \(\sigma = 0.7\) and a batch of \(B = 64\) records. They are the correct one, one with the variance bug and one with no noise. The variance bug removes noise only because \(\sigma^2 < \sigma\) when \(\sigma\) is below 1, and above 1 it would pass.
sigma=0.7  C=1.0  B=64  steps per run=2000  claim mu=1/sigma=1.429
correct: noise std 0.687 (claim 0.7)  FP 206/1000  TP 710/1000
correct: mu_lo=1.201  pass
variance for std: noise std 0.481 (claim 0.7)  FP 206/1000  TP 862/1000
variance for std: mu_lo=1.722  FAIL
no noise: noise std 0.000 (claim 0.7)  FP 0/1000  TP 1000/1000
no noise: mu_lo=5.360  FAIL
The correct optimizer’s bound on \(\mu\) is 1.201, below its claimed 1.429, so it passes. The variance bug’s bound is 1.722 and the missing noise’s is 5.360, so both fail. The test takes seconds, so run it on every commit.
Three things go wrong in practice.
First, a correct optimizer still fails with probability \(\beta\), here 5%, so an unseeded test fails one build in twenty. Fix the seed, or use a \(\beta\) of \(10^{-3}\) with more steps. Second, the script builds its own optimizer, so it tests Opacus, not your call to it. To test your code, have your setup function return the optimizer it makes, and drive that one. Third, the test never draws a batch or calls the accountant. So the same suite should assert that the loader is Opacus’s DPDataLoader and that a second library’s \(\varepsilon\) matches yours (Train a model with DP-SGD).

title: 52  Auditing private training
section: 52.4 From an attack to a lower bound
text:
52.4 From an attack to a lower bound
For a whole training run, the attack is a membership test on a planted canary. A trial is one training run, with or without the canary. Under \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP, every such test satisfies \[\mathrm{TPR} \le e^\varepsilon\,\mathrm{FPR} + \delta, \qquad 1 - \mathrm{FPR} \le e^\varepsilon\,(1 - \mathrm{TPR}) + \delta. \tag{52.3}\]
Solving these for \(\varepsilon\) turns measured rates into a lower bound on it. Write \(\overline{\mathrm{FPR}}\) for the one-sided Clopper–Pearson upper bound on the FPR at level \(\beta/2\), and \(\underline{\mathrm{TPR}}\) for the TPR’s lower bound. With probability at least \(1 - \beta\), the code is then not \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP, at the claimed \(\delta\), for any \(\varepsilon\) below \[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{lo}} = \max\Big\{\ln\frac{\underline{\mathrm{TPR}} - \delta}{\overline{\mathrm{FPR}}},\ \ln\frac{1 - \overline{\mathrm{FPR}} - \delta}{1 - \underline{\mathrm{TPR}}}\Big\}. \tag{52.4}\] The bound needs independent trials. It also needs a threshold chosen on other trials than those it counts, because a threshold tuned on them inflates it.
No library installed with this book computes the bound, so the script imports eps_lower_bound from the book’s helper module, practitioner_privacy_tests.py. Suppose an attack catches the canary in 500 of 1,000 runs that include it, and raises one false alarm in 1,000 runs without it.
for false_pos, true_pos in ((1, 500), (0, 1_000)):  # out of 1,000 runs without and with the canary
    eps_lo = eps_lower_bound(false_pos, true_pos, 1_000, DELTA)
    print(f"FP {false_pos}/1000  TP {true_pos}/1000: certified eps lower bound {eps_lo:.2f}")
FP 1/1000  TP 500/1000: certified eps lower bound 4.43
FP 0/1000  TP 1000/1000: certified eps lower bound 5.60
The raw rates alone would suggest 6.21, but confidence is expensive, and the certified bound is only 4.43. Even a perfect attack certifies only 5.60 from 1,000 trials per hypothesis. So do not expect an end-to-end audit to certify all of a large claim.

title: 52  Auditing private training
section: 52.5 A one-run audit of the trained model
text:
52.5 A one-run audit of the trained model
Thousands of runs are out of reach for a real model, so Steinke, Nasr & Jagielski (2023) get many trials from one run. Plant a number \(m\) of canaries, include each one by its own fair coin, train once and score every canary. Then fix a list length \(r\). Guess “in” for the \(r/2\) highest scores and “out” for the \(r/2\) lowest, and make no guess about the rest. Write \(W\) for the number of correct guesses.
Under \(\varepsilon\)-DP, no attack guesses one canary’s coin right with a probability above the limit \(p_\varepsilon\) given below. So the count \(W\) is no more likely to reach any value \(v\) than a binomial count with that success rate is: \[\Pr[W \ge v] \le \Pr\big[\mathrm{Bin}(r, p_\varepsilon) \ge v\big], \qquad p_\varepsilon = \frac{e^\varepsilon}{1 + e^\varepsilon}. \tag{52.5}\] An observed count that this binomial reaches with probability below \(\beta\) rules out that \(\varepsilon\), and the certified bound is the largest \(\varepsilon\) ruled out. Under \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP, the paper adds at most \(2m\delta\) to that probability. The coins must be independent and fair. Several list lengths need a Bonferroni correction, which runs each test at \(\beta\) divided by their number.
The script runs it on the released pipeline of Train a model with DP-SGD on the Adult census data. It adds only the canaries, 1,000 held-out rows with flipped labels. The coins put 537 of them in the training set, and the release’s noise multiplier gives \(\varepsilon = 3.91\) for this larger set at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). A non-private model uses the release’s baseline recipe, and a memorizing control runs non-private Adam for 60 epochs with small batches. Each canary is scored by minus its loss, and Table 52.1 gives each model’s best of six list lengths from 20 to 1,000.



Table 52.1: One-run audit of the released pipeline on Adult with 1,000 mislabeled canaries, at 95% overall confidence and \(\delta = 10^{-5}\).

Both release-recipe models certify nothing, and the reason is the recipe, not privacy. Ten epochs with large batches barely fit the flipped labels, so included canaries have the same loss as excluded ones, with or without noise. Only the memorizing control separates its canaries. Even it certifies just 0.53 for a model with no finite \(\varepsilon\), because each canary is a single trial. A perfect list of all 1,000 guesses would certify at most 5.27.
So use the one-run audit to expose a bug, when a DP model certifies more than its claim, never as evidence of privacy. Report it with its threat model, a black-box attacker who sees only the final model. Also report a control that shows the attack can detect leakage on your data.
Stronger black-box attacks, such as the likelihood ratio attack (LiRA) of Pre-release privacy risk assessment, train shadow models. These are copies of the model, trained with its exact recipe on similar data. Run them before release and keep their results with the release documents (Release and governance). LiRA’s TPR at a low FPR shows what a realistic attacker learns. But its (model, record) pairs share models, so they are not independent trials, and give no certified bound.

title: 53  Adaptive data analysis
text:
53.1 What it is
When you tune on a held-out validation set, you read the scores and try new settings, so each question depends on earlier answers. Such adaptive reuse overfits the holdout set, whose scores then overstate how the model does on new data.
Each such question is a statistical query, which averages a per-record answer between 0 and 1 over the \(n\) records you hold. A classifier’s accuracy is an example. Its population value is the same average over new data. Suppose the records are drawn independently and a number \(k\) of queries are fixed before any answer is seen. Then the largest gap between the two values is on average at most \[\sqrt{\frac{\ln(2k)}{2n}}. \tag{53.1}\] The number of queries enters through a logarithm, so it hardly matters.
Adaptive queries break this, because a later query can be built to fit the sample’s own noise. Blum & Hardt’s boosting attack does so on a leaderboard whose labels are coin flips, where nothing can beat 0.5 on new data. Yet after 1,000 submissions on as many holdout records, it reports 0.7182.
Differential privacy (DP) is the remedy, because answers that reveal little about any record cannot be used to overfit it. Let a mechanism’s answers be on average within a distance \(\alpha\) of the empirical values. Let the whole exchange be DP at a privacy level \(\varepsilon\), with a small slack \(\delta\), for samples that differ in one replaced record. The transfer theorem then bounds the expected largest error against the population by \[\alpha + e^\varepsilon - 1 + \delta, \tag{53.2}\] whatever the analyst does with the answers. For small \(\varepsilon\) the middle term is about \(\varepsilon\), so the bound is useful only well below \(\varepsilon = 1\). It protects the validity of the answers, not the people in the holdout set.

title: 53  Adaptive data analysis
text:
53.2 When you meet it
You meet adaptivity when a validation set, a test set or a leaderboard answers more than one round of questions, as in hyperparameter search. A round is a batch of questions fixed before any of its answers is seen. The bounds below grow with the number of rounds. Table 53.1 gives the choice for each situation.



Table 53.1: How to reuse a holdout set, by situation.









Situation
What to do




A final evaluation
Keep a test set and use it once


Few adaptive rounds, plenty of data
Give each round its own slice of data


Many adaptive rounds, scarce data
Answer through noise, or use Thresholdout


A search that is private in the holdout set
Nothing more, since the transfer theorem covers the winner


A public leaderboard
Show a new score only when it beats the best by a margin (Blum & Hardt’s Ladder)

title: 53  Adaptive data analysis
text:
53.3 How to use it
The simplest fix is sample splitting, which answers each of \(r\) rounds on its own \(n/r\) records. The expected largest error is then at most \(\sqrt{r\ln(2k)/(2n)}\) for \(k\) queries in all, so the data you need grow in proportion to \(r\). Take 10,000 validation records and a search over 1,000 configurations, each chosen from the earlier scores, so \(r = k = 1{,}000\). Splitting then gives a bound of 0.6165, useless for scores between 0 and 1. A bound of 0.05 would need 1,520,181 records, where fixed queries would need 1,521.
Answering every query with Gaussian noise, under the transfer theorem, needs records that grow only like \(\sqrt k\). Its constants are large, though, so splitting stays cheaper up to a few hundred adaptive queries.
Thresholdout (Dwork et al. 2015) answers from a training set while the training value agrees with the holdout value. Such answers reveal nothing about the holdout set. When they differ by more than a noisy threshold, it records a detection and returns a noisy holdout value. So its privacy cost grows with the number of detections, not of queries. But its formal \(\varepsilon\) in the full edition’s experiment is about 29, and no mainstream library ships it. So treat it as a brake, not a guarantee.

title: 53  Adaptive data analysis
text:
53.4 What goes wrong
The common failure is not an attack but a long search that picks each setting from earlier validation scores. A fixed grid scored once, as in scikit-learn’s GridSearchCV, is a single round, so Equation 53.1 bounds its winner’s overstatement. So count rounds, and report how many a validation number has been through. Practice is often milder than the worst case, but the risk is real when records are few and rounds many.

title: 54  Release and governance
text:
54.1 Why this matters
A model trained with differential privacy (DP) is not finished when training stops. Someone else, a privacy reviewer or a data protection officer, decides whether it may ship. They will ask what the guarantee covers, whether its number is right and what it means under the law. None of them can rerun your training. So the claim must travel with everything needed to check it.
This chapter packages a small network for release, trained on 30,000 people from Adult with the private form of stochastic gradient descent (SGD), called DP-SGD. It is the model of Train a model with DP-SGD, whose target privacy level \(\varepsilon\) was 4. The script practitioner_release.py runs every computed step in a few seconds. It starts from the run record that the training script writes, passed with --record PATH, or else from a built-in copy of the book’s record.

title: 54  Release and governance
text: uv run python code/part05-dp-ml/practitioner_release.py

title: 54  Release and governance
text:
54.2 Assemble the run record
The record must hold what the accountant needs. An accountant is the code that turns a run’s settings into \(\varepsilon\) (Report and review an ε claim). It reads four of them, the noise multiplier \(\sigma\), the sampling rate \(q\), the number of steps and the slack \(\delta\). It also takes four things for granted, so the record states those too.
They are the privacy unit, here one person, and the neighbouring relation, adding or removing a unit or replacing one. The others are the sampler, how the code drew each batch, and that no other use of the private data went uncounted. The training script reads the sampler from the loader Opacus returned rather than typing it, and records the seed and whether Opacus’s secure_mode was on.
The record also gives \(n\), the number of units, and the library versions. It says how the hyperparameters were chosen and whether any preprocessing saw private data. In the excerpt, data is the training script’s record and RELEASE_CONTEXT holds the release owner’s additions.
merged = RELEASE_CONTEXT | data  # the training record, plus what the release owner adds
rec = load_record(merged)
for key, value in asdict(rec).items():
    print(f"{key}: {value}")
problems = record_problems(merged)  # missing fields, sampler not Poisson, delta above 1/n^1.1, tuning
limitations = record_limitations(merged)  # stated, so not a problem, but the statement must disclose them
print(f"record problems: {len(problems)}")
for problem in problems:
    print(f"  - {problem}")
print(f"record limitations: {len(limitations)}")
for limitation in limitations:
    print(f"  - {limitation}")
unit: person (one row of Adult)
neighbours: add/remove
n: 30000
delta: 1e-05
sigma: 0.972900390625
sample_rate: 0.03333333333333333
sampler: poisson
secure_mode: False
seed: 0
steps: 300
...
record problems: 0
record limitations: 1
  - secure_mode=False: Opacus drew the noise from a seeded, non-cryptographic generator so the numbers reproduce; floating-point attacks on the noise are not excluded. Retrain with secure_mode=True to ship
The record’s \(\delta\) follows the book’s default of \(\delta \le 1/n^{1.1}\) rounded down to a power of ten, \(10^{-5}\) for Adult (Choosing ε). Its three values of \(\varepsilon\) come from the training script’s cross-check. Opacus’s privacy loss random variable (PRV) accountant gave the first. The privacy loss distribution (PLD) and looser Rényi differential privacy (RDP) accountants of Google’s dp_accounting gave the others.
The tuning entry matters most to a reviewer. Every run that helps choose a hyperparameter looks at the data, and the final run’s \(\varepsilon\) leaves those runs out. Here non-private runs chose the learning rate on 2,000 held-out Adult rows that play the part of public data. And \(\varepsilon = 4\) was fixed before any private run. Those 2,000 people come from the same survey and get no guarantee, so the statement names them.
With that stated, the run’s \(\varepsilon\) is also the \(\varepsilon\) of the whole procedure. If you tune on private data, report both, as in Hyperparameter tuning.
A record problem stops the release, such as a missing field, a sampler that is not Poisson, a \(\delta\) above \(1/n^{1.1}\) or unreported tuning. The one limitation here is secure_mode, left off so that the book’s numbers repeat. The statement discloses it, and a model you ship is retrained with it on.

title: 54  Release and governance
text:
54.3 Recompute the guarantee
Next, recompute \(\varepsilon\) from \(\sigma\), \(q\) and the number of steps alone, with a different library from the one that trained. A recomputation inside the training code would reuse any wrong number. The default is the PLD accountant of dp_accounting, which rounds the privacy loss up so that its \(\varepsilon\) is never too small. Read it at the record’s \(\delta\) and at one a hundred times smaller. Then read the trade-off curve, the largest true positive rate (TPR) that any membership test can reach at each false positive rate (FPR) (Choosing ε).
pld = privacy_loss_distribution.from_gaussian_mechanism(sigma, sampling_prob=sample_rate).self_compose(steps)
eps_pld = pld.get_epsilon_for_delta(delta)
eps_pld_small = pld.get_epsilon_for_delta(delta / 100)
eps_rdp = rdp_epsilon(sigma, sample_rate, steps, delta)
eps_rdp_small = rdp_epsilon(sigma, sample_rate, steps, delta / 100)
tpr = {fpr: tpr_bound(pld, fpr) for fpr in FPRS}  # largest TPR of any membership test
eps PLD at delta=1e-05: 3.981
eps RDP at delta=1e-05: 4.503
eps PLD at delta=1e-07: 5.191
eps RDP at delta=1e-07: 5.736
TPR bound at FPR 1e-03: 0.0123 (PLD curve)  0.0536 (pair eps, delta only)
TPR bound at FPR 1e-02: 0.0652 (PLD curve)  0.5355 (pair eps, delta only)
record's PRV eps: reported 3.99, recomputed 3.98: consistent
The recomputed PLD value, 3.981, agrees with the training run’s PRV value, and RDP’s 4.503 is higher because RDP is looser. Report the tight value with its accountant’s name, and never set one accountant’s \(\varepsilon\) against a budget computed by another. The curve gives a number a non-specialist can use. At an FPR of \(10^{-3}\), no membership test can reach a TPR above 0.0123, while the pair \((3.98, 10^{-5})\) on its own would allow 0.0536.
The script flags a reported \(\varepsilon\) more than 0.05 below the recomputation, a claim that is too good. The subtler failure is a recomputation that agrees on wrong inputs. For example, the code shuffles the data into fixed batches, but the accountant assumes Poisson sampling (Amplification by subsampling). No number shows that, so the record’s sampler, read from the loader, is what catches it.

An accountant proves a theorem about an algorithm, not about the code that runs it. So the release also needs evidence about the code and the model. title: 54  Release and governance
text:
54.5 Write the statement
The statement goes in the model card’s privacy section. The script’s format_statement builds it from the record, so no number is typed by hand. The block below omits lines that repeat the record.
Guarantee: (3.98, 1e-05)-DP per person (one row of Adult), add/remove neighbours,
  for the whole training run on Adult (UCI 2), 30,000 training rows (n = 30,000).
  Also (5.19, 1e-07)-DP. Any membership test has TPR at most 0.0123 at FPR 1e-3.
Mechanism: DP-SGD, poisson sampling q = 0.0333, noise multiplier 0.9729,
  clipping norm 1, 300 steps (10 epochs).
Accounting: prv, Opacus 1.6.0; recomputed with dp_accounting PLD (RDP gives 4.50).
...
Noise generator: Opacus secure_mode=False, seed 0.
...
Not covered: data outside the training set, API outputs that use other private data, other releases.
Below the statement, add the evidence of Table 54.1, each item with the attacker it models. The last line deserves the most care. The guarantee covers the weights and anything computed from them alone, because post-processing cannot weaken DP. An example is the logits that the deployed application programming interface (API) returns. An output that also uses other private data, such as a retrieval index, is a new release. So is a second model trained on the same people.

title: 54  Release and governance
text:
54.6 Map the claim to regulation
This section is not legal advice, since every answer depends on facts beyond the model.
In the European Union, Recital 26 of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) exempts anonymous information. It asks about the means of identification “reasonably likely to be used”. Pseudonymised data, which only information kept separately links to a person, remain personal data under Article 4(5).
For AI models, Opinion 28/2024 of the European Data Protection Board (EDPB) sets a test. A model is anonymous only if the likelihood of extracting personal data about its training set is insignificant. Each claim is assessed case by case. The opinion names DP and attack tests, such as membership inference, as measures to weigh. It warns that a test shows resistance only to the attacks tested. The trade-off curve speaks to extraction as well as membership, because it caps reconstruction too (Choosing ε).



Table 54.2: What DP evidence answers, and leaves open, for the legal questions a release meets.

What DP does not answer

Training still processes personal data, so the GDPR applies to it, lawful basis included. Article 35 requires a data protection impact assessment (DPIA) before processing likely to result in a high risk. The DPIA is the natural home for the statement. In the United States, the safe harbor route of the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) removes listed identifiers (§164.514(b)(2)), which DP does not do. Its expert determination route can cite DP evidence but not be replaced by it. California’s law, as amended by the California Privacy Rights Act, adds duties against re-identification for the business.
None of these texts says that DP makes a model anonymous by itself. A DPIA entry built from this chapter’s evidence can read as follows, with the bracketed parts filled in by the controller and counsel.

The model was trained on personal data under [lawful basis, Art. 6]. Training used DP-SGD with a guarantee of \((3.98, 10^{-5})\)-DP per person, add/remove neighbours, for the whole training run. No membership test against the released weights can exceed a TPR of 0.0123 at an FPR of \(10^{-3}\), and the same curve caps reconstruction. The code passed a CI test of its noise and clipping, and a one-run audit of the released pipeline found nothing, while a memorizing control certified 0.53. [A shadow-model attack was / was not run.] These tests show resistance only to the attacks run. DP does not remove identifiers and is not pseudonymisation. Whether the bound makes the model anonymous is for [counsel], and we make no claim of automatic anonymity. Not covered: the 2,000 stand-in rows, the test rows, outputs that use other private data, and later model versions.

title: 54  Release and governance
text:
54.7 Review someone else’s claim
Run the same steps in reverse when someone else hands you a model. Ask for the record of Section 54.2, and refuse a claim that cannot be recomputed. Recompute \(\varepsilon\) from the claim’s own parameters, and check its \(\delta\) against the number of units. Report and review an ε claim gives the checks on the accountant and the sampler.
The script reviews a claim made up for this book, with every flaw a review should catch. It claims \(\varepsilon = 1\) at \(\delta = 10^{-3}\) for a model trained on 50,000 records, over 5,000 steps with noise multiplier 0.8. Its batches of 256 were shuffled and of fixed size but are accounted as Poisson sampling. And the claim states no unit, no clipping norm and no tuning.
def review(claim: dict[str, Any]) -> list[str]:
    """Recompute a claim from its own parameters and list what does not hold up."""
    findings = record_problems(claim)  # includes a sampler that is missing or not Poisson
    sigma, q, steps, delta = claim["sigma"], claim["sample_rate"], claim["steps"], claim["delta"]
    pld = privacy_loss_distribution.from_gaussian_mechanism(sigma, sampling_prob=q).self_compose(steps)
    recomputed = {"PLD": pld.get_epsilon_for_delta(delta)}
    if "rdp" in str(claim.get("accountant")).lower():  # also the accountant the claim names
        recomputed["RDP, the accountant named,"] = rdp_epsilon(sigma, q, steps, delta)
    for name, eps in recomputed.items():
        if eps > claim["epsilon"] + 0.05:
            findings.append(f"eps={claim['epsilon']} does not follow: {name} gives {eps:.2f} at its delta")
    delta_ok = delta_for(claim["n"])
    findings.append(f"at delta={delta_ok:.0e} (1/n^1.1) PLD gives eps={pld.get_epsilon_for_delta(delta_ok):.2f}")
    return findings
claim: Our model is trained with differential privacy, epsilon = 1.
findings: 10
  - missing field: unit
  - missing field: neighbours
  - missing field: max_grad_norm
  - missing field: secure_mode
  - sampler 'shuffled fixed-size batches' is not Poisson subsampling: Poisson-subsampled accounting does not apply
  - delta=1e-03 is above 1/n^1.1 (use 1e-06)
  - tuning not reported: the cost of choosing hyperparameters is unknown
  - eps=1.0 does not follow: PLD gives 2.17 at its delta
  - eps=1.0 does not follow: RDP, the accountant named, gives 2.55 at its delta
  - at delta=1e-06 (1/n^1.1) PLD gives eps=3.75
By the vendor’s own parameters the claimed 1 is 2.17, and the RDP accountant it names gives 2.55. At a \(\delta\) the book accepts it is 3.75. Even that is too low, because shuffled fixed-size batches get no amplification by Poisson subsampling. The true \(\varepsilon\) can be far above all these numbers.
The script cannot see a wrong unit, since it takes \(n\) as given. If the records are messages and a customer sends many, screen the per-customer \(\varepsilon\) with User-level differential privacy yourself. Send the findings back with a request for a corrected record.

title: 54  Release and governance
text:
54.8 After release
The guarantee is fixed at release, but every retraining on the same people is a new release that composes with the old ones. For identical runs, compose the PLD of one run with itself once per version, pld.self_compose(steps * versions). State the budget per model version and in total over a fixed period. If the total over a schedule is too large, calibrate each version to a share of it.
Deletion requests need their own answer, because DP deletes nothing. It says the model is about as likely as one trained without the person, but their row is still in the data. So honour a request by removing the row, from the stand-in and test rows too, and retraining on a fixed schedule. Whether that is fast enough for the GDPR’s Article 17 is a question for counsel.
Give each model version its own record and statement, and name in advance the incidents that reopen a release. A failing CI test, an audit bound above the claim, or a bug in the sampler or the accountant needs a corrected statement or a retrained model.

Unit, \(n\), \(\delta\), neighbours, sampler read from the loader, \(\sigma\), \(q\), steps, clipping norm, accountant and version, secure_mode, seed, tuning, preprocessing, public data
record problems: 0; secure_mode on for the shipped model


\(\delta\)
\(\delta \le 1/n^{1.1}\), rounded down to a power of ten
\(n\) counts units, not rows


Tuning
Choices on public data, or every private run counted
Run and procedure \(\varepsilon\) both reported


Recomputed \(\varepsilon\)
PLD in dp_accounting, at \(\delta\) and \(\delta/100\), and TPR from the curve
Reported value not below the recomputation


Audits
CI test; one-run audit of the released pipeline with a memorizing control; shadow-model attack
CI passes on the released commit; no bound above the claim; the control detects leakage; any attack not run is named


Groups
Per-group accuracy with exact intervals
Test set not private, or its release accounted


Statement
Generated from the record
Every number recomputable; “not covered” filled in


Regulation
DPIA entry mapping the evidence to each legal question
Reviewed by counsel; no claim of automatic anonymity


Third-party claim
Recompute from its own parameters
Unit, sampler, \(\delta\) and tuning all stated


After release
Budget per period; retraining and deletion schedule; incident triggers
Versions composed; each has its own record

title: 54  Release and governance
text:
54.10 References

Near, Darais, Lefkovitz & Howarth, Guidelines for Evaluating Differential Privacy Guarantees (NIST SP 800-226, 2025): what to ask of any DP claim.
European Data Protection Board, Opinion 28/2024 on certain data protection aspects related to the processing of personal data in the context of AI models (December 2024): when a model can count as anonymous.
Ponomareva et al., “How to DP-fy ML: A Practical Guide to Machine Learning with Differential Privacy” (JAIR 2023): its reporting section lists what a privacy statement contains.

Derivations. This workflow has no counterpart in the full edition.
